title: In progress, 2026-10-14
text:
Notes on the chord-change lessons built in this session. Nothing here is committed unless git log says so.


Twelve lessons now share one look: numbered steps, each a chord chart (TuneChart) with a staff under it and the Backing Track band, then usually a builder and an ear test.








Lesson
File
Notes




Blues changes
lessons/blues-changes.qmd
Existing. Now has a grand staff under every chart. Hand-written script.


C, Am, F, G
lessons/pop-changes.qmd
Hand-written script, same shape as the blues one.


Four-chord loops
lessons/four-chord-loops.qmd
Hand-written script. Eight loops, builder, ear test.


Cadences
lessons/cadences.qmd
Engine. Plagal taught as the “fake” cadence (the argument is in section 4).


Guide tones
lessons/guide-tones.qmd
Engine. Staff shows a single line; the band’s piano plays it.


Minor changes
lessons/minor-changes.qmd
Engine. Written in A minor (tonic 9).


Borrowed chords
lessons/borrowed-chords.qmd
Engine.


Turnarounds
lessons/turnarounds.qmd
Engine.


Reharmonizing
lessons/reharmonize.qmd
Engine. Ode to Joy with four sets of chords, melody played by the band.


Pop changes for guitar / piano / bass
lessons/pop-changes-guitar.qmd, -piano, -bass
Engine, with fretboard, keyboard or bass diagrams.



The nine newest .qmd files were generated by a script (not kept in the repo) that pasted the same style block, bottom strip and script tags into each, then a ChordLesson.init({...}) config. To change the shared page furniture, edit each .qmd or write the generator again. To change behaviour, edit the engine.




apps/shared/lessons/chord-staff.js (LessonChordStaff): the staff under a chart. Modes: chords (grand staff, block chords and bass note), third, seventh, guide (one line), bass (bass clef). Also describe(sym, transpose, flats) for the diagrams.
apps/shared/lessons/chord-lesson.js (ChordLesson): steps, builder, ear tests, key strip, diagrams (guitar, piano, bass), and a tune’s melody above the chart. Config is documented in its header.
apps/shared/lessons/tunes.js: added BluesTunes.ode (key C), and inKey now uses a tune’s own key instead of assuming F.
apps/shared/tune-chart.js: bars with a chord under a third of the bar wide are drawn smaller (tc-tight), which fixed the cramped numerals in ~/Desktop/cramped.png. Script version is ?v=31 in the lessons that load it.




tests/band/lessons/loops.cdp.js (“CHORD LESSONS OK”): every new page has the right number of staves, the key menu respells them, the sounding bar lights on chart and staff, the ear tests give a verdict and reveal the chart, the guide-tone staff has one note per chord, the guitar lesson draws four diagrams, tight bars get tc-tight. tests/band/lessons/blues.cdp.js still passes. Setup is in tests/band/README.md (render the pages into tests/band/lead/site/lessons, serve on port 8500).



All of it. I checked layout in screenshots and that the pages run without errors, but not how it sounds. In particular:

the guide-tone lines played by the band’s piano (does the melody sit well over the comping?);
the “busy” setting in the reharmonizing lesson, and whether the chords really fit Ode to Joy note for note;
the minor, borrowed and turnaround lessons in each feel (Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Motown, Medium swing, Bossa nova);
the staff lighting during playback on a phone-width screen.





Song names in four-chord-loops.qmd: Let It Be, No Woman, No Cry, Don’t Stop Believin’, Zombie, Despacito, Stand by Me, I Got Rhythm, Louie Louie, Wild Thing, Sweet Home Alabama, Hit the Road Jack were written from memory.
The cadences lesson states a position (plagal is not a cadence) and cites William Caplin’s Classical Form for it. Please check the citation against the book before it is relied on.
Guitar diagrams come from the band’s open-shape library, which ignores the note after a slash. G/B shows the G shape. The lesson says so.
“Mario cadence” in borrowed-chords.qmd (♭VI–♭VII–I) is a popular name, not a textbook one.
Prose in the nine newer lessons was written in one pass and read only by me.





No lesson links yet from the blues lessons to the new ones.
The instrument lessons stop at secondary dominants. No two-fives or builder.
The guitar and bass lesson pages are long (a diagram per chord per step); they may want a “show one chord at a time” control.
The generator script should be kept in scripts/ if the nine pages are going to be edited in bulk.
Quiz questions pick answers at random, and the second cadence question uses my own wording for how each ending “feels”. Rewrite it in your own words.





Generator kept: scripts/chord-lessons.mjs holds the shared furniture (front matter, style block, bottom strip, script tags with versions); each lesson is scripts/chord-lessons/<name>.json (title, body prose, init config). --check compares with lessons/<name>.qmd, --write [name] writes, --extract rebuilds the JSON from the .qmd files. Eight of nine reproduced the existing files byte for byte; guide-tones differed only in key order (JS puts the integer-like key "251" first), same content at runtime. To bump a script version for all nine, edit SCRIPTS and --write. If you hand-edit a .qmd, run --extract first or the next --write overwrites it.
Links from the blues lessons (one bullet or line each): changes -> cadences/turnarounds/guide tones/borrowed chords; guitar, piano, bass -> their pop-changes page; melody -> guide tones and reharmonizing; improvising -> guide tones. blues-drums.qmd untouched.
“Show one chord at a time” (chord-lesson.js?v=2, all nine pages regenerated with the new version): a button above the diagrams on guitar and bass pages (not piano, which is one card). Off by default; on, only the sounding bar’s chords are shown (the first bar’s when stopped), and it follows the band. Test added in loops.cdp.js; loops.cdp.js and blues.cdp.js pass. Not looked at on a phone.
Still not done: two-fives/builder in the instrument lessons, rewriting the quiz wording.




reading-swing.qmd, changes-now.md, the tests/abc folder and many changes to the band and tools files were in the tree when this was written and are not part of this work. _quarto.yml and lessons/index.qmd have both sets of edits in them.



Committed (in the commits up to e4f1887): the seven blues lessons (lessons/blues-*.qmd, apps/shared/lessons/blues-kit.js, diagrams.js, score.js, tunes.js, drumkit.js), the Lessons landing page, scale charts in every .bl-scale panel and .bl-notes, the play row beside each chord grid, staff margins (no first-line indent, nothing cut off, two bars a line under 600 px), drum-note tooltips and the clickable kit picture. Tests: tests/band/lessons/{blues,instruments,more,tune,layout}.cdp.js, t_drumstaff.js, t_tune.js; setup in tests/band/README.md; history in apps/shared/band/NOTES.org.
Uncommitted blues-lesson edits now in the tree (step 8 “Grabbing the crash” in blues-drums.qmd, chokeBars in blues-kit.js, tunes.js, _blues-kit.qmd versions) are another session’s, not this one’s.
Open for this thread: - Nobody has listened: the kit picture’s sounds (cross-stick uses the rim sample), the swung ▶ Play, the arp bass line. - A player should check: piano fingerings (modes take the fingering of the major scale with the same notes, so C Mixolydian’s left hand starts on 1); the violin first-position chart; the Oscar Pettiford credit on Blues in the Closet (X:1009). - Saxophone charts: not started, on purpose (the user has a plan for them). - Offered, never answered: guitar and piano steps show chords as whole notes, not the comping rhythm. - The tune’s pickup is not played at the top of each chorus; the melody is played by the band’s chord instrument. - tests/band/pat/t_tunes.js expected 10 built-in setups and there were 12 (failed before this work). - The lyrics site’s copy of the engine (bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh) was not rebuilt.

title: In progress, 2026-10-14
text:
Done

Backing Track → melody entry. tools/_backing-track.qmd: a button “Open in the melody entry tool” (#bt-mel-entry) in the Melody panel. It opens chord-entry.html#from=tune&d=… the way the lyrics site’s Band panel does, with the changes, tempo, style, title and the melody so far (gridMelody). A pickup in front of bar 1 is not sent; the panel says so.
Pickups between sections (tools/_chord-entry.qmd):

On loading a .cho, the words before a section’s first chord (“Gone a[Eb]way”) become its pickup (lyr[k].lead), if the last bar of the section before has notes to spare (pickOf, choSections records pick). Before this, the pickup count was lost on every reload.
If there are no notes for those words, the load note says so (“…has no notes for it: record Verse 3 with the pickup played in the count-in”).
mergeTake: a take to the end of a section keeps the next section’s pickup notes at the end of its last bar, unless the take played into them. (Re-recording the Bridge used to wipe Verse 3’s “Lat-er”.)

Syllables in the words box. The first lyric box (“The words, by syllable”) shows the words hyphenated once the dictionary has loaded (splitWords, once per section, lyr[k].split). Hyphens there drive the drafts. The Split into syllables button (#ce-words-split) splits typed or pasted words that have no hyphen yet. Words split only by their vowels are listed in the warning line.
Count-off menu (#ce-countin beside Hear it in the Check panel: 1, 2 or 4 bars, default 1, kept in localStorage ceCountIn). It sets the band player’s countIn (player clamp raised from 2 to 4) for Hear it and band takes, and the page’s own click for click takes (sess.count = bars x one bar’s beats, accent on every bar of the count-off). The take engine is unchanged: only the last count-off bar is read (pickup notes), earlier ones are dropped as before. 4 bars are “1 2 3 4” bars; only a count-off of 2 keeps the half-speed first bar. chord-entry.js tag is now ?v=10 (its content did not change; the page and player.js?v=122 did). Test: tests/band/entry/countin.cdp.js (“COUNT-IN OK”).

title: In progress, 2026-10-14
section: One shared ABC parser, toward a notation system with MIDI and audio entry (a separate session)
text:
One shared ABC parser, toward a notation system with MIDI and audio entry (a separate session)
The goal, agreed in chat: one notation system built from the tune, tonal and rhythm assessments, Song Builder and Chord/Melody Entry. You set the parameters first (key, meter, allowed rhythm cells, strictness), then enter by MIDI, tapping or microphone, and a decoder ranks what you might have meant (an extended MelodyDwim). Microphone input is built last, but the design allows for it from the start: every event carries a confidence, and noisy MIDI stands in for the microphone in tests.
Done, not committed (the tests/abc entry under “Other people’s changes” above is this): - apps/shared/abc-core.js (AbcCore): tokenizer, header fields, key signatures, note→MIDI, chord symbols. - apps/assessment/abc-pitch.js, apps/rhythm-assessment/abc-rhythm.js, apps/tune-assessment/abc-tune.js are now thin wrappers over it, with exactly the old output. Each throws a clear error if abc-core.js was not loaded first. - <script src="/apps/shared/abc-core.js?v=1"> before the parser in 13 .qmd pages (seven practice pages, tools/_backing-track, tools/_chord-entry, lessons/_blues-kit, blues-changes, four-chord-loops, pop-changes). tests/band/tune/t_score.js and t_oracle.js load it too. One pointer line was added to CLAUDE.md. - Tests: node tests/abc/compare.js → “ABC SAME” (frozen old parsers in tests/abc/baseline/ against the new ones, on every tune, pattern, rhythm and benchmark plus edge cases; also checks every page loads the core first). The test was checked by planting five errors in the core; it catches all of them. SITE=<rendered pages> node tests/abc/pages.cdp.js → “PAGES SAME” (13 pages in headless Chrome, old parsers against new). quarto preview copied everything into _site, and every _site page that loads a parser has the core tag. - Later: re-rendered tools/backing-track.qmd into tests/band/lead/site (its copy predated the core tag); entry/melody-bt, side, entry pass again. Every lesson page in the test site loads the core.
Found, deliberately not fixed (it changes grades): - The tonal assessment grades 53 of the 148 live patterns (pattern-set.js) on the wrong pitches. abc-pitch.js knows only C major and C minor. Any key starting with a letter then “m” (Dm, also Gmix) is read as C minor, and other keys as C major. The staff shows the right key, but grading expects e.g. F where the staff shows F♯ in D. apps/assessment/app.js also assumes C for the key menu names and the resting-tone target (60 + transpose). Fix: grade with AbcCore.keyAccidentals, then rework those two places. Students’ past results were scored the old way.
Next, in order: 1. (Recommended first) fix the tonal key bug above. 2. The event model: { t_on, t_off, pitch candidates, confidence, source }, built on AbcCore.tokens. Keep written events (one per notehead, which the rhythm assessment’s notehead colouring needs) separate from sounding notes (ties merged). 3. The profile schema (key/mode, allowed degrees, meter, subdivision, swing, triplets, RhythmCells vocabulary, strictness). 4. A decoder on MIDI that wraps Chord Entry’s quantizer, plus a noisy-MIDI test helper (jitter, cents drift, merged and split notes). 5. MelodyDwim ranking by profile. 6. Presets (Assess, Dictate, Build, Chart). 7. Tap entry. 8. Microphone note segmenter (YIN + onsets).
Watch: swing should come from the one shared setting the swing worktree (changes-now.md) is building, not a new copy.
Update (agent, 2026-10-14 afternoon) — Next steps 1 and 2 done, not committed. - Tonal key bug fixed. apps/assessment/abc-pitch.js grades with AbcCore.keyAccidentals (new exports keySignature, tonicPc). apps/assessment/app.js: key menu names come from the pattern’s own key (“D”, “E dor”, “A mix”, …; keyNameAt); the resting-tone target, the tonality cadence and the “no response” reference use writtenTonicMidi + transpose (tonic of the written key, C4..B4, not 60); the sung-response staff is written in the pattern’s key and spelled against its signature (midiToAbcToken(midi, ksig); with no signature it spells exactly as before); currentMinor now means “minor third” (minor, dorian, …), so Gmix is no longer treated as minor and Ddor is. - tests/abc/compare.js still verifies everything else identical and now reports the intended difference: 53 of 148 pattern-set patterns grade on different pitches, and for them the test checks the change is only the key-signature shift per note. title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
For a Claude session asked to add a style (“add a samba”, “a second-line groove”, “a gospel 6/8”). Read this first, then the header comments of the files it names. NOTES.org beside this file is the history of the band and its open questions.


A style is a row in styles in catalog.js: a name, a group (the genre heading in the Style menu), and defaults that belong together.
{ id:"bossa", label:"Bossa nova", group:"Latin", genres:"Bossa nova, slow samba",
  feel:"straight", bass:"bossa", rhythm:"bossa", drums:"bossa", voicing:JAZZV,
  desc:"Root-and-fifth bass with pickups, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave." }

bass, rhythm, drums are ids of entries in the bass, comp and drums lists of the same file. rhythm may be several joined by + (a blend).
voicing is { piano, guitar }: a voicing style id for each (PLAINV, STRUMV, JAZZV are ready-made).
Optional: sound ({ bass:"upright"|"electric", cymbal:"ride"|"hat"|"bell", piano, guitar, lead, kit }), where piano and guitar are sound ids from sounds.js (BandSounds.sounds("guitar") lists them: jazz, steel, nylon, clean and distorted electric), push (chords anticipate), full (the piano’s triads keep all three notes), bass and drums may each name several patterns joined by + (a blend: one of them per bar, planned four bars at a time by BandHarmony.blendOpts; shares in opts.bassMix / opts.grooveMix), calm (strike and hold the chords around cadences and in bars with more chords than usual: BandHarmony.calmAt; a chart marks phrase ends with "^phrase" and single bars with "^plain"), halfRhythm (comping rhythm ids, a+b: what the comping plays in bars of half time instead of its own rhythm), time ({ feel:"half", parts }), ext:true (unmarked extensions on offer). A style with no sound gets upright bass, ride, piano, jazz guitar.

A style made only of parts that already exist is one line in styles plus the fit lists (step 3). Most requests need at least one new part. Decide that first: listen in your head to what the bass, the chord instrument and the drums each play in that music, and check each against the existing entries before writing a new one.




Write the new parts, each in its own engine file. Copy the nearest existing pattern and read the comment block above the table you are adding to.

Bass line: LINES in bass.js (a fixed figure over the chord’s root, fifth, octave).
Comping rhythm: GRID in comp.js for a set pattern, FIG for a one-bar swing figure.
Drum groove: GROOVES in drums.js (bars for 4/4, threeBars for 3/4, triplet for 12/8 feels).
Congas: PATTERNS in congas.js (see Congas below).
Positions are beats from 0; x.5 is the off-beat eighth (swung by the player unless the event says straight:true). Velocities are 0..1 and the player scales them by the band’s intensity.
Use ctx.phrase.bar (0..3) to shape four-bar phrases and ctx.intensity for how hard the band is playing. phraseDyn, leanDyn and spread in comp.js are the shared dynamic shaping: use them rather than fixed velocities.
Every pattern must cope with 3/4 and with a bar holding two chords. The tests check both.

Describe each new part in catalog.js: an entry in bass, comp or drums with id, label, feel (swing, straight or any), group, tags and a desc that says what is played on which beats, in a musician’s words. The desc is shown on the page and on the Accompaniment Styles page.
Say where each part fits: add its id to FITS.bass, FITS.comp or FITS.drums with the style ids it belongs in (your new one, and any existing style it also suits). Locked, a menu lists only what fits the chosen style, so a part missing from FITS cannot be chosen. Add the new style id to the voicing lists it should offer (JAZZ, POP, PLAIN, or a VOICE row).
Add the style row to styles, in its group. The id is permanent: saved setups, links and song files name it. Never rename one.
Tests (plain node, run from the test’s own directory):

tests/band/pat/t_patterns.js runs every style and option against every meter. It has a want table of where chords must land for set patterns; add your rhythm there.
tests/band/pat/t_pop.js lists the style ids of some groups in order; update the list if you added to one.
tests/band/styles/t_sections.js, tests/band/fills/t_fills.js, tests/band/meter/t_change.js must still pass.

Publish it to the pages. In tools/_backing-track.qmd and tools/_accomp-styles.qmd, raise the ?v= number on every script you changed (browsers cache them). Then quarto render tools/backing-track.qmd and check that .gitignore did not change (Quarto appends to it). The lyrics site copies the engine: bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh.
Say what was not verified. Nothing here can be listened to from a terminal. Report the pattern in beats, what the tests cover, and that it needs ears. Do not commit unless asked.




The conga player (congas.js) is a part of its own beside bass, comping and drums: it has its own fader, staff and MIDI track, and any style may have it. Adding a pattern:

PATTERNS in congas.js: id: { bars: [...], three: [...], triplet: [...] }. bars is one or two 4/4 bars (a two-bar pattern follows the bar number); three is one bar of 3/4 and triplet one bar of 12/8, both optional. A bar is a list of rows [pos, drum, stroke, hand, vel]: drum is "c" (conga, the higher drum) or "t" (tumba); stroke is H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muffled, B bass; hand is "L" or "R". Positions are beats; 12/8 positions are thirds of a beat (x.333). A pattern with no bar for the meter plays the steady one, so it can stay short.
congas in catalog.js: { id, label, feel, group, tags, desc }; the desc says which stroke falls on which beat, with which hand.
FITS.congas: the style ids it belongs in (steady and none fit every style).
A style that should have them says congas:"id" on its row in styles. Left out, the style has none.
tests/band/congas/t_congas.js checks every pattern in every meter, and that the other players play the same notes with or without them.

Sounds: the congas are one sample set (congas in sounds.js) built from the soundfont’s three conga notes; a new stroke is a new piece name there, a trim, and its place in BandNotation.congaName and the GM table in midi.js.




The Style menu of the Backing Track page; ?style=id in its address.
A tune’s ABC: %%style bossa nova above the first P: line (the whole tune).
One section: %%style bossa nova on the line under its P: line, or "^style bossa nova" in a bar (from that bar to the next section; "^style none" ends it early). The form bar carries style, and BandCatalog.sectionOpts turns it into the options for those bars. Single parts can follow the name: %%style Swing; voicing drop2; rhythm charleston; bass two; drums funk; feel straight. The comping moves to the instrument the style is built around (sound.lead), if it has one. The page’s blend sliders and walk amount do not apply inside such a section. On the Backing Track page the Band menus change to a section’s settings as it starts, and a change made there stays with that section (opts.sectionOverrides, which the player puts before the section’s style).
A crash grabbed with the hand: "^choke" in a bar (the crash on its beat 1, stopped before beat 2), beside "^fill" and "^stop".
Two built-in setups in presets.js (“Style demo: …”) tour the jazz and the pop, rock and country styles a section at a time. Add a new style to the one it belongs in.
A lyrics-site song file (~/Projects/carols/site/extra/*.cho): {style: carol} above the first heading for the song, or under a heading for that section. See the top of tools/chordpro.py there.
A name matches an id, a menu label, or part of a label, ignoring case.





Plain JS globals, no build step, no dependencies. Match the comment density and voice of the file.
A new option is opt-in: an existing style must sound exactly as it did, and an option left unset must not draw from the random number generator (the tests compare runs).
Sample sets are named only in sounds.js. A new sound is one entry there (family, label, zones, and an optional amp chain); the Comping menu, the player and styleOpts pick it up from that entry. Add its General MIDI program to PROGRAM in midi.js, and its samples to tests/band/meter/fetch-samples.js.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
A style is a row in styles in catalog.js: a name, a group (the genre heading in the Style menu), and defaults that belong together.
{ id:"bossa", label:"Bossa nova", group:"Latin", genres:"Bossa nova, slow samba",
  feel:"straight", bass:"bossa", rhythm:"bossa", drums:"bossa", voicing:JAZZV,
  desc:"Root-and-fifth bass with pickups, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave." }

bass, rhythm, drums are ids of entries in the bass, comp and drums lists of the same file. rhythm may be several joined by + (a blend).
voicing is { piano, guitar }: a voicing style id for each (PLAINV, STRUMV, JAZZV are ready-made).
Optional: sound ({ bass:"upright"|"electric", cymbal:"ride"|"hat"|"bell", piano, guitar, lead, kit }), where piano and guitar are sound ids from sounds.js (BandSounds.sounds("guitar") lists them: jazz, steel, nylon, clean and distorted electric), push (chords anticipate), full (the piano’s triads keep all three notes), bass and drums may each name several patterns joined by + (a blend: one of them per bar, planned four bars at a time by BandHarmony.blendOpts; shares in opts.bassMix / opts.grooveMix), calm (strike and hold the chords around cadences and in bars with more chords than usual: BandHarmony.calmAt; a chart marks phrase ends with "^phrase" and single bars with "^plain"), halfRhythm (comping rhythm ids, a+b: what the comping plays in bars of half time instead of its own rhythm), time ({ feel:"half", parts }), ext:true (unmarked extensions on offer). A style with no sound gets upright bass, ride, piano, jazz guitar.

A style made only of parts that already exist is one line in styles plus the fit lists (step 3). Most requests need at least one new part. Decide that first: listen in your head to what the bass, the chord instrument and the drums each play in that music, and check each against the existing entries before writing a new one.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
Write the new parts, each in its own engine file. Copy the nearest existing pattern and read the comment block above the table you are adding to.

Bass line: LINES in bass.js (a fixed figure over the chord’s root, fifth, octave).
Comping rhythm: GRID in comp.js for a set pattern, FIG for a one-bar swing figure.
Drum groove: GROOVES in drums.js (bars for 4/4, threeBars for 3/4, triplet for 12/8 feels).
Congas: PATTERNS in congas.js (see Congas below).
Positions are beats from 0; x.5 is the off-beat eighth (swung by the player unless the event says straight:true). Velocities are 0..1 and the player scales them by the band’s intensity.
Use ctx.phrase.bar (0..3) to shape four-bar phrases and ctx.intensity for how hard the band is playing. phraseDyn, leanDyn and spread in comp.js are the shared dynamic shaping: use them rather than fixed velocities.
Every pattern must cope with 3/4 and with a bar holding two chords. The tests check both.

Describe each new part in catalog.js: an entry in bass, comp or drums with id, label, feel (swing, straight or any), group, tags and a desc that says what is played on which beats, in a musician’s words. The desc is shown on the page and on the Accompaniment Styles page.
Say where each part fits: add its id to FITS.bass, FITS.comp or FITS.drums with the style ids it belongs in (your new one, and any existing style it also suits). Locked, a menu lists only what fits the chosen style, so a part missing from FITS cannot be chosen. Add the new style id to the voicing lists it should offer (JAZZ, POP, PLAIN, or a VOICE row).
Add the style row to styles, in its group. The id is permanent: saved setups, links and song files name it. Never rename one.
Tests (plain node, run from the test’s own directory):

tests/band/pat/t_patterns.js runs every style and option against every meter. It has a want table of where chords must land for set patterns; add your rhythm there.
tests/band/pat/t_pop.js lists the style ids of some groups in order; update the list if you added to one.
tests/band/styles/t_sections.js, tests/band/fills/t_fills.js, tests/band/meter/t_change.js must still pass.

Publish it to the pages. In tools/_backing-track.qmd and tools/_accomp-styles.qmd, raise the ?v= number on every script you changed (browsers cache them). Then quarto render tools/backing-track.qmd and check that .gitignore did not change (Quarto appends to it). The lyrics site copies the engine: bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh.
Say what was not verified. Nothing here can be listened to from a terminal. Report the pattern in beats, what the tests cover, and that it needs ears. Do not commit unless asked.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
The conga player (congas.js) is a part of its own beside bass, comping and drums: it has its own fader, staff and MIDI track, and any style may have it. Adding a pattern:

PATTERNS in congas.js: id: { bars: [...], three: [...], triplet: [...] }. bars is one or two 4/4 bars (a two-bar pattern follows the bar number); three is one bar of 3/4 and triplet one bar of 12/8, both optional. A bar is a list of rows [pos, drum, stroke, hand, vel]: drum is "c" (conga, the higher drum) or "t" (tumba); stroke is H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muffled, B bass; hand is "L" or "R". Positions are beats; 12/8 positions are thirds of a beat (x.333). A pattern with no bar for the meter plays the steady one, so it can stay short.
congas in catalog.js: { id, label, feel, group, tags, desc }; the desc says which stroke falls on which beat, with which hand.
FITS.congas: the style ids it belongs in (steady and none fit every style).
A style that should have them says congas:"id" on its row in styles. Left out, the style has none.
tests/band/congas/t_congas.js checks every pattern in every meter, and that the other players play the same notes with or without them.

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
This lesson is for a bass player. The bass is the instrument that plays the lowest note of every chord, so on the changes of C, Am, F, G it is the part that decides which passing chords are heard. Each step has the line in bass clef, a fretboard for it and the chart.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
C, Am, F, G. One note for each chord, the root. The bass-clef staff shows the line and the fretboard shows where to play it, on a four-string bass in the lowest position that has the note.

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
2. Extensions
Cadd9, Am7, Fadd9, Gsus2. The roots are the same. The extensions are for the chord instruments, so the bass line does not change.

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
3. The walking line
C, G/B | Am, C/G | F, F♯dim | G. Now the bass is the part that carries the passing chords: C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G. Every note is one step from the last. This is the line to learn.

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
4. Leading into the next chord
C, E7 | Am, C7 | F, D7 | G7. The bass plays the root of the dominant, which is a fifth above the note that follows. E, then A. C, then F. D, then G.

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
Where to go next

Play the walking line along with the band at three tempos.
Take the line to the key menu and play it in G, D and A.
The blues bass lesson goes further with the walk.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
A song in C major is not limited to the chords of C major. It may borrow chords from the parallel minor (C minor) or from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat 7). The borrowed chord has a note that is not in the key, and it sounds like a colour change. This lesson adds those chords one at a time to a plain I, IV, V, I.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
1. The plain version
C, F, G, C. Every chord is in the key of C major.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
2. The minor iv
C, F, Fm, C. Replace the IV with the iv. F minor has A♭, a note that is not in C major and that falls to G, the 5th of C. It is the sound of a major song turning wistful for one bar.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
3. The ♭VII
C, F, B♭, C. B♭ is the chord of the flat seventh (the 7th of the mixolydian mode). It falls a step to C. It sounds natural after F because the two roots are a whole step apart and the chords share the note F.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
4. The ♭VI and ♭VII together
C, A♭, B♭, C. Two borrowed chords, each a whole step above the last, rising to C. A♭ has A♭, C and E♭ (a minor-key chord), and B♭ has B♭, D and F. It sounds big and triumphant, and is sometimes called the “Mario cadence”.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
5. All three together
C, Fm, A♭ B♭, C. The minor iv in bar 2, then the ♭VI and ♭VII together in bar 3.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
The turnaround is a short chord pattern that sends a tune back to its beginning: I, vi, ii, V. Jazz players have been changing it for a century. This lesson starts with the plain one and adds the standard changes one at a time, and ends with the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
1. The plain turnaround
C, Am, Dm, G: I, vi, ii, V. The bass follows the circle of fifths: C, then A, D, G, and back to C.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
2. Sevenths
Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Every chord gets its 7th. The 7th of one chord is often a step from the 3rd of the next, which is what makes the guide-tone line smooth (see the lesson on guide tones).

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
3. A dominant on the vi
Cmaj7, A7, Dm7, G7. Make the vi a dominant. A7 is the V of Dm7, and its C♯ pulls up to D.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
4. Start on the iii
Em7, A7, Dm7, G7. iii, VI, ii, V: the turnaround begun a step earlier. Em7 is a good stand-in for Cmaj7 (it has E, G and B, three of its four notes), and it makes a chain of fifths that is a link longer.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
5. Tritone substitution
Cmaj7, E♭7, Dm7, D♭7. Replace each dominant with the one a tritone away. A7 becomes E♭7 and G7 becomes D♭7. The bass line now falls by half step wherever a substitute is used: E♭ to D, D♭ to C.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
6. Rhythm changes
C A7 | Dm7 G7 | Em7 A7 | Dm7 G7. The first four bars of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (in B♭ in the original, here in C). Two chords in every bar. Jazz players have written hundreds of tunes on these changes.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Classical singing fills a room without a microphone. It does that through resonance, not force: a steady breath, tall and pure vowels, and a seamless legato line that carries from the bottom of the voice to the top. Most of its training comes from the Italian bel canto (“beautiful singing”) tradition. This lesson follows that tradition’s order: breath, onset, vowels, registers, agility and the long note.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; tenors and basses read treble-clef notes an octave lower. Step up exercises climb a half step at a time, as in a teacher’s warm-up. Click a heading to fold a section away.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Posture and the appoggio breath
Stand tall but not stiff: feet hip-width apart, weight forward slightly, sternum comfortably high, shoulders down, head balanced. Breathe in low and wide, so the lower ribs, belly and back expand.
As you sing, keep the ribs open and let the belly come in slowly. Singers call this balance appoggio (“leaning”): the breath is supported rather than pushed out, so the tone stays steady.
Exercise: breathe in for 4 counts, then hiss out on “sss” for 12 counts, keeping the ribs wide. Next time, go for 16 counts, then 20.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Onset and legato
Begin each phrase with a clean, balanced onset: air and tone together, with no click and no rush of air first. Then join the notes so the sound never breaks between them. That’s legato, the basis of classical singing.
Sing this five-note scale on a single “ah”, sliding nothing and dropping nothing between notes.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: Pure vowels: i e a o u
text:
Pure vowels: i e a o u
Italian has five pure vowels: [i] as in si, [e] as in che, [a] as in la, [o] as in no, [u] as in tu. Unlike English vowels, they don’t glide into a second sound: Italian no is [nɔ], never “no-oo”. Classical singers learn to sing every language on these clean vowel shapes.
Sing them on one pitch, keeping the same space at the back of the mouth as the lips change shape.



Then sing them on a scale.



The IPA chart shows these and the other sounds singers meet in Italian, German, French and English.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Resonance and the tall vowel
A classical tone rings because the throat stays open and the soft palate is lifted. That’s the feeling at the start of a yawn, or of a pleasant surprise. Singers call the ring squillo, and the warmth that comes with it chiaroscuro (light and dark).
Exercise: sing an easy “ng” (as in sing) on a middle note, then open slowly to “ah” without moving the pitch. Keep the buzz you felt in the “ng”.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Registers and the passaggio
Every voice has a lower register (chest) and a higher one (head), with a transition zone called the passaggio. Classical training aims for one even sound across it. To do that, singers modify vowels slightly as they go up: “ah” darkens a little toward “aw”, and “ee” toward “ih”. That keeps the throat open and the tone even.
The arpeggio below climbs through the voice. Step it up a half step at a time, and as you near the top of your comfortable range, round the vowel and lighten the sound rather than push.




If the voice cracks around the passaggio, that’s normal at first. Sing the same arpeggio more quietly, on “oo”, where the voice blends most easily, then return to “ah”.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Agility: the nine-note scale
Quick runs (coloratura) need a light, flexible voice with the breath still steady. This scale of nine notes up and down is a classic warm-up. Sing it slowly and clean at first, keeping each note distinct, never “ha-ha-ha”.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: The long note: messa di voce
text:
The long note: messa di voce
Messa di voce means “placing the voice”: one long note that grows from soft to loud and back to soft, with the pitch and the vowel unchanged. It’s the most demanding exercise in breath control, and a lifelong one.



Practice: start on a comfortable middle note, and make the swell only as big as you can keep steady.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Vibrato
A trained classical voice has a natural vibrato: a regular, even pulse in pitch, about five to seven times a second. It isn’t made deliberately. It appears when the breath is steady and the throat is free. If yours wobbles slowly or flutters fast, the cause is usually in breath or tension, and is best fixed with a teacher, not by trying to control the vibrato itself.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: Words: diction in Italian, German and French
text:
Words: diction in Italian, German and French
Classical singers sing in many languages, and each has its rules:

Italian: pure vowels; double consonants held longer (nòtte, “night”); a flipped or rolled R.
German: long and short vowels clearly different; final consonants crisp; the “ich” sound [ç] and the “ach” sound [x]; ü [y] and ö [ø] with rounded lips.
French: nasal vowels ([ɑ̃] in chant, [ɔ̃] in mon); the rounded [y] of tu; a smooth line with every syllable even.

The IPA chart gives each of these sounds with examples. Singers write IPA under the words of a song to learn its pronunciation before they sing it.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Reading and solfège
Classical singers read music. Tonal do re mi introduces solfège, which names the notes by their place in the key, so a singer can hear a line before singing it. Sing this phrase on solfège.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Where to go next

Pop singing: speech-level singing, mix, belt and runs.
Jazz singing: swing, scat and the changes.
The IPA chart for diction in other languages.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Four chords, C, Am, F and G, are under more pop songs than any other progression: I, vi, IV, V. It can sound plain, and it can sound rich, depending on what the players do to it. Almost every move is one of four: add a note to each chord, walk the bass between chords, approach a chord with its own dominant, or split a bar into a two-five. This lesson adds those moves one at a time, on the same four bars. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four choruses after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. (The numerals only name the chord’s root, so a III7 in bar 1 is the dominant of Am, and a vii7 before it is its two.)

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
1. The basic changes
One bar each of I, vi, IV and V. Plain major and minor triads. The bass moves down a minor third, then down a third, then up a step, and the G at the end pulls back to the C.



Learn this version first. Every other version on the page is this one with something added, so you should be able to hear the plain one underneath.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
2. Add extensions
Extensions are notes added on top of the triad without changing what the chord is. Cadd9 adds a D. Am7 adds a G, and Fadd9 adds a G. Gsus2 takes out the B and puts in an A, so the chord has no third: it is neither major nor minor. It sounds suspended, and the ordinary G that follows it, or the C it leads to, feels like the answer.



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ. Listen to bar 4: the leading tone B, which is what pulls G to C, is not there.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
3. Add passing chords
Two bars are split in half, so that the bass can walk instead of jump.

Bar 1: C, G/B. The bass steps down C, B and arrives on A in bar 2. The G/B is a G chord with its third in the bass.
Bar 2: Am, C/G. The bass keeps stepping down, A then G, to land on F in bar 3.
Bar 3: F, F♯dim. Now the bass goes up, F, F♯, and arrives on G in bar 4. The F♯dim is built from F♯, A and C, three of the four notes of D7, so it pulls up to G.




Listen to the bass. There is no jump anywhere in the line: every note is one step from the last. A slash chord such as C/G is the C chord with G as its lowest note.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
4. Secondary dominants
A dominant seventh chord pulls to the chord a fifth below it. The home key has one, G7, which pulls to C. A secondary dominant is the dominant of some other chord of the key, played just before that chord, so that chord gets to sound like home for a moment.

E7 goes to Am. It has a G♯, which is not in the key of C.
C7 goes to F. It has a B♭, which is not in the key of C either.
D7 goes to G. It has an F♯.
G7 goes to C: the usual dominant, now with its seventh.




Each bar now has a note from outside the key, and each of them leads by half step into the next bar’s chord (G♯ to A, B♭ to A, F♯ to G). That is why the progression sounds like it is travelling.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
5. ii-V-Is
A dominant can have a chord in front of it, the ii chord, a fifth above, so that the approach itself is a progression: ii, V, then I. Here each secondary dominant gets its own two.

Bar 1 keeps C for two beats, then Bm7 E7, a two-five into Am.
Bar 2 keeps Am for two beats, then Gm7 C7, a two-five into F.
Bar 3 is Fmaj7 for two beats, then Am7 D7, a two-five into G.
Bar 4 stays on G7.




Strictly, the two-five into a minor chord uses a half-diminished ii (Bm7♭5), but plain Bm7 is the common way to write it in pop and the band plays it as written. Compare the last chord of each of the first three bars with section 4: it is the same dominant, with a two in front.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:

Choose one option for each bar and the chart rewrites itself. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. All of the options fit together, so there is no wrong combination: try a plain first bar with a busy last bar, or the reverse.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
Travis picking is a fingerpicking pattern in which the thumb plays a steady bass on every beat and the fingers play the melody or the chord notes on the strings above it, between the thumb notes. It is named for Merle Travis, from Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, and was spread by Chet Atkins and, later, by folk and country guitarists everywhere. The thumb is a bass player, and the fingers are a rhythm section that plays off it. This lesson builds it a step at a time, from the thumb alone to the band, with hammer-ons and pull-offs added at the end.
The Backing Track band plays the pattern as the comping rhythm Fingerpicking: Travis pattern. There is a lesson on that pattern in the band’s own terms, Comping rhythm: Travis pattern, and one on the simpler pattern before it, John Prine fingerpicking. This lesson is the hands.
How to read the examples. Each exercise is written on a staff and in tablature. Tablature has one line a string, with the high E on top and a number for the fret. The staff is written an octave above where a guitar sounds, as guitarists read it. Press ▶ to hear it, and ↻ Loop to repeat it. The strings are numbered 6 (low E) to 1 (high E). The right hand uses p for the thumb, and i, m and a for the index, middle and ring fingers.
Here is what you are working toward, played by the band. Switch the other players off to hear the guitar alone, and slow the tempo with the slider at the bottom of the page.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
1. The thumb alone
Start with the thumb, and only the thumb. On a chord, the thumb plays four bass notes in a bar, one on every beat: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, and the inner string again. For C the root is the 5th string, the alternate bass is the 6th string (fret 3, which is a G), and the inner string is the 4th string, fret 2 (an E). Hold the C shape and play 5, 4, 6, 4.






The alternate bass is the string on the other side of the root, so the thumb swings between a low note and a higher one. That is where the oom-pah comes from, and this pattern is the same as the band’s bass line in its folk and country styles.

Easy because: one finger plays one note on every beat, and your fretting hand holds a chord you already know.
Hard because: the thumb has to find three strings without looking, and keep going in time.
What goes wrong:

The thumb plays the wrong string, usually the next one over.
The beat is uneven because the 5-to-6 jump takes longer than 5-to-4.
The strings ring into each other. Rest the side of the right hand lightly on the bridge to damp the bass, and the notes come out shorter and cleaner.


Practice: play it with a metronome at 60, with your eyes closed, for a minute. Then do the same on G, Am and D (section 4 has the strings).

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
2. Pinches on beat 1
Now add a note on beat 1 only. Pick a treble string with a finger at the same moment as the thumb plays the root: that is a pinch. For C, use the B string (fret 1) with the middle finger. The other beats stay the same, thumb alone.




Easy because: the thumb pattern is unchanged, and only one other note arrives, always on the same beat.
Hard because: the thumb and the finger have to start the note at the same instant. If they drift apart it sounds like a clumsy strum, not a pinch.
What goes wrong: the finger plays first or late. The pinch is louder than the thumb notes that follow.

Practice: play only the pinches, with the thumb and finger leaving the strings together, then add the other three beats.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
3. Fingers between the thumb notes
Now give the fingers their place. On each beat the thumb plays its note on the beat, and a finger plays a note on the “and” after beats 2, 3 and 4. Beat 1 stays a pinch, so there is nothing on its “and”. Count it “1 2-and 3-and 4-and”. The fingers play the treble strings: the middle finger on the B string and the ring finger on the high E string work, or the index finger on the G string. Use whichever fingers you prefer, and keep them the same from bar to bar.



This is the Travis pattern. The thumb and the fingers alternate, so each one has a note, then a gap, then a note, and your hand feels like two people taking turns. Listen to the band play it in the demo above, and look at the staff to see how it matches.

Easy because: the thumb part is the same one from section 2, and the fingers play only three notes in a bar.
Hard because: the thumb and the fingers have to be independent. The thumb keeps its beat while the fingers play off it, and the thumb wants to follow the fingers.
What goes wrong:

The thumb stops or stumbles when the fingers come in.
The finger notes land on the beat instead of after it.
The treble notes are as loud as the bass notes. Play the thumb a little louder and the fingers more lightly.


Practice: count out loud, “one, two-and, three-and, four-and”. Slow it down until it is steady, then bring it up in small steps. Spend a week on this step before the next.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
section: 4. On C, G, Am and D
text:
4. On C, G, Am and D
The same pattern needs a root, an inner string and an alternate bass for each chord. The thumb always plays the root of the chord on beat 1.




C: root on string 5, inner string 4 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 6 (fret 3). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
G: root on string 6 (fret 3), inner string 4 (open), alternate bass on string 5 (fret 2). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
Am: root on string 5 (open), inner string 4 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 6 (open). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
D: root on string 4 (open), inner string 3 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 5 (open). The strings below the root, 6, stay silent. Treble: strings 2 and 1.





Easy because: the pattern is the same each time, and the four chords are open shapes you know.
Hard because: the thumb has to learn a new set of strings for each chord. D, with only four strings in use, is the one that trips people up.
What goes wrong: the thumb plays a string that is not in the chord, and the bass sounds wrong. The alternate bass on D should be the open 5th string, not the low E.

Practice: one chord for four bars, until the thumb finds the strings by feel. Then the next chord. For the chord shapes and the fretting hand see guitar chord shapes by hand.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
5. Changing chords
Now move from one chord to the next without breaking the thumb’s beat. The thumb keeps going while the fretting hand moves. The change lands on beat 1 of the next bar, on the root. The thumb notes on beats 3 and 4 are the time you have to move: let go of the old shape on beat 4 and have the new one down for beat 1.




Easy because: you can think of a bar at a time, and a bar of a chord you have already played is a bar you know.
Hard because: the picking hand cannot slow down while the fretting hand moves, and the roots of the chords move around on strings 4 to 6.
What goes wrong:

The pattern stops dead at the change, because the picking hand waits for the fretting hand.
The thumb plays the old chord’s root on the new chord.
The last beat of a bar is rushed.


Practice: play C and G, two bars each, with a metronome. Do not stop. If the change is late, drop one beat of the picking (rest the fingers) and keep the thumb going. Then play it with the band.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
section: 6. Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs
text:
6. Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs
Hammer-ons and pull-offs make the pattern sound like Chet Atkins instead of a practice exercise. The hand technique is in Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar; you should be comfortable with sections 1 to 4 of that lesson first.
Hammer onto the 3rd of the chord, on beat 1. The 3rd of a major chord is the note that makes it major, and in an open chord the string next to the root is often an open string a hammer-on away from it. On G, the thumb picks the open 5th string (A) and hammers to fret 2 (B, the 3rd). On C, it picks the open 4th string (D) and hammers to fret 2 (E, the 3rd). The hammered note takes the place of the pinch on beat 1, and then the pattern goes on.



Pull-offs in the treble, between the thumb notes. The “and” after beat 2 can be two quick notes instead of one: pick the higher note, then pull off to the lower. On C the high E string is picked at fret 3 and pulled off to the open string. On Am the B string is picked at fret 1 and pulled off to the open B string.




Easy because: the thumb never changes. The hammer-ons and pull-offs are all in the fingers, and each one fits in one place in the pattern.
Hard because: the fretting hand has to do something while it is also holding the chord, and the picking hand has to stay steady while it waits for the hammer or the pull.
What goes wrong: the decorated beat gets rushed, or the thumb loses its place. The hammer-on is too soft to hear. A pull-off is not loud enough to match the picked notes.

Practice: put one decoration in a four-bar phrase, in the same place each time, until you do not have to think about it. Then try a second one.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
7. With the band
Now play the part with the band. The chart is G, C, D, G. The band’s guitarist plays the pattern in section 3, and its bass plays the root and alternate bass with the thumb. Take the guitar off (the Chords button) and play the part yourself. Start at 70 beats a minute and speed up when it is steady.



The second button is the simpler pattern the band calls thumb, pinch-and. Use it to rehearse the thumb with fewer finger notes, and then play the Travis pattern.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
8. A neighbour: chicken pickin’
Chicken pickin’ is a cousin of Travis picking that sounds very different. It is a country guitar technique played with a flat pick and the middle and ring fingers (hybrid picking). The pick plays a bass or chord note, and the fingers snap the treble strings, pulling each one up and letting it slap against the frets. Notes are also muted by the picking hand, and the short, dry, clucking sound that results gives it the name. It began in the Telecaster-based country playing of the 1950s and 1960s, and you can hear it in the work of James Burton, Albert Lee and, more recently, Brad Paisley. This lesson does not teach it. If you can play the Travis pattern, you already have the independence of thumb and fingers that it takes.
Unlocks: the band’s other fingerpicking pattern, Prine; Hammer-ons and Pull-offs.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
This is how a pianist plays chords on a 12-bar blues, built up from one finger. You need to be able to find notes on the keyboard by name. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has a keyboard diagram, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. Above the keys there is one coloured lane for each chord, with a square over every key that chord uses, so you can compare chords by looking straight up and down. Middle C is marked in green. Click a chord’s name at the left of its lane to hear it. Under the keyboard the same notes are written on a grand staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its pianist plays exactly the notes shown, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the piano to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the squares show chord tones or note names.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of C7 is C. A blues has three chords and so three roots. Play them with the left hand, low on the keyboard, one long note per bar.



Count the form as you play: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes. Starting on the root, take every other note of the scale: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Here are all four notes of each chord in the right hand, root at the bottom. The 5th is dashed because it is the first note to leave out. Click a chord name to hear the notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
3. Guide tones over a root
Now play only the 3rd and 7th in the right hand, with the root in the left. Look down the lanes: the right hand’s two notes hardly move. Going from I7 to IV7, each note drops a half step, and they swap jobs: the 3rd becomes the ♭7th and the ♭7th becomes the 3rd. For V7 both notes sit a half step above the I chord’s.
To keep the hand still, the two notes are not always in the same order. Sometimes the 3rd is on the bottom and sometimes the 7th. Switch the labels to chord tones to see which.



The band’s pianist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm once the changes are comfortable.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
4. Shells in the left hand
Put root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone and the right hand is free for a melody. A three-note chord with the 5th left out is a shell voicing. To keep the hand in one place the notes are rearranged from chord to chord, so the root is not always on the bottom.



Play a chorus of shells with the left hand only. Then add one note of your own in the right hand per bar. Any chord tone will do.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
5. Rootless voicings
When there is a bass player, the root is taken care of, and the left hand can spend its fingers on colour instead. A rootless voicing is the two guide tones plus two notes from higher up the chord: the 9th (a whole step above the root) and the 13th (the same note as the 6th). There are two forms, one with the 3rd on the bottom and one with the 7th on the bottom, and they alternate so the hand barely moves. This is the standard left-hand sound of jazz piano since the late 1950s.



The dashed square is the root, shown only so you can see where the voicing sits in relation to it. Leave it to the bass.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is a half step lower than a dominant chord’s. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide tones take turns to fall by a step: the 7th of each chord drops to become the 3rd of the next.



The same chorus with rootless voicings in the left hand:

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
section: 7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is over guide tones and a root.



The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a half step to become the ♭7th of IV, the same move your right hand makes. Once the guide tones are secure, play the riff in the right hand and rootless voicings in the left:

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and work the same steps there. Start with F, B♭ and G.
Loop a chorus with the piano left out and comp for yourself.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and find the guide tones of each new chord.
The Chord Sheet tool (Tools menu) draws these and other voicings for any chords you type in, one at a time or superimposed.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
An oscillator is the part of a synthesizer that makes a repeating wave. Its two settings are the shape of the wave and how fast it repeats (the frequency, heard as pitch). This lesson plays the classic shapes from the harmonic series lesson on a real oscillator, then makes the pulse wave move.
How to use the page. Press ▶, or play the computer keys (a w s e d…), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard; the widget sounds while a key is held. Keep the volume in the bottom bar low to start with. The bright waves are loud.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
Four shapes



Play the same note with each Wave and watch both pictures:

Sine: one spike in the spectrum.
Triangle: a few odd harmonics that die away fast. Softer than you’d guess from the pointed shape.
Sawtooth: a comb of every harmonic. The brightest and the most useful, because a filter can carve almost anything out of it.
Square: only every other spike. Listen for the hollow, woody tone.

Move Pitch up and down. On the spectrum the whole comb slides along together, keeping its pattern. That pattern (the timbre) is independent of the pitch.

Frequency and pitch. Each octave doubles the frequency: A2 is 110 Hz, A3 220 Hz, A4 440 Hz. That’s why the spectrum’s frequency axis is drawn with every octave the same width.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
Pulse width
A pulse wave is up for part of each cycle and down for the rest. The fraction of the cycle it spends up is the pulse width (or duty cycle). At 50% it is a square wave.



Drag Pulse width slowly from 50% down to 5%. The sound goes from hollow to nasal to thin and reedy. On the spectrum, gaps appear and move: at width 1/k, every kth harmonic is missing. Widths of 30% and 70% sound the same: one is the other upside down.
Inside the browser there is no pulse oscillator, so the widget makes one the way some analogue synths did: it takes a sawtooth and subtracts a delayed copy of the same sawtooth. The delay, as a fraction of the cycle, is the pulse width.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
PWM: pulse-width modulation
Now let something move the width for you. PWM rate is how many times a second the width swings, and PWM depth is how far.



A slowly swinging pulse width gives the rich, chorus-like shimmer of 1980s string machines and synth pads: the gaps in the spectrum sweep up and down, a little like a phaser. Turn the rate up to 5 Hz or so for a wobble. The thing doing the moving is an LFO, a low-frequency oscillator, which gets its own lesson.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
A jazz singer is part of the band. The tone is conversational, the rhythm swings, and the melody is something to reshape rather than repeat. This lesson moves from tone and swing to scat, blue notes, singing the chords, and the back-phrasing of a ballad.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower. The playback is straight, but swing the eighth notes when you sing (see the next section). Click a heading to fold a section away.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Tone: talk the tune
Jazz singers from Billie Holiday to Shirley Horn sound like they are telling you something. Keep the tone close to your speaking voice, with clear words.
Vibrato is a natural, regular wobble in a held note’s pitch. Use it as a colour, not a constant. A common habit is to start a long note straight and let the vibrato bloom near the end.
Sing the note below, straight for two beats and then letting it relax into vibrato.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Swing eighths
In swing, a pair of eighth notes is played long–short, roughly like the first and last notes of a triplet: “doo-ba doo-ba”. Accent the off-beats (the “and”s) a little, and let some notes almost disappear. Those are ghost notes, shown in parentheses in the syllables under the staff.
The playback here is straight; sing it swung. For a swung band to sing with, try Reading swing or the Backing Track on a swing style.




Tap your foot on beats 2 and 4, not 1 and 3. That is where the drummer’s hi-hat closes in a swing feel, and it puts your body in the groove.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Scat syllables
Scat is improvising with syllables instead of words. The syllables work like articulation on a horn:

“doo” for a smooth, legato note.
“ba” and “da” for a note with an attack.
“dat” and “dot” for a short note at the end of a phrase.
“bee”, “bop”, “doo-dle” for quick runs.

Start by copying a horn line. Sing this phrase with the syllables written under it. Then make up your own syllables on the same notes.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
section: Blue notes and the blues scale
text:
Blue notes and the blues scale
The blues scale adds the “blue notes” to a minor pentatonic: in C, that’s C, E♭, F, F♯ (the ♭5), G and B♭. The ♭3 and ♭7 sung over major chords give blues and jazz their bite. Slide into them, and bend them slightly sharp.



Practice: sing the scale over a 12-bar blues in C with the Backing Track, then improvise a two-bar phrase using only C, E♭, F and G.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Singing the changes: arpeggios
Improvisers outline the chords as they go by. Sing each chord’s tones from the root up: 1, 3, 5, 7. Here is a ii–V–I in C, the most common progression in jazz.



Then sing them going down, from the 7th of each chord, and you’ll see how the notes join up.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
section: Guide tones: the line inside the changes
text:
Guide tones: the line inside the changes
The 3rd and 7th of each chord are its guide tones. Sung in a row they make a smooth line that moves by a half step or not at all, and it outlines the harmony with only two notes per chord. Guide tones covers the idea in depth.



Practice: sing the guide tones while the Backing Track plays a ii–V–I. Then add one passing note between each pair.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Back-phrasing a ballad
On a ballad, jazz singers float the words over the beat. They start a phrase late and then catch up, stretch one word, and rush the next. This is back-phrasing. The band keeps strict time; the singer’s line is free on top of it.
Here is a phrase written plainly, then back-phrased, with each entry a beat or more late and some notes pulled together.






(The words are a stand-in to sing on, not a real tune.)
Practice: sing a ballad you know with a slow backing track. Say the words in rhythm first, as speech, then sing them with the same freedom.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Trading fours
In a jam the soloists trade fours: each takes four bars in turn, often answering what the last one played. Practise call and response: play the call, then sing a four-bar answer that starts with the same rhythm and ends somewhere new.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Where to go next

Pop singing: mix, belt and runs.
Classical singing: breath, pure vowels and legato.
Improvising on a blues: the same ideas for any instrument.

title: Sound 10: The Compressor
text:
A compressor is an automatic hand on the volume knob. When the sound gets louder than a set level, it turns it down; when it gets quieter, it lets it back up. The loud parts and the quiet parts end up closer together. Almost every vocal, bass line and drum track on a record goes through one.
How to use the page. The source starts as an uneven riff (some notes loud, some barely there). The graph shows input level across and output level up. The red dot is the sound right now, and the red bar on the right is the gain reduction: how many decibels the compressor is turning the sound down at this moment.

title: Sound 10: The Compressor
text:
The controls




Threshold: the level where the compressor starts working. Anything quieter passes through unchanged; on the graph the line follows the dashed diagonal until the threshold.
Ratio: how hard it turns down what goes over. At 4 : 1, a sound 8 dB over the threshold comes out only 2 dB over. At 20 : 1 almost nothing gets over: that’s a limiter.
Knee: how gently it starts. A soft knee bends into compression gradually.
Attack: how fast it reacts when the sound goes over. Slow attack lets the very start of each note through before clamping down, which keeps drums punchy.
Release: how fast it lets go when the sound drops back.
Make-up gain: compression makes everything quieter, so you turn the whole thing back up. Now the quiet notes are louder than before.

Press Bypass on and off with the uneven riff: compressed, the quiet notes come forward and the loud ones stop jumping out.

title: Sound 10: The Compressor
text:
Hearing attack and release
Switch the source to the drum loop, set the ratio to 8 : 1 and the threshold to about −30 dB.

Attack 1 ms: the snare’s crack is flattened; the drums sound small and thick.
Attack 30 ms: the crack gets through before the compressor reacts; the drums punch.
Release 30 ms with a fast attack: the sound “pumps”, rising between hits. Dance music uses this on purpose.

title: Sound 10: The Compressor
text:
Parallel compression
Turn Mix down to 50%. Now you hear the untouched drums and a heavily squashed copy together. The natural hits stay sharp and the squashed copy fills in between them. Engineers call it “New York” compression.

title: Sound 10: The Compressor
text:
Your own playing
Choose Microphone (headphones on) and play or sing from very soft to loud. With a threshold of −40 dB and a ratio of 6 : 1, watch the gain reduction bar follow you. The site’s backing band runs through a compressor too (threshold −12 dB, ratio 4 : 1, attack 3 ms), and these sound pages end in a limiter so that nothing comes out too loud.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
This is a first lesson for someone who has never played congas. You will learn five ways to strike the drum, how they are written, and the most common conga part there is, the tumbao. You need one drum. If you have no drum yet you can still follow the notation and listen to the band play each step.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to play them yourself. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.
About the sounds. The sounds on this page are General MIDI stand-ins. The computer has only an open tone, a muted tone and a low drum, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones you hear here are approximations. Listen to a real player for the sound.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
The drums
The conga is the higher drum of a pair, and the one this lesson uses. The tumba is the lower drum. A conga player often has both, and step 6 uses the tumba for a moment; everything else on this page is played on one drum.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Sitting and hands
This is ordinary advice, not a method. Sit upright, near the front of the chair, with the drum between your knees. Tilt it slightly away from you, or put it on a stand, so the bottom is open and the sound can come out. Keep your wrists and hands loose: a tight hand makes a dead sound and tires quickly. Take rings off. If anything hurts, stop and rest; a drum head is hard, and a beginner’s hands need time.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
The five strokes
The names and the first description of each stroke are from the teacher’s handout. Each button plays the stroke.
Bass tone ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand. It is the lowest sound the drum makes.
Open tone ▶ Hear it Strike near the edge of the head with the base of your fingers. Use the first four fingers at the edge and let them bounce off, so that the drum rings.
Muted tone ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand, creating a deep tone. Teachers differ on this name. Some say “muffled”, and some mean a tone where the fingers stay on the head after the strike. The handout’s description is the one used on this page.
Slap tone ▶ Hear it Strike the edge of the head with flat fingertips to create a high, pinging sound. The slap is the hardest stroke to learn and takes time. Do not expect it to ring on the first day.
Heel-toe ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the heel of the palm, then rock forward to slap with the fingers. It is a rocking motion of the hand: first the heel, then the fingertips. It is a quiet stroke, used as filler between the louder ones. On this page the two halves are written as two notes, heel and toe.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Reading a conga part
Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space of the staff. The head says how it is struck: a plain head for the open tone and the bass tone, an ✕ for the slap, a triangle for the heel and the toe, and a diamond for the muted tone. The open tone and the bass tone look the same, so read the letter.



In a part, two lines of words sit under the notes. The first line is the stroke: H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass. The second line is the hand: L left and R right. A left-handed player can reverse the hands. A low drum, when there is one, is written on a lower space.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
1. The two notes everyone hears
The tumbao is built up from the end of the bar. Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” and play only on the last two. Use the right hand for both, one after the other.



These are the two notes a listener notices. When they come in the right place, the rest of the part has somewhere to go.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
2. The right hand
Now add the slap on 2. The right hand plays all of it: the slap on 2, then the two open tones on 4 and the and of 4. Between them the right hand rests, and you keep counting.



If the slap will not come, play it as an open tone for now and come back to it. Take it slowly.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
3. The left hand
Put the right hand away and play the other half. The left hand plays heel on 1, toe on the and of 1, toe on the and of 2, heel on 3 and toe on the and of 3. It is the rocking heel-toe stroke, quiet. The gaps left in the bar are where the right hand will go.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
4. Both hands, slowly
Put the two hands together. The strokes in order are Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, and the hands are L L R L L L R R. The left hand plays every quiet heel and toe; the right hand plays the slap and the two open tones. This is the tumbao, as the handout writes it: a pattern of heel-toe-slap-toe figures and a pair of open tones. The sticking is the one given for the tumbao by Rebeca Mauleón in Salsa Guidebook, as quoted in the Wikipedia article on the tumbao.



This step is slow, and the band has no drummer, so the congas are easy to hear. Loop it and play along until your hands do not argue.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
5. With a band
The same part in the Cha-cha, at a moderate tempo, with the drummer in. The tumbao is the most common pattern on congas and bongos, and it fits cha-cha, son and boogaloo. The Feel menu at the bottom plays it in the other two.



Listen for the clave in the other instruments: a rhythm of five notes over two bars, three in one bar and two in the other, that the whole band is built around. You do not need to play it to play the tumbao, but it explains the next step.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
6. Two drums
Players who have two drums use the second one in the tumbao. Here, in Son montuno, every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. It is the bar with three clave notes (the second bar of a 2-3 clave, as Mauleón’s book has it, again via the Wikipedia article). Look at the two bars written large: the second has the notes on a lower space.



Stay on one drum until step 5 is easy. The two-drum bar is an extra, not a part of the basic tumbao.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Where to go next

Play step 5 with Leave out the congas ticked for ten choruses without losing the beat.
Take the tumbao to a tune: Watermelon Man for Congas plays it in a 16-bar blues.
Tools → Backing Track has a Congas menu that works in any style: put a tumbao under a tune you know.
Listen to a real conga player and copy what you hear. A page cannot give you the sound of the hands.

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:

Tumbao, Wikipedia: the heel-toe-slap-toe, open-open figure and its sticking (citing Rebeca Mauleón, Salsa Guidebook).
Conga, Wikipedia.
Congas: first steps, Thomann.
