title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
The tonewheel organ (the Hammond B-3 and its relatives) is in gospel, soul, blues, jazz and rock. It looks like a piano but behaves very differently: a key has no touch, a note sounds for as long as you hold it, and the sound is built by the player from nine pitches. Then it goes through a chorus, a volume pedal, and a speaker that spins.
The organ on this page is the band’s own: nothing is recorded, every note is built from the same parts as the real instrument. (How it’s built and where the numbers come from: apps/shared/band/ORGAN.md. It’s a model, so some of its levels are informed guesses.) Everything you set here is also what the organ plays in the band at the bottom of the page.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
1. The organ
Hold a key on the keyboard, or press Hold a chord, then work the controls while it sounds.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
2. Tonebars (drawbars)
Each of the nine bars adds one pitch to every key you press. Each bar is named by the length of an organ pipe in feet: the 8′ is the note you play, 16′ is an octave below, 4′ an octave above, and so on. The white bars are octaves of the note. The black ones are the 5ths and 3rd above it, which give the sound its colour. The two brown bars are the sub-octave pitches.
Each bar has nine positions, 0 (in, silent) to 8 (all the way out, loudest). Each step is about 3 dB. A registration is written as the nine numbers in three groups: 88 8000 000 means the first three bars all the way out and the rest pushed in.
Try this:

Start from 00 8000 000: the note alone, nearly a pure tone. Pull out the 4′, then the 2′, and watch the pitches stack up on the right.
Pull out the 1⅗′ alone over the 8′. That’s the 3rd, two octaves up. The organ’s 3rd and 5ths are slightly out of tune with a pure harmonic, because they come from tonewheels tuned to the keyboard. That’s part of the sound.
Pick 88 8888 888: the whole organ.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
3. Chorus and vibrato
A scanner sweeps the sound through a very short delay, 6.9 times a second. On its own that wobbles the pitch: vibrato (V3). Mixed half and half with the plain sound the wobble becomes a shimmer: chorus (C3), the setting most players leave on for jazz, gospel and soul. Switch between Off and C3 chorus on a held chord to hear it.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
4. The swell pedal
Because a key sounds the same however hard you press it, the organist plays dynamics with the right foot. The swell pedal is a volume pedal that never quite closes: at its quietest the organ is 24 dB down and the bass is kept up so the sound doesn’t go thin. It sits before the amplifier, so opening it also makes the sound grittier.
Organists open the pedal through the end of a phrase into the next one, pull it back sharply after a big hit, and ride it the way a singer leans into a long note.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
5. The Leslie speaker
The organ’s sound goes into a cabinet where it is split: the high notes go into a horn and the low notes into a drum, and both spin. As each one turns toward you it gets a bit louder and higher; as it turns away it gets softer and lower. That’s the swirl.

Slow (“chorale”): about 48 turns a minute. A gentle movement.
Fast (“tremolo”): about 400 turns a minute. A shimmering, urgent sound.
Stop: the rotors stand still.

The best part is the change. The light horn reaches its new speed in about a second and a half; the heavy drum takes about five. Switch from Slow to Fast on a held chord and listen to it wind up, then switch back and hear it wind down. The picture spins at the model’s speeds.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
6. The organ in the band
Here the organ comps in three styles. Unless you’ve taken them over above, the band’s organist works the pedal and switch by itself: the pedal follows how hard the band is playing and opens into each new phrase, and the Leslie goes fast at the end of a phrase that leads into a chorus. In swing, the speaker stays slow until the very end. Untick Let the band’s organist… above (or just move the control) to take them over.
Soul jazz, organ comping a boogaloo:



Swing, organ comping a jazz blues:



Ballad, long organ chords under a slow song (try 68 8600 000 and a low pedal):

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
7. Try it

Set 00 8000 000, chorus Off, Leslie Stop. That’s a plain electronic tone. Now put back the chorus, then the Leslie on Slow, then pull out the 16′ and 5⅓′. Each step makes it more like the organ on a record.
In the boogaloo, take over the Leslie and switch it to Fast just before bar 9 each time round.
In the ballad, take the pedal and play the dynamics: low through the first two bars, opening through bar 4 into the top.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
A pitched note has its energy at a few frequencies (the harmonics). Noise has its energy spread over all of them at once, with no pattern and no repeating shape. It’s the hiss of a cymbal, the breath in a flute, the “s” and “f” in speech, wind and rain. Synthesizers include a noise source for exactly these sounds.
How to use the page. Press ▶ to hear the colour you chose, or press one of the Made from noise buttons. Noise is loud for its size: start with the volume low.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
The colours of noise




White noise has equal energy at every frequency. Because each octave up holds twice as many frequencies as the one below, it sounds very bright: a hiss.
Pink noise has equal energy in every octave, so it falls away toward the highs. It sounds more even to the ear, like steady rain or a waterfall, and sound engineers use it to test speakers.
Brown noise (named after Brownian motion, not the colour) falls away faster still: a deep rumble, like surf heard from inside a house.

Watch the spectrum as you switch. White is flat, pink tilts down gently, brown tilts down steeply. The oscilloscope never settles into a shape, because noise never repeats.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
Sounds made from noise
Noise on its own is not very musical. Its use comes from shaping it: a filter picks out a band of frequencies, an envelope makes it short or long, and an LFO makes it move.







Button
Recipe




Wind
pink noise through a narrow band-pass filter whose centre drifts slowly


Surf
pink noise through a low-pass, both the volume and the brightness swelling every eight seconds


Hi-hat
white noise, only the highs, cut off within 50 ms (longer for the open hat)


Snare
a burst of noise for the wires with a short low tone for the drum head


Steam
white noise with the lows removed


Rain
soft pink noise for the background, plus thousands of tiny filtered clicks for drops



Every drum sound in the site’s backing band except the kick is made from noise in roughly this way.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
A lead sheet writes swing eighths as plain eighth notes, and that is not an error. The way they are written is shorthand, the way a chord symbol is. It tells you which notes come where, and the style tells you how to play them. This lesson covers what the shorthand means, how much room it leaves you, and how to know when it does not mean swing. The two examples are Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet, which swings, and Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man, which does not.
How to use the page. Every example is written out and can be played. Press ▶ Play to hear it. Examples that have a Swing slider let you set how long the first eighth of each pair is held, from even (50%) up to a dotted-eighth-and-sixteenth (75%). The Tempo box sets the speed. Play each example at more than one setting before you read on.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 1. What the page says, and what it means
text:
1. What the page says, and what it means
Here is the first bar of Blues in the Closet exactly as a lead sheet writes it.


Played as written, the eighths are even: each beat is split exactly in half. No jazz player reads it that way. In a swing tune each pair of eighths is played long-short: the note on the beat is held longer and the note on the “and” comes late. The usual way to explain it is with a triplet: the beat is split into three, the first note gets two thirds and the second gets one.


Arrangers almost never write that, because it is hard to read and because, as the rest of this lesson shows, it is not quite right either. Instead they write plain eighths and put a word or a sign at the top of the chart:

Swing, Med. swing, Shuffle, Bluesy, or just a tempo and a style name.
The sign ♫ = ♩ ♪³: “a pair of eighths equals a quarter and an eighth under a triplet”.
Nothing at all. On a jazz lead sheet, swing is the default, and you are expected to know it.

The one way not to read swing eighths is as a dotted eighth and a sixteenth. That is a ratio of 3 to 1, and at most tempos it sounds stiff and jerky, like a march. Compare it with the triplet version above.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 2. Swing is a range, not a ratio
text:
2. Swing is a range, not a ratio
The triplet is a useful first picture and a poor final answer. Measurements of recordings find that players swing anywhere from nearly even to a little past the triplet, and that the same player changes ratio with the tempo. The rough rule:




Tempo


Typical long:short


Slider


What it sounds like






Ballad, slow blues (under 80)


about 2:1, sometimes more


65–70%


Lazy, heavy triplet feel, often a 12/8 shuffle




Medium (100–160)


between 3:2 and 2:1


60–67%


The “standard” swing of a blues like Blues in the Closet




Up-tempo (over 220)


close to even


52–58%


Eighths almost straight; the swing is in the accents




The band on this site follows the same rule: its swing starts at 68% at 100 beats a minute and slides toward 60% as the tempo rises. Try it here. Set the slider to 66% and raise the tempo to 240: it becomes hard to play and starts to sound like a shuffle. Then lower the slider to 55% at the same tempo.



Everything else the shorthand leaves to you
The ratio is only one of the choices a plain line of eighths leaves open. Others matter at least as much, and the lead sheet says nothing about any of them.

Accents on the off-beats. Swing players lean on the “and”, not the beat. A line of eighths is usually played doo-BAH doo-BAH, with the beat note soft and the off-beat note pushed. This is why fast swing still swings at nearly even eighths.
Ghosted notes. A note in the middle of a run may be barely played at all, more felt than heard.
Length. A written quarter note is often played short (dit), especially on beats 2 and 4 and at the end of a phrase. A written eighth tied over the bar line is played long.
Where in the beat. Some players sit right on the beat, others play a fraction behind it (“laid back”) against a drummer who is on top of it. Neither is written; both are swing.
Small changes to the rhythm. Players anticipate a note by an eighth, delay one, or add a pickup. On a lead sheet, that is interpretation, not a wrong note.

What is not up to you: where the bar lines are, where the notes fall in the beat (on it or on the “and”), and the form. A swing eighth on the “and” of 2 is late, but it is still the “and” of 2.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
3. Blues in the Closet
Blues in the Closet is a medium-tempo jazz blues, usually played somewhere between 120 and 180 beats a minute. Here is the whole melody, in F, as it is written in the tune library.


There is no “Swing” marking on it, and none is needed: it is a bebop-era blues, every recording of it swings, and the eighth-note pairs are written the way every jazz player expects. Play it at 50% and then at 64% to hear what the marking would have told you.

The places that change when it swings

The pickup and the ties. The tune starts on the “and” of 4 and ties it into the bar. In swing, that pickup is late (it is the short note of a pair), so the first note of the tune arrives just before the bar line and pulls the band into it. The same figure ends bars 4 and 8. These anticipations are the strongest swing feature in the tune: give them a little accent.
The figure A F. In every bar the melody drops from the 3rd to the root in a pair of eighths. Swung, it is long-short, and the short F is the one to lean on.
The tied F in bar 2. A/F/- F/ C is four eighths, with the second tied to the third. Swung, the tied F lands on the late “and” of 2 and sustains through beat 3. Played even, the syncopation is weaker and the bar sounds square.
The long notes. The C in bars 4 and 8 is a dotted quarter tied to a quarter. It can be held full length or cut off early; both are common. The rest that follows is where the rhythm section, or another player, answers.



A range of good readings
Three players reading the same lead sheet would not play the same thing, and all three would be right. Try these settings and decide which one you like:




Setting


Tempo


Slider


Feel






Relaxed


120


66–68%


Close to the triplet, heavy, bluesy




Medium


150


60–64%


The usual jam-session reading




Up


200+


55–58%


Nearly even; put the swing in accents on the off-beats




What no setting allows is 50% at a medium tempo with every note accented equally. That is the one clear misreading.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing
text:
4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing
Watermelon Man (from Takin’ Off, 1962) is also a blues, with 16 bars instead of 12, and it is written in exactly the same way: plain eighth notes, no triplets, no dots. Here are its first eight bars and the four-bar riff that follows.


On the page it looks like Blues in the Closet: eighth notes, ties over the bar line, anticipations. The difference is the style. This is a straight-eighth tune: the eighths are even, and they stay even when the tempo drops. It is often marked “Funky”, “Latin”, “Even 8ths” or “Straight 8ths”, but on many lead sheets it is not marked at all, and you are expected to know it from the record, the same as with a swing tune.
Now move the slider to 66% and play it again. Bars 9 to 12 suffer most: z2 cc g2 a2 starts on an off-beat pair, and swinging it turns a crisp, funky riff into something closer to a nursery rhyme. The off-beat F in bars 2 and 6, which should snap against the beat, goes soft.

“Somewhere between”
Even this tune is not perfectly even. Hancock said that Billy Higgins played it “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. That is a slider setting of perhaps 53 to 56%, which is not enough to sound like swing but is enough to keep the line from sounding mechanical. Mongo Santamaría’s hit version a year later is a cha-cha, and its eighths are straight. Both are good readings of the same lead sheet; a 66% swing is not.
So the range of acceptable readings exists for straight tunes too. It is just centred in a different place.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
5. The contrast, side by side






Blues in the Closet


Watermelon Man






Written as


Plain eighths


Plain eighths




Played as


Swing, long-short


Even, or very nearly




Slider


55–68%, by tempo


50–56%




Where the energy is


Accents on the off-beats, late pickups


Crisp, equal subdivisions locked to a backbeat or a Latin pattern




How you know


Jazz blues, bebop era, every recording


The record, the style (“funk”, “Latin”, “even 8ths”)




The point is that the notation is identical. Everything that separates these two tunes in performance comes from outside the notes: the style, the era, the recording and the band.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
6. Reading a new lead sheet
When you open a chart you have not played before, before you play a note:

Look at the top of the page for a style or feel word, a ♫ = ♩ ♪³ sign, or “even 8ths”.
Look at the tempo. The faster it is, the straighter the swing.
Know where the tune comes from. A jazz standard or a bebop blues swings unless told otherwise. A funk, Latin, rock, soul or bossa nova tune does not.
Listen to a recording. It is the only thing that settles the question, and it tells you about the accents and the note lengths too, which no lead sheet shows.
Listen to the band. If the drummer plays the swing ride pattern, match its ratio; if the drummer plays straight eighths on the hi-hat, play straight. The ratio is shared, not chosen alone.

Then practise both tunes in this lesson at three tempos each, and play the slider settings from the tables until you can hear the difference without looking.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the bass player’s chair, starting from one note per chord. You need to know how to fret a note and pluck it. Everything else is built here, one step at a time. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams read like a bass standing upright in front of you: the low E string is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear its notes. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff, and below the chord chart is the bass line the band is playing. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, the bar on the chart and the diagram of the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the bass and the band’s bass player stops so that you can take the part. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. A blues has three chords, so it has three roots, and they sit close together. Find the key note on the E string. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on the next string up. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on that same string. Your hand does not have to move.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.
Start with two notes in each bar, on beats 1 and 3.



Count the bars as you play: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. When that is steady, play the root on every beat. Press Superimposed to see all three roots on one fretboard.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
2. Root, fifth and octave
The fifth of a chord is one string up and two frets up from its root. The octave (the root again, higher) is two strings up and two frets up. Index finger on the root, ring or little finger on the other two: the three notes make a box that has the same shape on every chord. Move the box to each root you learned in step 1.



The band’s bass plays root on beat 1 and fifth on beat 3. Play that first, then try root, fifth, octave, fifth, one note to a beat.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
3. The 3rd and the 7th
The root and fifth say which chord it is but not what kind of chord. Two other notes do that job.

The 3rd says major or minor. In a dominant seventh chord (G7) it is a major 3rd: one string up and one fret back from the root.
The 7th in a blues chord is a flat 7th (written ♭7), a whole step below the octave: two strings up at the same fret as the root.

Together they are called the guide tones, because they are the notes that change the most tellingly from one chord to the next. Root, 3rd, 5th and ♭7th are the four chord tones. Click each chord’s name to hear them climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



The band’s bass plays exactly that: root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7th, one note on every beat, the same shape in every bar. The line is written out below the chord chart. It is not a walking line yet. It is the four chord tones in order, so that your hand learns each shape and your ear learns what each note sounds like against its chord.
Work up to it in three stages, each for a few choruses:

Root on beat 1, 3rd on beat 3. Two notes to a bar.
Root, 3rd, 5th, and rest on beat 4.
All four notes, as the band plays them.

Then switch to Superimposed and look at I and IV together. The 3rd of the I chord is one fret below the root of IV, and the ♭7th of I is one fret above the 3rd of IV. Those half steps are how the chords connect.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
4. Walking
In step 3 every bar went the same way: up the chord from the root. A walking line also has one note on every beat, but it chooses its notes so that each bar leads into the next. Three changes turn the step 3 line into a walking line: the notes after the root can come in any order, the octave joins them, and the last note of the bar points at the next root. A recipe that always works:

Beat 1: the root of the chord.
Beats 2 and 3: any two other chord tones (3rd, 5th, ♭7th, or the octave).
Beat 4: an approach note, one fret below or one fret above the root of the next bar’s chord.

When the next bar is the same chord, beat 4 can be any chord tone. The diagram shows the chord tones of all three chords at once. A split dot is a note two chords share.
Between the chord tones you can also step along the scale that goes with the chord. Over the I chord that is the scale from step 3, the major scale with its 7th lowered a half step (called Mixolydian). Here it is in one place on the neck, with the run written in tablature. Beats 2 and 3 can borrow its notes, so a bar can climb step by step instead of jumping.






Listen to the band’s bass player for a chorus, then tick Leave out the bass and walk it yourself. Slow the tempo down as far as you need. A plain line that lands on the root at every chord change is worth more than a busy one that does not.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord. Its 3rd is a minor 3rd, three frets above the root on the same string. Everything else about the shape stays the same.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Play the root on the beat each chord arrives and one other note after it: root and 3rd, or root and an approach note into the next root.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford, who wrote this tune, was a bass player. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12 to turn it round. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, so the bass has room to be heard.



Play roots through the form first, two to a bar, and listen to how the riff sits against them. Then walk it. In bars 4 and 8 the melody holds one long note: that is the place for your line to lead clearly into the next chord. In bar 12, aim for the root of the V chord and then back to the top.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and find the same shapes in the new place. Start with F, B♭, A and E.
Loop a chorus with the bass left out and record yourself over the band.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and walk through it with the recipe from step 4.
Next on bass: pop changes for bass, roots and the walking line.

title: Lessons
text:
The site's backing band plays every example in these lessons. Choose an instrument, a topic, or both. They run roughly from simpler to more involved.


  All
  Bass
  Guitar
  Piano

  Congas

  Saxophone
  Voice
  Another instrument


  Any topic
  Blues
  Jazz
  Pop
  Latin
  Harmony
  Rhythm

  Reading

No lessons match both choices yet.


  
    Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
    Starting from the melody: hitting the change in bar 5, the blues and pentatonic scales, and a scale for each chord. Scales are shown as tablature, keyboard fingerings or a violin fingerboard, whichever you play.
  
  
    Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
    For any instrument that plays one note at a time. Roots, chord tones, guide-tone lines, a riff, and the melody of Blues in the Closet, written in your own key.
  
  
    Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
    What the chords of a blues are and how players vary them, from three chords to a jazz blues, with a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.
  
  
    Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
    Roots, then root and fifth, then the chord tones as a written line, then walking. Fretboard diagrams, bass-clef notation and the band's own bass line written out.
  
  
    Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
    Two- and three-note chords built from the 3rd and 7th, on strings 5 and 4 and on strings 4 and 3, with the same shapes a tritone higher. No barre chords.
  
  
    Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
    Left-hand roots, guide tones in the right hand, three-note shells and rootless left-hand voicings, each on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.
  
  
    Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
    How to read a drum part, then the beat, the ride pattern, swing time, fills that mark the form, the shuffle, the slow 12/8 and straight eighths.
  
  
    Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
    Why swing eighths are written as plain eighths, how far the long-short can stretch with tempo and style, and the range of good readings, with Blues in the Closet swung and Watermelon Man straight for contrast. Every example plays, with a swing slider.
  
  
    Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
    For a drummer who can already play a basic beat. The three sounds of the hi-hat, then quarter notes, eighths, accents, off-beats, an open note, open off-beats, sixteenths with one hand and with two, the foot alone and the swing hi-hat.
  
  
    How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
    The drums, how to sit, the five strokes (bass, open, muted, slap, heel-toe) and how they are written, then the tumbao built in six steps with the band: open tones, right hand, left hand, both hands, a cha-cha band and two drums.
  
  
    Watermelon Man for Congas
    The tumbao over a 16-bar blues: the form, the break on bar 14, the melody, and the same part in Mongo Santamaría's cha-cha and in a boogaloo.
  
  
    Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
    The four chords under most pop songs, made richer one move at a time: extensions, passing chords, secondary dominants and ii-V-Is. With a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.
  
  
    Pop Changes for Guitar
    The C, Am, F, G changes as fretboard diagrams: open shapes, extensions, passing chords and secondary dominants.
  
  
    Pop Changes for Piano
    The C, Am, F, G changes with a left-hand root and a right-hand chord, on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.
  
  
    Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
    The root of each chord, then the stepwise walking line through the passing chords, in bass clef and on a fretboard.
  
  
    Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
    Thirteen steps from open triads and power chords through barre chords, 7ths, shells and top-string triads to drop 2, drop 3 and altered dominants, each with diagrams, a staff and sound.
  
  
    Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand
    The same chords ordered by what the fretting hand finds hard, from one-finger shapes to barres, muted strings and stretches, with what goes wrong at each step.
  
  
    Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
    From one finger on one string to trills, licks and the Sus embellishment on open D, A and C, each written in notation and tablature that plays.
  
  
    Travis Picking on Guitar
    The thumb alone, pinches, fingers between the thumb notes, then C, G, Am and D, chord changes, hammer-ons and pull-offs, and the band. Ends with a note on chicken pickin'.
  
  
    Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
    Thirteen steps from triads and inversions through slash chords, 7ths, guide tones and shells to rootless, drop 2, spread, quartal and upper-structure voicings.
  
  
    Piano Voicings by Hand
    The same voicings ordered by what the hands find hard: span, black keys, two hands together, leaps, stretches and independence.
  
  
    Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
    Major and minor triads with the root, 3rd or 5th in the bass, their figured-bass names (⁶ and ⁶₄) and slash-chord names (C/E, C/G), on piano and guitar.
  
  
    Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
    Breath, onsets, speech-level singing and the mix, words, safe belting, pentatonic runs, cry and flips, phrasing with a mic, and singing a third above. Exercises move into your range.
  
  
    Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
    Conversational tone, swing eighths and ghost notes, scat syllables, the blues scale, arpeggios and guide tones through a ii-V-I, back-phrasing a ballad, and trading fours.
  
  
    Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
    Appoggio breathing, onset and legato, the five Italian vowels, resonance, registers and the passaggio, the nine-note scale, messa di voce, vibrato, diction and solfège.
  
  
    Four-Chord Loops
    The loops under a great many songs (I V vi IV, vi IV I V, the fifties loop, the turnaround, a borrowed chord, two minor loops) one at a time, each on a chart and a staff, with a loop builder and an ear test.
  
  
    Cadences, and the One That Is Not
    Authentic, half, deceptive, plagal and backdoor endings, each as a four-bar phrase on a staff, with the argument for why the plagal "Amen" is not a cadence, a phrase builder and two ear tests.
  
  
    Guide Tones
    The 3rd and 7th of each chord written as a single line over four-chord loops, a two-five-one and the turnaround. The band plays the line.
  
  
    Changes in a Minor Key
    From natural-minor i, iv, v to the harmonic-minor V7, the Picardy third, a walking bass and the ii°-V-i, in A minor.
  
  
    Borrowed Chords
    The minor iv, the ♭VII and the ♭VI borrowed into a major key, one at a time, with a chord-by-chord builder and an ear test.
  
  
    Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
    I-vi-ii-V made richer: sevenths, a dominant on the vi, starting on the iii, tritone substitutions and the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.
  
  
    Reharmonizing a Melody
    One tune, Ode to Joy, with four sets of chords under it, played with the melody. Mix the settings two bars at a time.
  
  
    Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
    The four jobs in a rhythm section, built up one player at a time. Switch players in and out while the band plays and see each part written out.
  
  
    Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
    Why the bass follows the kick, how the groove sets the feel, walking in swing and the tumbao in Latin music.
  
  
    Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
    Comping: strum patterns, voicing and register, the off-beat chop, jazz comping, and two chord players without a fight.
  
  
    Arranging 4: The Organ
    A playable tonewheel organ: pull the nine tonebars, switch the chorus, work the swell pedal and spin the Leslie, then hear it in the band.
  
  
    Accompaniment Patterns
    A lesson for every bass line, comping rhythm, drum groove and conga part the band plays, each built up from simpler ones, played on the band and written out.
  
  
    Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
    The harmonics of a note written out over any root, with how far each is from the piano. Build square, triangle, sawtooth and pulse waves from sine waves.
  
  
    Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
    The classic synth waves on an oscilloscope and spectrum, pulse width, and PWM.
  
  
    Sound 3: Noise
    White, pink and brown noise, and wind, surf, hi-hats, snares and rain made from it.
  
  
    Sound 4: Filters
    Low-pass, high-pass, resonance, band-pass, notch and EQ, on noise, music or your own voice.
  
  
    Sound 5: LFOs
    Vibrato, tremolo, wah and auto-pan from one slow oscillator, and what happens when it speeds up.
  
  
    Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
    A two-oscillator synth with filter, envelopes and LFO, played from the keys or MIDI, with presets for bass, brass, pads and plucks.
  
  
    Sound 7: FM Synthesis
    Carrier, modulator, ratio and index: sidebands on the spectrum, and bells, electric piano and bass from two sine waves.
  
  
    Sound 8: Wavetable Synthesis
    Morph through a table of wave shapes by hand or with an LFO.
  
  
    Sound 9: Distortion
    Soft clip, hard clip, tube-like, wavefolder and bit crusher, and the harmonics each one adds.
  
  
    Sound 10: The Compressor
    Threshold, ratio, knee, attack and release, with a live gain-reduction meter.
  
  
    Sound 11: Reverb
    A convolution reverb with a room you build: decay, pre-delay, damping and early reflections.
  
  
    Sound 12: Chorus and Flanger
    Moving short delays, the Doppler effect, and the comb filter.
  
  
    Sound 13: Phaser
    All-pass filters, phase and sweeping notches.
  
  
    Sound 14: The Vocoder
    Talk into the microphone and play chords: the voice shapes the synth band by band.

title: Sound 12: Chorus and Flanger
text:
When a choir or a string section plays a note, no two players are exactly in tune or exactly in time. The tiny differences make the sound wide and shimmering instead of one thin line. A chorus effect fakes that with a single sound: it adds copies of the sound, each delayed by a few milliseconds, and an LFO keeps changing those delays.
How to use the page. The source starts as chords. Use headphones if you can: the copies are spread left and right. The strip under the controls draws each copy’s delay time over the last four seconds.

title: Sound 12: Chorus and Flanger
text: The effect

title: Sound 12: Chorus and Flanger
section: Why a moving delay changes the pitch
text:
Why a moving delay changes the pitch
A delay on its own only makes a sound later. But when the delay is getting longer, the sound coming out is slowed down a little, so it’s a little flat. When the delay is getting shorter, the sound is sped up, so it’s a little sharp. It’s the Doppler effect of a passing siren. So an LFO on the delay time is a gentle vibrato on the copy. Mixed with the original, the slightly detuned copy beats against it, and that beating is the shimmer.
Press Vibrato: the mix is 100% wet, so you hear only the moving copy. Its pitch wobbles. Now press Chorus and the same wobble mixed with the dry sound becomes a shimmer.

title: Sound 12: Chorus and Flanger
text:
The controls

Delay: the average delay. About 15 to 30 ms for chorus. Below 10 ms the copy no longer sounds like a separate player; above 35 ms it starts to sound like a slap-back echo (try Doubler: a single slowly moving copy at 35 ms sounds like the part was recorded twice).
Depth: how far the delay swings, and so how far the pitch wobbles.
Rate: how fast. Slow (0.3 to 1 Hz) is lush; fast is seasick.
Voices: more copies, each with its own swing, spread across the stereo field.
Feedback: feeds the delayed copy back into the delay.

title: Sound 12: Chorus and Flanger
text:
The flanger
Press Flanger. The delay is now very short (1 to 5 ms), and the feedback is high. At delays this short the copy doesn’t sound like a second player. Instead it cancels some frequencies and reinforces others in an evenly spaced pattern, a comb filter. As the delay changes, the teeth of the comb sweep up and down: the jet-plane “whoosh”. It was first done with two tape machines running together, an engineer pressing a thumb on the flange of one reel to slow it. Try it on the drum loop and on the noise source, where the moving comb is easiest to see on the spectrum.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
One melody can sit on many sets of chords. A chord is right for a melody note if the note is in it (a chord tone) or if it passes quickly (a passing note). This lesson takes one tune, Ode to Joy, and puts four sets of chords under it.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it twice after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart. The tune is written above the chart and its notes light up as they sound. ▶ Play with the band plays the melody on the piano with the chords under it.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
1. A plain setting
C and G, mostly. Two chords. Every note of the tune is a chord tone or a passing note on one of them. This is how the tune is usually harmonised in a school songbook.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
2. Sevenths on the dominants
G7 for G. The tune does not change. The chord under it does: G7 adds an F, and the F is a note the tune already passes through in bar 2. Now it is a chord tone.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
3. Secondary dominants
Am in bar 3, E7 in bar 4, and Am then D7 in bar 7. The notes of the tune are the same. Under bar 4, E7 has the tune’s E as its root and its D as the 7th. In bar 7, D7 holds the tune’s D, and the E after it is the 9th.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
section: 4. A chord for every pair of notes
text:
4. A chord for every pair of notes
C F | C/E Dm7 | Am7 | Dm7 G7 | C F | C/E Dm7 | Am7 | Dm7 C. Now the chords change every two beats and the bass moves by step: C, F, E, D. It is the tune as a jazz pianist might play it, and it sounds quite different even though the tune has not changed a note.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
Build your own
Choose one of the four settings for each pair of bars, and mix them. The tune is above the chart. All of the settings fit the tune, so there is no wrong combination.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
Where to go next

Pick your own tune and try three sets of chords on it. Play the melody note by note against each chord.
The question to ask of every chord is: is this melody note a chord tone, or is it passing?

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
This is the 12-bar blues for instruments that play one note at a time: violin, saxophones, and anything else with a single line. It starts with one note per chord and ends with a line that spells out a jazz blues. You need to be able to read notes in your instrument’s range. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom transposes the page. Violinists choose Violin, and the scale under Where the flat 7 comes from then also shows the finger for every note. Flutes stay on concert pitch. Alto and tenor players choose their saxophone, and every chart and line of notation is then written in their key, while the band plays in the concert key shown beside it. A B♭ tenor and an E♭ alto reading this page at the same time see different notes and sound the same ones.
How to use the page. Every step is a twelve-bar line. Under each note is the name of its place in the chord at that moment: R for the root, then 3, 5, ♭7. Press ▶ Play beside the notation to hear the line alone, or ▶ Play with the band to hear it over the rhythm section, where the piano plays it. Tick Leave out the melody to play it yourself. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation either way.
Sections 1 to 6 build the skills. Section 7 puts them to work on a tune, Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet. If you would rather start with the tune, go there first and come back.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after. A blues has three chords and three roots. Play each one as a long note and count the bars: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.



A bass player would play these notes. Playing them yourself is the quickest way to hear where the form turns.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
2. Chord tones, and the 3rd and 7th
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord. Here are the four notes of each chord, played up from the root.



The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones. They are the two notes that tell a listener which chord this is, and they are the notes a good melody leans on.

Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line. The explanation follows the key and instrument chosen in the strip at the bottom.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
3. Guide-tone lines
Play only a guide tone of each chord, and at each change move to the nearest guide tone of the new chord. The line barely moves: when I7 goes to IV7 the 3rd falls a half step and becomes the ♭7th of the new chord. One note per bar, and the whole harmony of the blues is in it.
Starting on the 3rd:



Starting on the 7th. Two players can take one line each.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
4. Guide tones in rhythm
The same notes become a background figure when they are given a rhythm. This one is the Charleston: a note on beat 1 and another on the “and” of 2. A horn section plays exactly this kind of thing behind a soloist.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
5. A riff
A riff is a short figure repeated through the form and adjusted to fit the chords. This one is the 3rd, 5th, 6th and 5th of the home chord. Over the IV chord only its first note changes: it drops a half step, which makes it the ♭7th of IV. Over the V chord the whole figure moves up to that chord.



Look at the names under the notes in bars 5 and 6. The fingers play almost the same thing, and every note has a new job.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord, with a minor 3rd. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide-tone line steps down: the 7th of each chord falls to the 3rd of the next.



The chord tones of the same chorus:

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
section: 7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford wrote this blues in the early 1950s. It is a riff blues: one two-bar idea, played three times over the twelve bars. Learn the first two bars and you know nearly all of it.




How it is built

Four notes. The whole melody uses the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. Look at the names under bars 1 and 2: R, 3, R, 4, 3, R.
Three lines. Bars 1 to 4, 5 to 8 and 9 to 12 are the same riff. Each ends on a long note, which is where the rhythm section answers.
Notes that arrive early. Several notes are tied across the barline. They are played an eighth note before the beat and held into the next bar. Clap the rhythm before you play it. These early notes are what make the riff swing.



The one note that changes
In bars 5 and 6 the riff’s second note is a half step lower than it was in bars 1 and 2. It is the only accidental in the tune. Over the home chord that note was the 3rd. The IV chord has that pitch a half step lower, as its ♭7th, so the melody moves with the chord. In bar 7 the home chord returns and so does the original note. This is the sound of a blues going to IV, and the melody tells you the chord has changed without any help from the band.
Hear that move by itself. This is the guide-tone line from section 3 on the tune’s changes. Play it, then play the tune again and listen for the same half step inside the riff.





The last line
Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five (ii7 then V7) instead of V then IV. The melody does not change at all, but look at the names under it: the same pitches are now the 9th and ♭7th of the ii chord. A riff this simple fits because every one of its notes belongs to the key.
The roots of the tune, to learn where the chords fall:





Practising it

Sing the riff with the band before you play it.
Play bars 1 and 2 alone until the tied notes sit right. Use ▶ Play beside the notation to check yourself.
Play the whole tune with Leave out the melody ticked.
Change the concert key. A riff you can play in three keys is a riff you know.

When the tune is secure, go on to the improvising lesson, which uses this melody as its starting point.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
Where to go next

Change the concert key and play every step again. F, B♭, C and G are the keys a blues is most often called in.
Loop a chorus with the melody left out and make up your own line from the chord tones, landing on a guide tone at each change.
Take a chorus from the changes lesson and write its guide-tone line.
Write guide-tone lines over other progressions in the guide tones lesson, or put new chords under a melody in reharmonizing.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text: The quarter note gets one beat in common time. In a 4/4 measure you can fit four of them — one per beat. We count them simply: 1 – 2 – 3 – 4.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text:
Hear it, then say it
Before reading a single quarter note, you should be able to audiate a steady beat — feel it internally — and chant a neutral syllable on each beat. Only after the sound is secure do we attach the symbol.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text:
Practice steps

Tap a steady beat with your foot.
Chant “bah” on each tap for four beats.
Now look at four quarter notes and chant them while tapping.

When you’re ready, head to Practice → Rhythm Patterns and play a few quarter-note patterns. Your time on this page and your plays over there are both recorded automatically.






Tip



This page is being timed. Stay as long as you need; switch tabs and the timer pauses. Come back and it resumes.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
This lesson orders chord shapes by what the fretting hand finds hard, starting from a first lesson on guitar. Each step adds one physical demand: more fingers, a stretch, a barre, a muted string, a shift along the neck. Each step says what makes the shape easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Guitar chord shapes has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.
How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left. Each dot shows its chord tone, R for the root. The numbers under each diagram are the frets from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger). Press ▶ to hear a shape.
Finger numbers and barres. The button below puts the finger numbers in the dots instead of the chord tones, on every diagram on the page. Where one finger lies across several strings, a shaded bar joins those dots. The bar is drawn only where a barre is new: the small barre in G-B6, the first full barres in G-B8 and G-B9, and the barre with a silent string in G-B13. Tick the box to draw it on every diagram.
Finger numbers on guitar and on piano. The two instruments count differently. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1, then middle 2, ring 3 and little finger 4, and a thumb fretting a bass note over the top of the neck is written T. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, and the left hand is numbered the same way as the right, so its little finger plays the lowest note. A “3” is the ring finger to a guitarist and the middle finger to a pianist. Picking-hand fingers on guitar have letters of their own (p, i, m, a), so they are never mixed up with these.
The two on the left are the guitar hands, and the pair on the right is the piano, for comparison. The numbers are the same in the lesson diagrams below.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
Hand position





Good position is what makes every shape below easier, so set it up before the first chord and check it again whenever a shape feels hard.

Thumb: behind the neck, roughly opposite finger 2, with the pad (not the flat of the thumb) on the wood. It is a rest to push against, not a clamp. Squeezing harder does not make the note clearer.
Fingertips: arch each finger so that the tip comes down on the string from above, just behind the fret wire (the side towards the tuning pegs). Close to the fret needs the least pressure and buzzes least. The middle of the gap between frets needs more pressure and still buzzes.
Fingers: curved, with the knuckle joints bent. A curved finger lets the strings next to it ring.
Wrist and elbow: the wrist stays fairly straight, not bent sharply down or back, and the elbow hangs relaxed instead of pinned to the ribs or lifted. The palm stays a little away from the neck, so there is a gap you could slide a finger through.
Guitar angle: sit with the guitar body against your right thigh and the neck pointing slightly upward. Looking down at the fretboard should not need you to twist your wrist.
Easy because: with the thumb behind the neck, the fingers fall on the frets and need very little effort.
Hard because: it is not how the hand sits when it rests, so for the first weeks it takes thought.
What goes wrong:

The thumb climbs over the top of the neck. That makes the fingers flat, and they mute the strings next to them. (An occasional thumb over the top for a bass note is fine: that is the T in the diagrams.)
Flat fingers: the pad lies on the string and touches its neighbour.
The tip sits in the middle of the fret space, or on the fret wire, and the note buzzes or dies.
The wrist collapses and the palm presses on the neck, which is tiring and slows changes.
Long nails stop the fingertip landing; trim the fretting hand’s nails short.


Practice: place the fingers of a chord one at a time, checking each tip. Pick the strings one by one. If a string buzzes, move that fingertip closer to the fret before pressing harder.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B1 One or two fingers



Em7 takes finger 2. Em uses 2 and 3, and E5 does too, with the higher strings left silent. E7 uses fingers 2 and 1, and Am7 uses 2 and 1.

Easy because: one or two fingers, no stretch, and everything is within two frets.
Hard because: each finger has to press firmly enough to make a clean note, and the strum has to land on the right strings.
What goes wrong:

Fingertips hurt for the first week or two.
A string buzzes when the finger sits back from the fret instead of just behind it.
A fingertip leans on the next string and mutes it.


Practice: hold Em and pick one string at a time, so you can hear that each one rings. Five minutes a day builds calluses.
Unlocks: two-chord strums; G-A1 and G-A2.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B2 Three fingers, close together



Am and E are the same shape, moved over one string; both are fingered 2-3-1. A is 1-2-3, or a small index-finger barre across three strings. D is 1-3-2, with finger 1 on string 3, finger 3 on string 2 and finger 2 on string 1. Dm is the same three fingers in a different order, 2-3-1. D7 is 2-1-3: it is D with the middle finger moved to the other side, so the three fingers sit close together as in D.

Easy because: the fingers stay together and no finger reaches across another.
Hard because: three fingers have to land at once, and in A they crowd into one fret.
What goes wrong:

In D and D7, finger 3 touches the high E string and mutes it.
In A, the fingers collide.
Changing between E and A is slow.


Practice: move from Am to E. Fingers 2 and 3 move across one string together, and finger 1 stays on its fret, moving from string 2 to string 3. Go as slowly as you need to keep the shape.
Unlocks: four-chord loops that use only these chords; Boom-chick.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B3 Reaching: C and G



C is fingered 3-2-1, from string 5 up to string 2. Cadd9 adds finger 4 on string 2 in place of finger 1. G is 2-1-3, or 3-2-4 with finger 4 on both of the top two strings.

Easy because: everything is within the first three frets.
Hard because: in C the fingers spread diagonally over three frets and three strings. In G the fingers are far apart across the neck, and the strings between them have to ring open.
What goes wrong:

In C, finger 1 leans on the high E string.
The thumb rides high over the neck, which shortens the reach. Keep it low, behind the neck.


A note on the B string in G. In G the B string rings open, and it sits right beside the finger on the high E string. That finger, finger 3 or 4, can lean back and touch the B string, and then the string goes dull or silent. The chord is still G, because the B on string 5 still sounds, but it is thinner and the strum sounds uneven. To avoid it, press with the tip and keep the knuckle arched. Damping the B string can also be a choice: let the finger on string 1 lie lightly against it, and the chord loses one of its two B’s and sounds more open. The X in the second diagram marks the B string damped.



Practice: form C, lift all three fingers together, and put them down again without looking. Repeat ten times.
Unlocks: C, Am, F, G, and the pop changes of G-A1 and G-A4.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B4 Four fingers: open 7ths



C7 is C with finger 4 added on string 3. B7 uses all four fingers in a cluster: 2-1-3-4. Fmaj7 is a small shape on the top four strings.

Easy because: each shape is a small change from one you already know.
Hard because: four fingers are down at once, including the weak little finger, and B7 is a cramped cluster.
What goes wrong:

The little finger lands on the pad instead of the tip and mutes the next string.
The change from C to C7 is slow because finger 4 starts far away.


Practice: hold C and tap finger 4 on and off string 3, fret 3 (C to C7 and back), without lifting the other fingers.
Unlocks: Blues shuffle and the open-position 12-bar blues; G-A5.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B5 Reach: a wide stretch



The reach of a hand is how far apart the fingers can press at once. G7 is G with the little finger’s note moved down: finger 3 on string 6 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 1 on string 1 at fret 1. The fingers sit on the two outer strings and on opposite sides of the neck, so the hand opens as wide as it does in any open chord. Compare it with G above it.

Easy because: only three fingers, and the strings between them ring open.
Hard because: the hand has to open across all six strings and three frets at the same time. Small hands feel it most.
What goes wrong:

The thumb creeps up over the neck, which shortens the reach and makes it worse.
Finger 1 reaches the high E string at an angle and touches the string next to it.
The wrist bends sharply to make up the distance. Keep it fairly straight, with the elbow close to the body.


Practice: form G, then change to G7 by lifting finger 3 and putting down finger 1, with fingers 2 and 3 staying where they are. Do not hurry. If the stretch hurts, stop and rest, and do a little each day. The span grows with patience.
Unlocks: the G7 in blues and country changes; G-A5.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B6 Two strings under one finger
text:
G-B6 Two strings under one finger



In Dm7, finger 1 lies flat across strings 2 and 1 at the first fret. In F, fingers 3 and 2 go down beside that small barre.

Easy because: the barre covers only two strings.
Hard because: for the first time, one finger presses two strings, and it has to lie flat rather than on its tip.
What goes wrong:

String 2 is dull because it falls in the crease of the finger. Roll the finger slightly onto its outer edge.
The thumb creeps around the front of the neck.


Practice: put finger 1 alone across strings 2 and 1 and pick each string, until both ring. Then add the other fingers.
Unlocks: the F chord in the pop changes.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B7 Top-string triads



Moveable shapes. A chord shape can slide up and down the neck as long as it has no open string. An open string stays at the same pitch when the hand moves, so the shape would change. If every note is fretted, the whole shape moves together, and the chord’s name changes with the root. Of the shapes above, C xxx010 and Am xxx210 use open strings and stay where they are. C xxx553, C xxx988 and F xxx565 are fully fretted, so they move. The same is true of the barre chords in G-B8 and G-B9.
Three positions of the same triad. A triad has three notes, and any of them can be the lowest. On strings 3, 2 and 1 these are the moveable shapes. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Find the root and you know the chord.






In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is the lowest, and in second inversion the 5th is. The inversions lesson explains the names and how to write them, and pianists can see the same idea in piano inversions. The next step is voice leading: when you change chords, choose the inversion that is nearest, so each note moves a fret or two, or stays put. That is how a few small shapes on the top strings can follow a whole progression, and it is where this lesson leads.

Easy because: only three notes, and at most three fingers.
Hard because: strings 6, 5 and 4 must stay silent. Either pick only the top three strings, or let your fretting fingers rest lightly against the low strings to damp them. Higher up the neck the frets get closer together.
What goes wrong:

The open low strings ring.
The pick catches string 4.
The chord sounds thin. It is meant to: it is one part in a band.


Practice: play the three C shapes in a loop, picking the strings one at a time and then together.
Unlocks: funk and reggae chops; G-A9.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B8 Full barre, E shape



Finger 1 lies across all six strings, and the other fingers make the E shape in front of it: the open E chord, fingered 2-3-4 instead of 1-2-3, moved up so that the barre does the nut’s job. The root is on string 6, under the barre. Here the barre is at fret 5, which makes these A, Am, A7 and Am7.
Start at fret 5, not at F. The usual first barre chord is F, at fret 1, and it is the hardest place to learn it. Near the nut the strings sit highest above the frets and are under the most tension there, so the barre has to press hardest, and the frets are widest, so the hand has to stretch furthest. Around fret 5, closer to the bridge, the strings give more easily and the frets are closer together. Get the shape ringing there, then move it down a fret at a time (A♭, G, G♭) until you reach F. G-B10 does that move on purpose.

Easy because: the shape on top of the barre is E, which you already know.
Hard because: one finger presses six strings, which takes strength, and the hand tires quickly.
What goes wrong:

Strings buzz. Put the barre right behind the fret, and roll the finger so that its firmer outer edge, not the soft pad, meets the strings.
String 2 or 3 falls in a crease of the finger.
The elbow sticks out.

Fm and Fm7 are a little easier, since they need fewer fingers on top of the barre.

Practice: play the barre alone at fret 5, no other fingers, until all six strings ring. Hold for 10 seconds and rest for 20. Or put a capo at fret 5 and play E shapes above it, then do the capo’s job with your finger. When fret 5 is easy, do the same at fret 3, then fret 1.
Unlocks: every major and minor chord; G-A3.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B9 Barre, A shape
The A shape: the open A chord with a barre behind it on string 5, the root under the barre. String 6 is not played. At fret 5 these are D, Dm, Dm7, D7 and Dmaj7; the same shapes at fret 1 are B♭, B♭m and the rest, where the stretch and the pressure are greater for the same reasons as F.




Easy because: the barre covers five strings, not six.
Hard because: three fingers squeeze into one fret space on adjacent strings. Many players flatten finger 3 across strings 4, 3 and 2 instead, which takes practice of its own.
What goes wrong:

When finger 3 lies flat, it mutes string 1.
Finger 1 bends at the knuckle and lets string 1 go dead.


Practice: play Dm at fret 5 with the barre and finger 3 only, then add fingers 4 and 2. Then move it down to Cm (fret 3) and Bm (fret 2).
Unlocks: barre chords anywhere on the neck.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck
text:
G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck



The first three are the E shape (root on string 6) at frets 5, 3 and 1: A, G and F. The last three are the A shape (root on string 5) at frets 5, 3 and 2: Dm, Cm and Bm. They are written in that order, from fret 5 down, so that the move takes you from the easy end of the neck toward the hard one. Name the chord by the note under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape, on string 5 for the A shape.

Easy because: the shape doesn’t change, only the fret.
Hard because: you have to find the new fret without looking, and release just enough pressure to slide without the strings squeaking, all without dropping the beat.
What goes wrong:

A gap between chords.
Landing a fret off.
A scrape on the slide. Ease off the pressure, but don’t lift the fingers.


Practice: slide A down to G and back on a steady beat, then G down to F, using the fret markers at 3, 5, 7 and 9 as landmarks.
Unlocks: I–IV–V and the 12-bar blues in barre chords, in any key.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B11 Barre 7ths: finger independence



A7 and Am7 are the E shape at fret 5 with a finger taken away, so the barre itself plays the 7th on string 4; F7 is the same at fret 1. D7, Dmaj7 and Cmaj7 are the A shape, with the root on string 5. Learn them at fret 5 first, as in G-B8.

Easy because: A7 and Am7 are barres you already know, with a finger taken away.
Hard because: the little finger now has to press at the far end of a barre. Cmaj7 x35453 needs fingers 2, 3 and 4 spread across strings 4, 3 and 2.
What goes wrong:

The little finger collapses and mutes a neighbouring string.
It hasn’t the strength yet.


Practice: hold a barre and tap finger 4 on one string, fret by fret.
Unlocks: Bossa nova in barre positions; G-A6.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B12 Skipped strings: shells



In the shapes with the root on string 6, the underside of finger 1 (on the root) also touches string 5 to mute it. In the shapes with the root on string 5, the finger on the root leans against string 4.

Easy because: three notes, three fingers, and the shapes move anywhere.
Hard because: the skipped string must not sound. It is muted by a finger resting on it without pressing, and the strings above the shape are muted too.
What goes wrong:

The skipped string rings, because the muting finger isn’t touching it.
Playing too hard, which brings the muted strings back.


Practice: strum all six strings with the shape held. Only three notes should come out.
Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, and blues for guitar; G-A8.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3
text:
G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3




Easy because: the shapes are a barre plus at most two notes, and Cm7 is a barre alone.
Hard because: you need barre strength, but string 5 under the barre has to be silent. Lift the barre slightly where it crosses string 5 so it only touches the string.
What goes wrong:

String 5 sounds.
String 1 rings.


Practice: play Cm7 alone, then add finger 3 for C7. Then try fingers 3 and 4 together for Cmaj7.
Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing; G-A11.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings
text:
G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings



Cmaj7 xx2413 is fingered 2-4-1-3. That’s an order the hand hasn’t used before.

Easy because: only four strings, close together.
Hard because: the fingers come in unusual orders, and some shapes combine a small barre, a skipped string and a stretch of three or four frets.
What goes wrong:

Hand ache from long sessions.
Grabbing the wrong finger.
One note losing pressure in the stretch.


Practice: learn one ii–V–I in drop 2, saying the finger numbers out loud. Then move it up two frets.
Unlocks: the Drop 2 voicing, jazz comping, and the altered chords of G-A13.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
Where the two sequences meet








Harmonic order
By hand





G-A1 Open triads
G-B1, G-B2, G-B3
The same chords, sorted by how many fingers they need and how far they reach.


G-A2 Fifths
G-B1
E5 is one of the first shapes.


G-A3 Barre chords
G-B8, G-B9, G-B10
The barre, then the slide.


G-A4 Sus and add9
G-B2, G-B3
One finger moved.


G-A5 Dominant 7th
G-B4, G-B5, G-B11
Open 7ths, then barre 7ths.


G-A6 m7 and maj7
G-B6, G-B11
Small barre, then full barre.


G-A8 Shells
G-B12
The first skipped strings.


G-A9 Top-string triads
G-B7
Physically easy, but they come later in the harmonic order.


G-A10 Drop 2
G-B14
The hardest fingerings.


G-A11 Drop 3
G-B13
A barre with a skipped string.



The orders differ most in the middle. In the harmonic order a shell (G-A8) is simpler than a full 7th chord. Physically it is harder, because the string between has to be muted. A player who knows G-B4 can try shells with the root on string 6 without learning the barre first.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text: The bass and drums are the foundation. If they agree, a band can lose everyone else and still sound like a band. This page is about how they agree. How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
1. The bass follows the kick
The kick drum and the bass are both low and both short at the start of a note. When they land together they sound like one big instrument. When they land apart, the bottom of the band sounds busy and blurred.
Below, the drums play the same pop backbeat throughout. Try each bass line against it. Look at the bass staff and the kick drum (the lowest notes on the drum staff) and see where they line up.



The dotted line is the one the style was written with: the bass plays exactly where the kick plays. The others still work, but they make a different song: roots on every beat is plainer, eighths push harder, root and fifth sounds like country.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
2. The drums choose the feel
Now keep the bass line and change the groove. Each one divides the beat differently or puts the backbeat somewhere else.



Half-time moves the snare from 2 and 4 to 3 only: the chords go by just as fast but the song feels half as fast. Arrangers use it for a breakdown or a big final chorus. Four on the floor puts the kick on every beat, which is why the root-eighths bass now sounds like it’s doubling something.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
section: 3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time
text:
3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time
In jazz the roles change. The ride cymbal carries the time, the kick drum mostly keeps out of the way, and the bass plays a note on every beat. That’s a walking line: the root on beat 1, other notes of the chord and scale in between, and a note on beat 4 that leads into the next chord.
Compare it with the lighter two-feel (half notes) that a band often plays on the melody before walking for the solos, and with plain chord tones.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
4. Latin: the bass anticipates
In son montuno and salsa, the bass plays the tumbao: it doesn’t land on beat 1 at all. The new chord’s root arrives early, on the and of 2 and on 4, and rings over the barline. The clave and congas mark the beat instead.



Switch the congas off, then the drums. With only the bass left, you can hear that it is always a beat ahead of the chord chart.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
5. Try it

In section 1, play the Root eighths line, then switch the drums to Half-time in section 2. Which bass line would you choose for a half-time chorus?
Next: Guitar and keyboards.
