title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
This lesson orders piano voicings by what the hands find hard, starting from a first lesson. Each step adds one task: more notes, a wider span, black keys, two hands at once, leaps, and finally hands that move independently. Each step says what makes the voicing easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Piano chord voicings has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.
How to read the diagrams. Each keyboard shows one voicing. The dots carry the chord tones, R for the root. The staff puts the right hand on the treble clef and the left hand on the bass clef. Press Show finger numbers below to put the fingering in the dots instead of the chord tones. The span is the distance from a hand’s lowest note to its highest, counted in half steps: an octave is 12. Press ▶ to hear a voicing.
Finger numbers on piano and on guitar. The two instruments count differently. On piano the thumb is 1 and the fingers go 2, 3, 4 to the little finger, 5, in both hands. Because the hands are mirror images, the right hand plays a chord from the bottom 1-3-5 and the left hand 5-3-1: the left hand’s little finger takes the lowest note. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1 and the little finger is 4 (the thumb, when it frets a bass note over the neck, is written T). So a “3” means the middle finger to a pianist and the ring finger to a guitarist. The fingerings here are the usual ones; a hand of a different size may choose another.
The two on the left are the piano hands, and the pair on the right is the guitar, for comparison. The left hand is the right hand’s mirror image, so thumbs meet in the middle.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
Hand position





Set this up before the first chord, and check it when a voicing feels clumsy.

Sitting: sit on the front half of the stool, far enough from the keys that your forearms are level, or slope slightly down towards the keys, with your elbows a little in front of your body. A stool too low pushes the wrists up; too high pushes them down.
Fingers: curved, as if holding a ball. The knuckles are arched and the fingertip pad lands on the key. Fingers 2, 3 and 4 are about the same length when curved, so they land together.
Wrist: level with the back of the hand and the forearm, neither drooping below the keys nor lifted above them. The hand can float a little as it moves; it does not rest on the keys.
Thumb: it plays on its side, near the corner of the nail, not flat on its pad. Keep it relaxed and slightly curved, level with the other fingers.
Where on the key: play white keys near the front edge, where they go down most easily. Play a black key in the middle, not on its edge. When a chord mixes the two, the longer fingers (2, 3 and 4) usually take the black keys further back, while the thumb and little finger stay on the white keys at the front.
Easy because: a curved hand has every finger above its key, so the hand needs no tension to hold the position.
Hard because: the fingers tire when starting out, and it is tempting to flatten them to reach.
What goes wrong:

Flat fingers: the pad lies on the key, the hand has less strength, and the fingers play neighbouring keys too.
A dropped wrist, with the knuckles sinking below the hand.
The little finger collapses, and its first joint folds in.
The thumb plays flat on its pad and sticks out, and the hand twists.
Shoulders lifted, with the arms held up from the shoulder instead of hanging.


Practice: put the hand on C, E and G in 1-3-5 with the wrist level. Press each key, and check the wrist and finger tips between presses. Keep the fingers curved when the hand moves to the next chord.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B1 White-key triads, one hand



RH 1-3-5, and LH 5-3-1 an octave lower.

Easy because: each finger has a white key of its own: thumb, middle finger and little finger, with a key left out between each.
Hard because: the three notes have to sound together and evenly. The thumb is strongest, so the bottom note comes out loud and the top note thin.
What goes wrong:

The notes split instead of sounding as one chord.
The top note is lost.


Practice: play a chord, lift the hand, and put it back on the next chord without looking. Keep the wrist level.
Unlocks: P-A1.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B2 Bass note plus triad: two hands
text:
P-B2 Bass note plus triad: two hands




Easy because: the left hand plays one note, so it has one job.
Hard because: the two hands have to land together, and the right hand jumps a 4th or more between chords.
What goes wrong:

The stronger hand arrives first and the other drags.
One hand lifts early.
Watching one hand loses the other.


Practice: play C–Am–F–G in half notes, counting out loud. Close your eyes after one time through.
Unlocks: P-A1; Piano ballad with Long notes.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B3 Inversions: small moves instead of jumps
text:
P-B3 Inversions: small moves instead of jumps



RH 1-3-5 for root position and second inversion; 1-2-5 for first inversion.

Easy because: the hand moves by a step instead of a jump, and there are only two finger patterns.
Hard because: the span grows to 8 or 9 half steps. The open space in a 1-2-5 shape tempts fingers 3 and 4 to fill it.
What goes wrong:

Squeezing with finger 2, which makes the chord uneven.
Choosing the wrong finger for the new note.


Practice: play C in root position, first and second inversion, up the keyboard and back. Then do the same on F and G.
Unlocks: P-A2.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B4 Black keys in triads



All RH 1-3-5.

Easy because: in D, A and E the black key falls under finger 3, the longest finger, which reaches in easily.
Hard because: in B♭ and E♭ the thumb or finger 5 lands on a black key. Those fingers are short and prefer white keys, so the whole hand has to move further in toward the fallboard.
What goes wrong:

The thumb slips off the black key.
Finger 5 flattens.
Reading the key signature becomes a second task.


Practice: play D, A and E first, and B♭ and E♭ after them. Then do the same with the left hand.
Unlocks: every key in the Key menu of the lesson pages, and four-chord loops in all twelve keys.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B5 Two-note guide-tone shapes



RH 1-3 for the 4ths; 1-4 for the tritone.

Easy because: only two notes, so the hand is always relaxed. The span is 5 or 6.
Hard because: the interval changes from chord to chord (4th, tritone, 4th), so the fingers have to adjust each time.
What goes wrong:

Reaching with the arm instead of letting the fingers open.
Losing track of which note is the 3rd.


Practice: hold one pair, then change to the next while keeping the arm still.
Unlocks: P-A7; Charleston comping and blues guide tones. This step comes before four-note 7ths (P-B6) because two notes are easier on the hand. In the harmonic order it comes after them.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B6 Four-note 7ths in one hand



RH 1-2-3-5. The span is 10 or 11.

Easy because: the notes are a 3rd apart, so the fingers fall on every other key.
Hard because: the hand opens to a 7th, and finger 5 has to reach while fingers 2 and 3 stay curved.
What goes wrong:

The thumb lies flat.
Finger 5’s note is weak.
The chord comes out uneven.


Practice: play each chord, then its closest inversion (as in P-A6), and compare how the hand feels. If the hand aches, leave out the top note.
Unlocks: P-A5 and P-A6; the 7th chords in blues for piano.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B7 Shells in the left hand
text:
P-B7 Shells in the left hand



LH 5-3-1 for 1–3–7. For 1–7–3 (span 16), LH 5-1 and the right thumb on the top note.

Easy because: three notes in one hand, about the same span as P-B6.
Hard because: the left hand is usually the weaker one, and mistakes are easy to hear down low. The 1–7–3 order is a 10th wide, too wide for most hands to play alone.
What goes wrong:

The thumb hangs over the edge of the key.
The middle note doesn’t sound.


Practice: play the three shells slowly and listen for every note.
Unlocks: P-A8; solo piano.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B8 Rootless voicings: four notes in the left hand
text:
P-B8 Rootless voicings: four notes in the left hand



LH 5-3-2-1 throughout. The span is 9 to 11.

Easy because: the A and B forms alternate, so the hand moves by a step or less. The B forms are the narrowest.
Hard because: four fingers sound at once in the weaker hand, and you need the forms in every key. Black keys fall under different fingers in each key.
What goes wrong:

Forgetting which form comes next.
One note missing.


Practice: learn the chain in F first, which sits well under the left hand, and then the chain in C. Then add a bass line in the right hand.
Unlocks: P-A9; Jazz ballad, Bossa nova, Boogaloo.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B9 Leaps: bass note, then chord
text:
P-B9 Leaps: bass note, then chord



The left hand alone, as in stride or boom-chick: a low bass note, then a chord about an octave and a half higher.

Easy because: the shapes are triads you already know.
Hard because: the hand jumps 1½ octaves on the beat. The eyes want to follow the hand, and the rhythm slips.
What goes wrong:

The chord is late or too loud because the hand crashes onto it.
Looking down and losing the place.


Practice: left hand only, bass–chord–bass–chord, with a metronome at 60. Move in an arc and shape the chord in the air before it lands. Close your eyes once the landing is reliable.
Unlocks: stride and boom-chick left hands; country and folk comping.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B10 Stacked 4ths: one shape that moves
text:
P-B10 Stacked 4ths: one shape that moves



RH 1-3-5, span 10. For the So What chord, LH 5-2-1 and RH 1-3.

Easy because: every interval is the same, so there is one hand shape.
Hard because: each stack of 4ths lands on a different mix of black and white keys, so the same shape feels different in each place.
What goes wrong:

The hand follows the key colours and loses the shape.


Practice: slide the stack of 4ths up the white keys from D to D, one hand at a time, noticing which positions feel best.
Unlocks: P-A12; modal jazz.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B11 Wide spans: octaves, 9ths and 10ths



LH 5-1 for the octave, the 9th and the 10th. LH 5-2-1, rolled, for C–G–E.

Easy because: most adult hands can play an octave, and a 9th is possible with a firm wrist.
Hard because: a 10th is beyond most hands played as one chord.
What goes wrong:

Forcing the stretch. Roll the chord from the bottom instead, and never play through pain.


Practice: roll C–G–E slowly and listen for the three notes blending into one sound. Then play it with the pedal.
Unlocks: P-A11; Arpeggio low and high, Ballad: syncopated, Piano ballad.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B12 Independence: a held shell, a moving right hand
text:
P-B12 Independence: a held shell, a moving right hand



LH 5-3-1, RH 1-3-5.

Easy because: the left hand holds still, and the right hand plays a plain triad.
Hard because: the hands play different rhythms, three notes each, and each hand plays a different chord.
What goes wrong:

Both hands playing on the same beat.
The black keys in the right-hand triad (C♯, F♯) being missed.


Practice: hold the shell on beat 1 and play the right-hand triad on the “and” of 2. Then on the “and” of 4. Tap your foot on the beat.
Unlocks: P-A13; Charleston, Reverse Charleston, Boogaloo stabs and Son montuno.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
Where the two sequences meet








By hand
Harmonic order





P-B1, P-B2
P-A1
The same notes: the triad, then both hands.


P-B3
P-A2
Inversions are a harmonic choice and a hand-size choice.


P-B2
P-A4
A bass line under still triads needs P-B2’s coordination.


P-B5
P-A7
Two-note shapes are easier on the hand than four-note ones.


P-B6
P-A5, P-A6
Four notes in one hand.


P-B7
P-A8
The same step.


P-B8
P-A9
The same step.


P-B9, P-B11
P-A10, P-A11
Wide voicings need leaps and stretches.


P-B10
P-A12

P-B12
P-A13

P-B4
every step

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
text:
This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
text:
The pattern
Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.
It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
section: Step 1: Strum: downstrokes on the beat
text:
Step 1: Strum: downstrokes on the beat
Start with something simpler. One ringing downstroke on every beat. The first strum to learn, and the usual one for a slow song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
text:
Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
text:
Step 3: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The thumb plays every beat: root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string. On 2 and 4 a finger pinches a treble string together with the thumb, and on the and after it plays the string below. Get the thumb going alone first; it must not stop when the fingers join.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 100 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
section: Step 5: Two chords in a bar
text:
Step 5: Two chords in a bar
Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
text:
Step 6: In 3/4
The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

title: Drum groove: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
text:
The pattern
Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
It belongs in Swing and Jazz ballad. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
text:
Step 1: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1), slowly
How to play it. Right hand on the ride cymbal on every beat; left foot closes the hi-hat on 2 and 4. Nothing else. This is the pulse every jazz drummer plays on top of.

All the accompaniment patterns · Bass lines

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
text:
The pattern
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad and Boogaloo. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
text:
Step 2: Roots on every beat
The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
section: Step 3: Chord tones (learning to walk), slowly
text:
Step 3: Chord tones (learning to walk), slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, one to a beat, the same shape every bar. On a minor seventh chord the 3rd is three frets above the root; on a dominant or major chord, four. Say the chord tones as you play them.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: accented eighths
text:
The pattern
The basic rock beat with the hi-hat leaning on the beats and the off-beats played lightly (shoulder of the stick on the beat, tip on the off-beat). Written with an accent over each beat.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock, Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Dance pop and Boogaloo. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: accented eighths
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: accented eighths
text:
Step 2: Hi-hat: accented eighths, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

text:

Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
text:
Step 2: Dotted (1, and of 2, 3)
The root on beat 1, again on the and of 2 and on beat 3, the same rhythm as the kick drum. Every second bar ends with an eighth note that leads into the next chord.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: 3+3+2 (tresillo)

How to play it. Count eight eighth notes and play on 1, 4 and 7: ONE two three FOUR five six SEVEN eight. That is beat 1, the and of 2 and beat 4. The first two notes are the root, the last the fifth. It is the dotted line with its third note moved later.

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:

A two-bar figure in 3/4 (one bar of 6/4): root, fifth, octave in quarter notes, then the third above that octave held for two beats and the fifth to lead back.

title: Bass line: Footprints: waltz ostinato
text:

Start with something simpler. The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.

title: Bass line: Footprints: waltz ostinato
text:
Step 2: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Jazz time
text:
The pattern
Follows the Feel menu. Swing: the ride pattern, hi-hat foot on 2 and 4, a feathered kick and a little snare. Straight eighths: eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, cross-stick on 2 and 4.
It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad and Boogaloo. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Jazz time
text:
Step 1: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Jazz time
text:
Step 2: Ride pattern (learning swing, 2)
The swing ride pattern and nothing else: the cymbal on every beat with a skip note before 3 and before 1 (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a), and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
The pattern
A short chord on the and of every beat and never on the beat: the ska and calypso afterbeat.
It belongs in Calypso, Ska / reggae and Freylekhs / polka. Here it is in the ska / reggae style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 1: Quarter-note chords
Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 3: Every off-beat, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Never on the beat: a short chord on every and. Count 1-AND-2-AND aloud, tap the beat with your foot and play only with the and. On guitar it is a chop, the chord choked right after it sounds.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band
text:
Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 80 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 5: On the guitar
The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

text:

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
The pattern
The boogaloo riff, but about half the four-bar phrases end with a bar of walking quarter notes that leads into the next phrase, and now and then two bars.
It belongs in Boogaloo. Here it is in the boogaloo style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
Step 1: Boogaloo riff
Start with something simpler. A repeated straight-eighths figure: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, then a fifth and flat seventh on beat 4 leading back to the root. The kind of line under Watermelon Man. In 6/8 and 12/8 it becomes a shuffle: each beat played long-short, climbing root, 3rd, 5th, 6th.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
Step 2: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
Step 3: Walking
One note on every beat (four quarter notes in 4/4, three in 3/4, dotted quarters in 12/8): the root on beat 1 when the chord changes, chord tones and scale steps in between, and an approach note on beat 4 that leads into the next bar.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
section: Step 4: Boogaloo riff, walking at times, slowly
text:
Step 4: Boogaloo riff, walking at times, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Riff most of the time; at the end of some four-bar phrases, walk one bar of quarter notes into the next phrase. The skill is the switch: feel where the phrase ends and land on the next root exactly on 1.

The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s bass off and take the part yourself.

text:

title: Bass line: Root eighths
text:
The pattern
The root on every eighth note, the beats a little louder: the rock bass line under With or Without You and a thousand others.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock and Emo / pop-punk. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Root eighths
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Root eighths
text:
Step 2: Roots on every beat
The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Root eighths
text:
Step 3: Root eighths, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Eight even roots a bar, a little heavier on the beats. On bass, alternate two fingers or use downstrokes with a pick, and mute with the fretting hand between notes so they do not blur. Lock with the kick drum: the beats are where it lands.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: open off-beats
text:
The pattern
Four on the floor: kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4, a closed hi-hat on each beat and an open one on every off-beat (the stick closing it each time). The Four on the floor groove without the clap.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock, Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Dance pop and Boogaloo. Here it is in the dance pop style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: open off-beats
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: open off-beats
text:
Step 2: Hi-hat: off-beats only
The closed hi-hat plays only the ands, 1-and 2-and 3-and 4-and. Kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4. In 3/4: kick on 1 and 2, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

text:

How to play it. Four on the floor: kick every beat, snare on 2 and 4, a closed hat on each beat and an open one on every and. The foot opens and closes in eighths.

title: Conga part: Tumbao, two drums
text:
The pattern
The tumbao in the first bar. In the second, the right hand plays two open tones on the lower drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel; then the left-hand toe and the two open tones of beat 4 on the higher drum. The low drum belongs to the bar with three clave notes, which is the second bar of the 2-3 clave.
It belongs in Son montuno, Cha-cha and Boogaloo. Here it is in the son montuno style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Conga part: Tumbao, two drums
text:
Step 1: Tumbao
Start with something simpler. The basic conga part, on one drum with the hands alternating: left-hand heel on 1, left-hand toe on the and of 1, a right-hand slap on 2, left toe on the and of 2, left heel on 3, left toe on the and of 3, then two right-hand open tones on 4 and the and of 4. Heel and toe are quiet; slap and open tones carry.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
The pattern
The Cuban bass line that never plays beat 1: the fifth on the and of 2, then on beat 4 the root of the NEXT bar’s chord, held over the barline.
It belongs in Son montuno and Cha-cha. Here it is in the son montuno style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
Step 1: Root and fifth
Start with something simpler. The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
Step 2: Bossa nova
Root on 1 and fifth on 3, each one set up by an eighth note just before it: the fifth on the and of 2, the next chord’s root on the and of 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Tumbao

Sixteen eighth notes over two bars grouped 3+3+3+3+2+2. First bar (shown): 1, the and of 2, 4. Second bar: the and of 1, 3, 4. Beautiful Day.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock and Dance pop. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Groups: 3+3+3+3+2+2
text:
Step 1: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
Start with something simpler. Three held chords in a bar of eight eighth notes, grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Clocks, Shape of You, Eye of the Tiger.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Groups: 3+3+3+3+2+2
text:
Step 2: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
The chords play the 3-2 son clave over two bars. First bar (shown): 1, the and of 2, 4. Second bar: 2 and 3. Faith, Desire, I Want Candy.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Groups: 3+3+3+3+2+2
text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Sixteen eighths over two bars grouped 3+3+3+3+2+2. Count the groups, not the beats: one-two-three, one-two-three, … one-two, one-two. Play a chord on the first of each group.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
The pattern
The backbeat at half speed: kick on 1 and the and of 2, one snare on beat 3.
It belongs in Piano ballad, Straight-eighth rock and Emo / pop-punk. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
Step 2: Rock backbeat
Eighths on the cymbal and a full snare on 2 and 4. The kick changes over four bars: 1, 3 and the and of 3; then 1, the and of 2 and 3; the last bar adds a pickup on the and of 4. Sixteenth-note fills.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

text:

How to play it. The backbeat at half speed: kick on 1 and the and of 2, a single snare on beat 3. The chords go as fast, the song feels slower.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: Travis pattern
text:
The pattern
The same thumb on every beat: root, inner string, alternate bass, inner string. The fingers pinch with it on beat 1, then play between the thumb’s notes: the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4.
It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: Travis pattern
text:
Step 1: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
Start with something simpler. Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

How to play it. The same thumb on every beat. The fingers pinch with the thumb on beat 1, then play in between the thumb notes: the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4. Thumb and fingers alternate like two players.

title: Conga part: Steady congas
text:
The pattern
A quiet part that suits any music: open tones on 4 and the and of 4, a slap on 2, and a light heel and toe between. In 3/4: heel toe on 1, slap toe on 2, two open tones on 3. In 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8: heel, toe, toe on each beat, the slap on beat 2 and two open tones to finish the bar.
It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad, Boogaloo, Bossa nova, Son montuno, Cha-cha, Tango, Calypso, Ska / reggae, Reggaeton, Straight-eighth rock, Emo / pop-punk, Acoustic strum, Piano ballad, Dance pop, Motown / soul, 12/8 doo-wop, Country train beat, Boom-chick, Freylekhs / polka, John Prine Fingerpicking, Waltz (in one), Hymn (four parts) and Folk carol. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
This lesson is for a pianist who plays pop and rock chords and hasn’t yet met jazz voicings. Its thirteen steps each change one thing from the step before: how many notes, which chord tones, or where they sit. Piano voicings by hand has the same chords in the order the hands find them easy.
How to read the diagrams. Each keyboard shows one voicing. The dots carry the chord tones, counted up from the root: R, 3, 5, ♭7, 9 and so on. The root is a filled square. The staff underneath puts the right hand on the treble clef and the left hand on the bass clef. Press ▶ to hear a voicing.
Fingers are numbered 1 (thumb) to 5 (little finger), listed from the lowest note up. Middle C is C4.
Each step has an ID, such as P-A3, that other lessons use to point back here. The chords stay the same throughout: C, Am, F and G for pop, and Dm7, G7, Cmaj7 for the ii–V–I. That way a step here can be played with the same notes as its partner in the physical order.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A1 Root-position triads over a bass root
text:
P-A1 Root-position triads over a bass root
A triad is root, 3rd and 5th. The 3rd decides major or minor, and the 5th gives weight. The left hand names the chord with its root, and the right hand fills it in. This is the sound of most pop piano, and every later step rearranges these notes or adds to them.



Fingering: LH 5 on the root. RH 1-3-5.
Practice: play the four chords on a steady beat. Notice that the right hand jumps every time. The next step gets rid of the jumps.
Unlocks: Piano ballad with Long notes or Quarter-note chords.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A2 Inversions and smooth voice leading
text:
P-A2 Inversions and smooth voice leading
Inverting a triad moves its lowest note to the top, so the hand can stay in one place. Here the note C stays put through the first three chords: it is the root of C, the 3rd of Am and the 5th of F. The other notes move by a step at most. This is voice leading: each note travels as little as it can, and the chords sound connected. The bass root still names the chord.



Fingering: RH root position 1-3-5, first inversion (3rd at the bottom) 1-2-5, second inversion (5th at the bottom) 1-3-5.
Practice: loop the four chords with your eyes closed after the first time round. The hand moves no more than a finger’s width. Then play the loop in F and in G.
Unlocks: Ballad: rocking, Ballad: half-broken, Arpeggio up and down.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A3 Sus and add9
Sus2 and sus4 replace the 3rd with the 2nd or the 4th. The chord is then neither major nor minor, and it wants to settle. Add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 9th, the 2nd an octave up, for the shimmering open sound of pop ballads. Put the 9th above the 3rd, not right next to the root, or it rubs.



Fingering: sus2 1-2-5; sus4 1-4-5; Cadd9 (3–5–9) 1-2-5.
Practice: play Gsus4 and then G. One finger moves, as C falls to B. Then go from C to Cadd9.
Unlocks: Piano ballad, Arpeggio low and high; the Cadd9 bars of pop changes for piano.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A4 Slash chords: a moving bass under still triads
text:
P-A4 Slash chords: a moving bass under still triads
The two hands now do separate jobs. The left hand walks the bass line C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G, and the right hand holds triads that barely move. A triad over a bass note other than its root makes a new chord with a new name. F over G, the last chord here, is the first jazz-flavoured sound in the sequence: G with ♭7, 9 and 11. P-A13 comes back to the idea.



Practice: play only the bass line, then only the right hand, then both together, slowly. Keep the right hand soft and let the bass line sing.
Unlocks: the passing chords in pop changes; Motown / soul.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A5 Seventh chords in close position
text:
P-A5 Seventh chords in close position
A seventh chord stacks one more 3rd on the triad, and the kind of 7th sets the colour. A major 7th (B in Cmaj7) is bright and floating. A ♭7 (B♭ in C7) is bluesy and restless. In a minor chord the ♭7 is soft. A dominant 7th has a tritone between its 3rd and its 7th (B and F in G7), which wants to resolve.



Fingering: RH 1-2-3-5.
Practice: play C, Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7, changing one finger at a time, and put each colour into words.
Unlocks: Medium swing with Quarter-note chords; the 7th chords in blues for piano.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A6 Inverted 7ths: the ii–V–I
Choose each inversion so that the hand barely moves. From Dm7 to G7, F and D stay, A falls to G and C falls to B. From G7 to Cmaj7, F falls to E, D falls to C, and G and B stay. Each time, the 7th of one chord falls a step to the 3rd of the next: C to B, then F to E. That falling 7th is the engine of jazz harmony.



Fingering: RH 1-2-3-5 for each.
Practice: loop the three chords in time and sing the top line, D–D–C. Then move to F (Gm7, C7, Fmaj7) and B♭.
Unlocks: Medium swing, Charleston, and ii–V–I turnarounds.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A7 Guide tones: 3rd and 7th
The 3rd and the 7th are the only tones that tell major from minor and dominant from major 7th, so two notes can stand for the whole chord. The root belongs to the bass, and the 5th adds little. Follow the lines: C falls to B while F holds, then F falls to E while B holds. Guide tones goes further.



Fingering: RH 1-3 for a 4th; 1-4 for the tritone.
Practice: play the ii–V–I in guide tones, then sing each line. Add a top note of your own, any chord tone.
Unlocks: Charleston and Reverse Charleston without clutter; blues for piano.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A8 Shells: 1–3–7 and 1–7–3
A shell is root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone, which leaves the right hand free for a melody. In 1–3–7 order the shape spans a 7th and sits comfortably under one hand. In 1–7–3 order the 3rd is on top, a 10th above the root. That sounds more open, and it is the classic jazz left hand, but most hands need the right thumb to take the 3rd. The root is in the shell because, with no bass player, someone has to play it.



Fingering: LH 5-3-1 for 1–3–7. For 1–7–3, LH 5-1 on root and 7th, and RH 1 on the 3rd.
Practice: play the ii–V–I in the left hand only, then add a melody in the right. Alternate 1–3–7 and 1–7–3 (Dm7 1–3–7, G7 1–7–3, Cmaj7 1–3–7) so the hand hardly moves.
Unlocks: solo piano and comping without a bass; blues for piano.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A9 Rootless voicings, A and B
text:
P-A9 Rootless voicings, A and B
With a bass player covering the root, the left hand plays the 3rd, the 7th and two colour tones: the 9th, plus the 13th on a dominant. Form A has the 3rd at the bottom and form B has the 7th at the bottom. Alternate them and each chord is only a step from the last. This has been the left-hand sound of jazz piano since the 1950s, and the site’s jazz styles use it. The Chord Library calls these Rootless A/B.



Fingering: LH 5-3-2-1 for A forms; 5-3-2-1 or 5-4-2-1 for B forms.
Practice: play the first chain (A–B–A) on a metronome, with the bass line D, G, C in the right hand. Then learn the chain that starts on B.
Unlocks: Jazz ballad, Medium swing with Charleston, Bossa nova, and Boogaloo.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A10 Drop 2
Take a four-note chord in close position and drop its second-highest note an octave. Dm7 in close position is D–F–A–C. The second note from the top is A, which drops to A3. The chord now spreads over an octave and a half, with the root back in the middle, and it sounds fuller and more orchestral. Put a melody note on top of a close chord, drop the second voice, and you have harmonised the melody.



Fingering: LH 2-1, RH 1-4 or 1-5.
Practice: take the first phrase of a melody you know. Play each melody note as the top of a close chord, then drop the second voice. Drop 3, where the third voice from the top drops, is the same idea one voice lower.
Unlocks: block-chord melody (George Shearing, Bill Evans), and Long notes under a singer.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A11 Spread voicings: low 5th, upper triad
text:
P-A11 Spread voicings: low 5th, upper triad
An open 5th low in the left hand is the cleanest bass a piano has, because it stays out of the muddy middle register. Above it, the right hand plays a triad built from the 3rd, 7th and 9th. For Cmaj9 that is E–B–D, a little like an Em triad over C, which is why a rich chord can feel simple to play. The site has no voicing style for spread voicings yet.



Fingering: LH 5-1, RH 1-3-5 (or 1-4-5 where the lower gap is wide).
Practice: hold the low 5th with the pedal, then place the right hand above it. Learn the low 5th as one shape.
Unlocks: Arpeggio low and high, Ballad: syncopated, Jazz ballad, and gospel and singer-songwriter ballads.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A12 Quartal voicings
Stacking 4ths leaves no 3rd in the chord, so it is neither major nor minor. It sounds open, modern and modal. The best-known example is the “So What” voicing from Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue (1959): three 4ths and a major 3rd on top. Every interval in a stack of 4ths is the same, so the shape can slide up and down and keep its sound. The site has no quartal voicing style yet.



Fingering: LH 5-2-1 with RH 1-3 for the So What chord; RH 1-3-5 for a three-note stack.
Practice: play the So What chord, then the same shape a half step higher, and back. Then slide a three-note stack up the white keys from D.
Unlocks: modal jazz and Bossa nova.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A13 Upper-structure triads
The left hand plays a shell that fixes the chord’s name and type. The right hand plays a plain major triad built from the extensions above it. D major over a C shell gives Cmaj7 with a 9th, a ♯11 and a 13th. A major over a G7 shell is the same colour on a dominant. This is P-A4’s idea again: a triad over a different bass note. The site has no voicing style for upper structures yet.



Fingering: LH 5-3-1, RH 1-3-5.
Practice: play G7 as a shell, then place the A triad on top. Then try the D♭ triad and hear how strongly it pulls to C.
Unlocks: ballad endings, tags and turnarounds; reharmonising.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
Where to go next

Piano voicings by hand has the same chords in physical order.
Guitar chord shapes has the same ideas on the guitar.
The Chord Library, set to Keyboard, has every close, shell, rootless and drop voicing of every chord.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text: A triad has three notes: the root, the 3rd and the 5th. You can stack them in any order. The note you put lowest decides which inversion you are playing. The chord keeps its name, because the three notes are the same. Only the arrangement changes, and with it the sound and the way the hand moves. This lesson covers major and minor triads: how to build the three positions, what they are called, and how to write them. Press ▶ to hear a shape.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
section: Root position, first inversion, second inversion
text:
Root position, first inversion, second inversion
In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is lowest. In second inversion the 5th is lowest. To invert a chord, take the lowest note and move it to the top, an octave higher. Do it once for first inversion and twice for second inversion. Do it a third time and you are back in root position, an octave up.
Finger numbers. Press Show finger numbers to see the fingering in the dots instead of the chord tones. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, in both hands, so the right hand plays a root-position triad 1-3-5 and the left hand 5-3-1. On guitar the index finger is 1 and the little finger 4. Notice that on piano the inversions change the fingering (first inversion in the right hand is 1-2-5), because the wide gap moves.

















Look at the dots. In the first chord the root is on the bottom. In the second the 3rd is on the bottom and the root has moved to the top. In the third the 5th is on the bottom. The same three letters, C, E and G, are in all of them.
Telling them apart on the page. Look at the lowest note and ask what it is for the chord. If it is the root, the chord is in root position. A 3rd means first inversion, and a 5th means second inversion. The way the notes sit also gives a clue. In root position the notes are stacked in 3rds (C to E to G). In first inversion the top two notes are a 4th apart (G to C). In second inversion the bottom two notes are a 4th apart (G to C).
Practice: play C in root position, then first inversion, then second inversion, then root position an octave higher. Say the name of the lowest note each time. Repeat on F and G.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Minor triads
Minor triads invert in the same way. The only difference is that the 3rd is a half step lower.



The intervals inside the chord are the thing that changes. A major triad is a major 3rd with a minor 3rd on top; a minor triad is the reverse. So root-position Am (A C E) has a minor 3rd (A to C) and then a major 3rd (C to E). First inversion (C E A) has a major 3rd and then a 4th. Second inversion (E A C) has a 4th and then a minor 3rd. Whatever the quality, a 4th sits at the top of first inversion and at the bottom of second inversion, and that 4th is how you spot an inversion by eye.
Practice: play Am in the three positions, then C and Am one after the other in first inversion. Notice that the two chords share two notes, and only one finger moves.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Names: figured bass
Classical musicians have a shorthand for the inversions that goes back to the 1600s. It is called figured bass, and it labels the chord by the intervals above the lowest note. You will still see it in theory books and in Roman-numeral analysis.

The 6 stands for the interval of a 6th above the bass note. In first inversion of C, the bass is E and the other notes are G (a 3rd up) and C (a 6th up). In second inversion, the bass is G, with C above it (a 4th up) and E (a 6th up). The figure for first inversion is simply ⁶, because the 3rd is understood and left unwritten. The second inversion needs both numbers, ⁶₄.
With Roman numerals the figures go beside the numeral: I is a tonic triad in root position, I⁶ is in first inversion, and I⁶₄ is in second inversion. In C major, I⁶ is C/E and I⁶₄ is C/G.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Names: slash chords
Pop, rock and jazz players use a simpler system. They write the chord, a slash, and then the bass note. C/E means a C chord with E in the bass: first inversion. C/G means a C chord with G in the bass: second inversion. A plain C means the root is in the bass, although the player decides which notes go above.

Say it as “C over E”. The note after the slash is always the bass. A slash chord can also have a bass note that isn’t in the chord at all, such as C/D. That is not an inversion, and we leave it for another lesson. Chart writers use the slash form because it tells the bassist what to play, and the chord symbol alone does not.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Inversions on the guitar
On the guitar an inversion is a different set of strings and frets, and the shape moves anywhere on the neck if it has no open string. These are on strings 3, 2 and 1. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Compare the F shapes with the C shapes on the piano above.






The numbers under each diagram are the frets from the low E string to the high E string, and x is a string you don’t play. Move any of these along the neck and the root moves with it. The F shapes become G shapes two frets higher. More about moveable shapes is in Guitar chord shapes by hand.
Practice: play the three F shapes in order, then slide each up two frets and name the new chord.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Why use them: voice leading
Without inversions, every chord change makes the hand jump. With them you can choose the position of each chord so that the notes move as little as possible, and some notes stay where they are. This is voice leading. It makes a progression sound smooth and connected, and it is much easier on the hand. For example, going from C to Am to F, the top note C stays put in all three chords, as the root, the 3rd and the 5th, while the other notes move a step at most. That example is worked out in piano chord voicings, and Piano voicings by hand shows how it feels under the fingers.
Practice: play C, then F in second inversion (F/C), then C again. The C stays where it is, and the other two notes each move a step. Then play C, F in root position, C and feel how much farther the hand travels.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
An arrangement is a set of decisions about who plays what, where, and when they keep quiet. This series takes the site’s backing band apart one player at a time. Each example below is the band itself: press ▶ Play, then use the buttons under Who plays to switch players in and out while it runs. Under the buttons, the last four bars the band played are written out, one staff per player, so you can see what you are hearing.
The four lessons:

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
1. Four jobs
A rhythm section shares out four jobs:

Time. The drums say where the beat is and how it is divided: straight or swung, busy or calm. Everyone else leans on them.
The bottom. The bass says which chord this is by playing its root, mostly on the strong beats, and it ties the harmony to the drums’ rhythm.
The harmony and the inner rhythm. Guitar and keyboards fill the middle: the rest of the chord, played in a pattern that sits between the drums’ hits.
The melody. A singer or soloist. The rhythm section’s job is to leave room for it.

A band sounds good when those jobs don’t step on each other. Most of arranging is deciding who doesn’t play.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
section: 2. Build it up one player at a time
text:
2. Build it up one player at a time
Start with only the drums, then add the bass, then the guitar. Listen for what each player adds. The drums alone have rhythm but no key. The bass adds the chord changes. The guitar adds the colour of each chord (major or minor) and fills the gaps in the rhythm.



Now take one away at a time. Without the bass, the band suddenly sounds thin and high. Without the drums, the guitar and bass have to keep time themselves and they sound loose. Without the guitar, the bass and drums still hold the song up: that’s why they are called the foundation.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
section: 3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house
text:
3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house
Look at the written parts while the band plays. The bass sits low, under the bass clef. The guitar sits in the middle. The drums aren’t pitched, but the kick is low, the snare is in the middle and the cymbals are high.
When two players share a register they blur together. The easiest fix is to move one of them. Here the piano comps in a ballad, then plays the same notes an octave higher, then an octave lower. Hear how the low one gets in the way of the bass and muddies the chords, and how the high one leaves the middle empty for a singer.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
4. Same chords, three bands
A style is a set of these decisions made together. These three play the same four chords. Switch players off in each to hear how the jobs are shared out differently.
Rock: bass on every eighth note, guitar strumming eighths, a backbeat on 2 and 4. Everyone plays the same grid, so it drives.



Reggae: the guitar plays only on the off-beats and the drums leave beat 1 empty. The bass carries the downbeat by itself. Take the bass out and the beat is gone.



Swing: the bass walks a note on every beat, the ride cymbal plays the swung pattern, and the piano plays short chords now and then, mostly off the beat. The piano part changes every time round: in jazz the comping is a conversation, not a fixed pattern.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
5. Try it

In each example, find the one player you could lose with the least damage. That player is the first to drop out when a singer comes in.
Turn on only bass and drums in the reggae example, then only guitar and drums. Which pair still sounds like reggae?
Next: Bass and drums.



  Tempo 
  ■ Stop

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text: A dot adds half the value of the note again. A dotted half note (normally two beats) becomes three beats. A dotted quarter becomes one-and-a-half.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text:
The dotted-quarter-plus-eighth figure
The classic figure is a dotted quarter followed by an eighth — the “long- short” pattern you hear at the start of countless tunes. It’s tricky because the eighth note lands on the and of beat two, not on a beat.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text:
Practice steps

Chant a steady “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &”.
Hold the dotted quarter across “1 & 2”, then say the eighth on “&”.
Try it slowly, then bring it up to tempo.

Then go to Practice → Tunes and find a tune that uses this figure. Play it a few times and listen for the long-short.






Tip



Notice this lesson tracks separately from the quarter-note lesson — the report will show your time on each page, not just “lessons” as a lump.

title: Motown / soul
text: Open the Motown / soul style in the Backing Track

title: Motown / soul
text:
What it is
The 1960s Detroit sound of Motown Records: a snare (often with a tambourine) hitting every beat, a busy electric bass, guitars chopping chords, and a song built for radio and dancing.

title: Motown / soul
text:
A little history
Berry Gordy started Motown in Detroit in 1959. Its records were cut by a house band later known as the Funk Brothers: drummer Benny Benjamin, bassist James Jamerson, pianist Earl Van Dyke, and others, playing in Studio A (“the Snakepit”). The songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote the mid-’60s run of hits for the Supremes and the Four Tops, many on a stomping four-beat snare. Jamerson’s bass lines, played with one finger on a Fender Precision, moved far more than any pattern can show. The band played uncredited until the film Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002).

title: Motown / soul
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Motown: root, fifth, octave, a stand-in for Jamerson’s lines.
Comping: the two-bar rhythm of You Can’t Hurry Love. Drums: snare on every beat.

title: Piano ballad

title: Piano ballad
text:
What it is
The slow pop or rock song led from the piano: octaves in the left hand, the chord broken or rocked in the right (often in first inversion, so the top moves smoothly), and a band that comes in half-time, with the backbeat on beat 3.

title: Piano ballad
text:
A little history
The piano was the home instrument of popular song long before rock: Tin Pan Alley sold sheet music for it. In the 1970s singer-songwriters at the piano (Carole King’s Tapestry, 1971; Elton John; Billy Joel) made the piano ballad a staple of rock. The 1980s power ballad put it under big drums, and from the 2000s Coldplay, Alicia Keys and Adele (Someone Like You, 2011, over nothing but broken piano chords) kept it at the top of the charts.

title: Piano ballad
text:
The band’s version

Comping: three right-hand patterns (rocking, half-broken, syncopated) in four-bar spans.
Bass and drums: half time; a quiet kick and a cross-stick on 3. The hi-hat sits low.

title: Acoustic strum
text:
What it is
The singer-songwriter’s band: a steel-string acoustic guitar strumming a syncopated pattern (down, down-up, up-down-up), a bass and kick together on 1, the and of 2, and 3, and a light backbeat.

title: Acoustic strum
text:
A little history
The steel-string guitar became a popular accompanying instrument through country and blues players in the 1920s-30s and the folk revival of the 1950s-60s (Woody Guthrie, then Bob Dylan, Joan Baez). From the late 1960s singer-songwriters (James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, Cat Stevens) put a band around the strummed guitar. The 1990s Britpop and “unplugged” years (Oasis’s Wonderwall) and the 2000s-2010s folk-pop of Jason Mraz, Mumford & Sons and Ed Sheeran kept it among the most common sounds in pop.

title: Acoustic strum
text:

Bass: Dotted (1, and of 2, 3), with the kick. Comping: a campfire strum. Drums: light.

title: Boom-chick
text: Open the Boom-chick style in the Backing Track

title: Boom-chick
text:
What it is
The oldest accompaniment in popular music: a bass note on the strong beats and a chord on the weak ones. In 2/4 or 4/4 it is boom-chick; in 3/4 it is oom-pah-pah.

title: Boom-chick
text:
A little history
Brass bands and dance orchestras of the 1800s split the beat between the tuba (or bass) and the horns or second violins: marches, polkas and waltzes all run on it, and so does the stride and ragtime piano left hand (bass note, chord, bass note, chord). Guitarists in American old-time and country music used the same idea, a thumbed bass on the beat and a strum after it: Maybelle Carter’s guitar with the Carter Family from 1927, and later the folk revival. Sing-along songs from campfire to music hall still use it.

title: Boom-chick
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: oompah. Drums: boom-chick.

title: Ska / reggae
text: Open the Ska / reggae style in the Backing Track

title: Ska / reggae
text:
What it is
Jamaican popular music since about 1960: guitar and keyboard chords on the off-beats (the skank), a bass that carries the melody of the groove, and, in reggae, a one-drop drum beat with nothing on beat 1 and the kick and snare (or rim) together on beat 3.

title: Ska / reggae
text:
A little history
Ska (c. 1960-66) came from Jamaican musicians playing American R&B for sound systems and stressing the off-beat; studio bands such as the Skatalites played it fast with horns. Around 1966 the tempo slowed into rocksteady, with the bass more prominent (Alton Ellis, the Paragons). By 1968 the beat had changed again into reggae: Toots and the Maytals’ Do the Reggay (1968) is one of the first records to use the word. Drummer Carlton Barrett of Bob Marley’s Wailers made the one-drop the standard reggae beat, and Island Records’ Catch a Fire (1973) took the Wailers worldwide. Later strands include dub, roots, lovers rock, dancehall (see Reggaeton) and Britain’s 2 Tone ska revival (c. 1979).

text:

Bass: Roots on every beat, plainer than a real reggae bass line, which moves and leaves gaps.

title: Son montuno
text: Open the Son montuno style in the Backing Track

title: Son montuno
text:
What it is
The groove of Cuban son and of salsa: a two-bar repeating piano figure (the montuno or guajeo), a bass that plays ahead of the beat (the tumbao), and a clave pattern every part is fitted to.

title: Son montuno
text:
A little history
Son grew up in eastern Cuba and reached Havana around 1910-20, played by small groups on tres (a guitar with three doubled strings), guitar, bongó, maracas, claves and a marímbula or bass. The second half of a son, the montuno, is a vamp where a lead singer improvises against a chorus. In the late 1930s and 1940s Arsenio Rodríguez enlarged the group into the conjunto: piano, trumpets, and a conga. He is credited with the anticipated bass: the bass skips beat 1 and lands on the and of 2 and on 4, so that each chord is heard a little before the bar it belongs to. Mambo bands (Pérez Prado, Machito) and the New York salsa of the 1960s and ’70s (Eddie Palmieri, Fania Records) built on the same parts.
Clave is the two-bar rhythm (3-2: three hits then two; or 2-3) that the parts are written around. The band plays 2-3.

title: Son montuno
text:
The band’s version

Bass: tumbao, anticipating each bar. Comping: the two-bar montuno.
Drums: clave. Congas: a tumbao moving to the second drum every other bar.

title: Bossa nova
text: Open the Bossa nova style in the Backing Track

title: Bossa nova
text:
What it is
Brazilian song style from Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s: samba slowed and quietened for a voice and a nylon-string guitar. The guitarist’s thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3 (in 2/4 counting, the two beats of the bar) while the fingers play syncopated chords that repeat over two bars.

title: Bossa nova
text:
A little history
Samba’s percussion section (the surdo bass drum, tamborim, agogô) was too loud for the small apartments and clubs of Copacabana. João Gilberto moved the parts onto the guitar: the thumb took the surdo, the fingers took the tamborim’s syncopations. His single Chega de Saudade (1958, song by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes) is usually called the first bossa nova record. Jobim’s harmony (major sevenths, ninths, chromatic inner lines) came from jazz and from Debussy and Ravel.
American jazz musicians took it up after Charlie Byrd and Stan Getz’s Jazz Samba (1962). Getz/Gilberto (recorded 1963, released 1964), with Astrud Gilberto singing The Girl from Ipanema, made it a world style. Jazz drummers turned the guitar’s rhythm into the brush or cross-stick pattern the band plays: a two-bar figure close to the son clave, over a steady bass drum on 1 and 3.

title: Bossa nova
text:
The band’s version

Bass: root and fifth with pickups. Comping: the two-bar pattern.
Drums: bossa clave on the cross-stick. Voicings: jazz voicings with added 9ths.
Feel: straight eighths. Bossa never swings.

title: Cha-cha

title: Cha-cha
text:
What it is
A medium-tempo Cuban dance rhythm, steadier and simpler than mambo, with a cowbell on every beat and the three quick steps (cha-cha-chá) on beat 3, the and of 3, and beat 4.

title: Cha-cha
text:
A little history
Violinist Enrique Jorrín, of the charanga orchestra Orquesta América, wrote La engañadora (1951, recorded 1953). The orchestra’s dancers found its rhythm easier than the danzón-mambo, and the steps’ scuffing sound named the dance. Charangas played it on flute, violins, piano, bass, timbales, güiro and conga; Orquesta Aragón made it famous across Latin America. By the late 1950s it was a ballroom dance in the US and Europe, and American pop recorded “cha-cha” versions of everything.

title: Cha-cha
text:
The band’s version

Bass: the cha-cha bass line. Comping: chords on the cha-cha figure.
Drums: a bell on the beats. Congas: a tumbao. Voicings: plain triads and sevenths.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
What it is
The slow 1950s ballad: piano chords repeated in triplets, three to every beat, over a slow backbeat, usually on the I-vi-IV-V chords, behind a lead singer and vocal group.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
A little history
Doo-wop came from African American vocal groups on street corners in New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Chicago in the late 1940s and ’50s, following the Ink Spots and the Mills Brothers. The backing singers sang nonsense syllables (doo-wop, sh-boom) in place of instruments. On record, small bands added a pianist hammering triplets, an idea from New Orleans rhythm and blues (Fats Domino) and the slow blues. The same 12/8 feel carries soul ballads into the 1960s, from Etta James’s At Last onward.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:

Bass: 12/8 ballad. Comping: triplets. Drums: slow 12/8 backbeat.
On a 4/4 chart the band plays the triplets over each beat.

title: Country train beat
text: Open the Country train beat style in the Backing Track

title: Country train beat
text:
What it is
The country rhythm that sounds like a steam train: a snare (often with brushes) on every eighth note, accented on 2 and 4, a bass on root and fifth, and a boom-chicka guitar.

title: Country train beat
text:
A little history
The sound is most associated with Johnny Cash’s Tennessee Two at Sun Records in Memphis: Luther Perkins’ muted boom-chicka electric guitar and Marshall Grant’s slapped bass on Folsom Prison Blues (1955) and I Walk the Line (1956). Drummer W. S. Holland joined in 1960 and the train beat became a drum pattern. Train songs had been part of country and blues since the 1920s (Jimmie Rodgers), and the beat has stayed in rockabilly, bluegrass-flavoured country and country rock.

title: Country train beat
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: a boom-chicka strum. Drums: train beat.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text: Open the Freylekhs / polka style in the Backing Track

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
What it is
The fast 2/4 of Eastern European dance music: the bass on every beat, alternating root and fifth, and the full chord on every off-beat (oom-pa oom-pa). A freylekhs (“joyful”) is the most common klezmer dance tune; the polka is its Central European cousin.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
A little history
The polka started in Bohemia in the 1830s and was danced across Europe and America within a decade. Its bands (brass, then accordion) gave it the bass-and-off-beat accompaniment. Klezmer is the instrumental music of Ashkenazi Jewish weddings in Eastern Europe. Immigrant clarinettists Naftule Brandwein and Dave Tarras recorded it in New York in the 1920s, with bands that played the same driving off-beats on piano, brass and drums. It faded after the war and came back in the 1970s revival (the Klezmorim, Andy Statman, Kapelye, later the Klezmatics). Songs like Hava Nagila and Hanukkah songs are still played this way.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth on every beat, with a run up into the next bar now and then.
Comping: chords on the off-beats. In half-time bars the piano switches to ballad patterns.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text: Open the Straight-eighth rock style in the Backing Track

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
What it is
The basic rock band: drums with a snare backbeat on 2 and 4 and even eighth notes on the hi-hat, an electric bass on the root in eighths, and guitar strumming every eighth note.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
A little history
Rhythm and blues of the late 1940s and early ’50s was mostly shuffled (swung) eighths. Through the 1950s, records by Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Ray Charles mixed straight eighths in, and by the early 1960s even eighths were the norm in rock and soul; Alexander Stewart traces the shift through New Orleans drummers such as Earl Palmer. The backbeat came from gospel handclaps and R&B. The British Invasion, then punk’s down-stroke eighths (the Ramones, 1976) and new wave, kept the plain driving eighths at the centre of the style.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root eighths. Comping: down-up eighths on the guitar. Drums: a backbeat whose kick varies from bar to bar. Chords are pushed (they arrive an eighth early) the way rock bands do.
