title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
For a Claude session asked to add a style (“add a samba”, “a second-line groove”, “a gospel 6/8”). Read this first, then the header comments of the files it names. NOTES.org beside this file is the history of the band and its open questions.


A style is a row in styles in catalog.js: a name, a group (the genre heading in the Style menu), and defaults that belong together.
{ id:"bossa", label:"Bossa nova", group:"Latin", genres:"Bossa nova, slow samba",
  feel:"straight", bass:"bossa", rhythm:"bossa", drums:"bossa", voicing:JAZZV,
  desc:"Root-and-fifth bass with pickups, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave." }

bass, rhythm, drums are ids of entries in the bass, comp and drums lists of the same file. rhythm may be several joined by + (a blend).
voicing is { piano, guitar }: a voicing style id for each (PLAINV, STRUMV, JAZZV are ready-made).
Optional: sound ({ bass:"upright"|"electric", cymbal:"ride"|"hat"|"bell", piano, guitar, lead, kit }), where piano and guitar are sound ids from sounds.js (BandSounds.sounds("guitar") lists them: jazz, steel, nylon, clean and distorted electric), push (chords anticipate), full (the piano’s triads keep all three notes), bass and drums may each name several patterns joined by + (a blend: one of them per bar, planned four bars at a time by BandHarmony.blendOpts; shares in opts.bassMix / opts.grooveMix), calm (strike and hold the chords around cadences and in bars with more chords than usual: BandHarmony.calmAt; a chart marks phrase ends with "^phrase" and single bars with "^plain"), halfRhythm (comping rhythm ids, a+b: what the comping plays in bars of half time instead of its own rhythm), time ({ feel:"half", parts }), ext:true (unmarked extensions on offer). A style with no sound gets upright bass, ride, piano, jazz guitar.

A style made only of parts that already exist is one line in styles plus the fit lists (step 3). Most requests need at least one new part. Decide that first: listen in your head to what the bass, the chord instrument and the drums each play in that music, and check each against the existing entries before writing a new one.




Write the new parts, each in its own engine file. Copy the nearest existing pattern and read the comment block above the table you are adding to.

Bass line: LINES in bass.js (a fixed figure over the chord’s root, fifth, octave).
Comping rhythm: GRID in comp.js for a set pattern, FIG for a one-bar swing figure.
Drum groove: GROOVES in drums.js (bars for 4/4, threeBars for 3/4, triplet for 12/8 feels).
Congas: PATTERNS in congas.js (see Congas below).
Positions are beats from 0; x.5 is the off-beat eighth (swung by the player unless the event says straight:true). Velocities are 0..1 and the player scales them by the band’s intensity.
Use ctx.phrase.bar (0..3) to shape four-bar phrases and ctx.intensity for how hard the band is playing. phraseDyn, leanDyn and spread in comp.js are the shared dynamic shaping: use them rather than fixed velocities.
Every pattern must cope with 3/4 and with a bar holding two chords. The tests check both.

Describe each new part in catalog.js: an entry in bass, comp or drums with id, label, feel (swing, straight or any), group, tags and a desc that says what is played on which beats, in a musician’s words. The desc is shown on the page and on the Accompaniment Styles page.
Say where each part fits: add its id to FITS.bass, FITS.comp or FITS.drums with the style ids it belongs in (your new one, and any existing style it also suits). Locked, a menu lists only what fits the chosen style, so a part missing from FITS cannot be chosen. Add the new style id to the voicing lists it should offer (JAZZ, POP, PLAIN, or a VOICE row).
Add the style row to styles, in its group. The id is permanent: saved setups, links and song files name it. Never rename one.
Tests (plain node, run from the test’s own directory):

tests/band/pat/t_patterns.js runs every style and option against every meter. It has a want table of where chords must land for set patterns; add your rhythm there.
tests/band/pat/t_pop.js lists the style ids of some groups in order; update the list if you added to one.
tests/band/styles/t_sections.js, tests/band/fills/t_fills.js, tests/band/meter/t_change.js must still pass.

Publish it to the pages. In tools/_backing-track.qmd and tools/_accomp-styles.qmd, raise the ?v= number on every script you changed (browsers cache them). Then quarto render tools/backing-track.qmd and check that .gitignore did not change (Quarto appends to it). The lyrics site copies the engine: bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh.
Say what was not verified. Nothing here can be listened to from a terminal. Report the pattern in beats, what the tests cover, and that it needs ears. Do not commit unless asked.




The conga player (congas.js) is a part of its own beside bass, comping and drums: it has its own fader, staff and MIDI track, and any style may have it. Adding a pattern:

PATTERNS in congas.js: id: { bars: [...], three: [...], triplet: [...] }. bars is one or two 4/4 bars (a two-bar pattern follows the bar number); three is one bar of 3/4 and triplet one bar of 12/8, both optional. A bar is a list of rows [pos, drum, stroke, hand, vel]: drum is "c" (conga, the higher drum) or "t" (tumba); stroke is H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muffled, B bass; hand is "L" or "R". Positions are beats; 12/8 positions are thirds of a beat (x.333). A pattern with no bar for the meter plays the steady one, so it can stay short.
congas in catalog.js: { id, label, feel, group, tags, desc }; the desc says which stroke falls on which beat, with which hand.
FITS.congas: the style ids it belongs in (steady and none fit every style).
A style that should have them says congas:"id" on its row in styles. Left out, the style has none.
tests/band/congas/t_congas.js checks every pattern in every meter, and that the other players play the same notes with or without them.

Sounds: the congas are one sample set (congas in sounds.js) built from the soundfont’s three conga notes; a new stroke is a new piece name there, a trim, and its place in BandNotation.congaName and the GM table in midi.js.




The Style menu of the Backing Track page; ?style=id in its address.
A tune’s ABC: %%style bossa nova above the first P: line (the whole tune).
One section: %%style bossa nova on the line under its P: line, or "^style bossa nova" in a bar (from that bar to the next section; "^style none" ends it early). The form bar carries style, and BandCatalog.sectionOpts turns it into the options for those bars. Single parts can follow the name: %%style Swing; voicing drop2; rhythm charleston; bass two; drums funk; feel straight. The comping moves to the instrument the style is built around (sound.lead), if it has one. The page’s blend sliders and walk amount do not apply inside such a section. On the Backing Track page the Band menus change to a section’s settings as it starts, and a change made there stays with that section (opts.sectionOverrides, which the player puts before the section’s style).
A crash grabbed with the hand: "^choke" in a bar (the crash on its beat 1, stopped before beat 2), beside "^fill" and "^stop".
Two built-in setups in presets.js (“Style demo: …”) tour the jazz and the pop, rock and country styles a section at a time. Add a new style to the one it belongs in.
A lyrics-site song file (~/Projects/carols/site/extra/*.cho): {style: carol} above the first heading for the song, or under a heading for that section. See the top of tools/chordpro.py there.
A name matches an id, a menu label, or part of a label, ignoring case.





Plain JS globals, no build step, no dependencies. Match the comment density and voice of the file.
A new option is opt-in: an existing style must sound exactly as it did, and an option left unset must not draw from the random number generator (the tests compare runs).
Sample sets are named only in sounds.js. A new sound is one entry there (family, label, zones, and an optional amp chain); the Comping menu, the player and styleOpts pick it up from that entry. Add its General MIDI program to PROGRAM in midi.js, and its samples to tests/band/meter/fetch-samples.js.
Write descriptions for a music teacher: beats and instruments, no code words.

Two built-in setups in presets.js (“Style demo: …”) tour the jazz and the pop, rock and country styles a section at a time. Add a new style to the one it belongs in.
A lyrics-site song file (~/Projects/carols/site/extra/*.cho): {style: carol} above the first heading for the song, or under a heading for that section. See the top of tools/chordpro.py there.
A name matches an id, a menu label, or part of a label, ignoring case.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
Plain JS globals, no build step, no dependencies. Match the comment density and voice of the file.
A new option is opt-in: an existing style must sound exactly as it did, and an option left unset must not draw from the random number generator (the tests compare runs).
Sample sets are named only in sounds.js. A new sound is one entry there (family, label, zones, and an optional amp chain); the Comping menu, the player and styleOpts pick it up from that entry. Add its General MIDI program to PROGRAM in midi.js, and its samples to tests/band/meter/fetch-samples.js.
Write descriptions for a music teacher: beats and instruments, no code words.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives one symbol to each sound, so a singer can read the same sounds in any language. Click a symbol for a description and reference words in English (General American and RP), Hindi, Marathi, German, French, Korean and Japanese. A language is left blank where it does not have the sound. This page has text only, no audio.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Notes for singers


How classical diction uses IPA
A transcription records sounds, not spelling. Coaches and diction books write a song’s text in IPA so everyone sings the same vowels and consonants, then add stress, linking and the places where a sung line differs from speech. Learn the sounds once and you can read the transcription for any language you meet.


Pure vowels
Most sung languages here are built on steady vowels (Italian, German, French, Japanese, Hindi, Marathi, Korean). In English, [eɪ], [oʊ] and [aɪ] are diphthongs: sing the first element for nearly the whole note and add the second at the very end. Italianate five-vowel thinking ([a e i o u], with open and closed e and o) is a good basis for all of them.


English
General American and RP differ most in r (after vowels), in the vowels of bath, lot and thought, and in the flap [ɾ] of water. Unstressed syllables have schwa in speech, but singers often give them a clearer vowel on long notes. Aspiration of initial p, t, k is a strong cue for audibility.


German
Final voiced stops are voiceless (Tag [taːk]). Two ch sounds: [ç] after front vowels and l, n, r; [x] after a, o, u, au. Vowel length is meaningful, and the stage r is the tongue-tip trill [r] while everyday speech uses [ʁ]. Vowel-initial stressed syllables begin with a light glottal onset [ʔ].


French
No diphthongs and no aspiration. Four nasal vowels, front rounded vowels [y ø œ], and the mute e, which is pronounced when sung. Liaison and enchaînement link words, and French syllables are even in stress.


Hindi and Marathi
Keep dental (त द) and retroflex (ट ड) apart, and learn the four-way contrast (p, pʰ, b, bʱ). Hindi drops the inherent a at the end of words, and sometimes inside them; sung text may restore it. Marathi has the extra affricates [t͡s d͡z] and the retroflex lateral [ɭ].


Korean
Three kinds of stop: lax, tense and aspirated. Lax stops are voiced between vowels. Tense and aspirated stops raise the pitch of the following vowel in speech. Final stops are unreleased.


Japanese
Five vowels, with [ɯ̟ᵝ] spread-lip rather than rounded. Long vowels, double consonants and moraic ん count as extra time. Vowels i and u are often devoiced between voiceless consonants in speech. Japanese [ɾ] is a single tap.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Language notes


About the examples
Examples use broad transcription of standard forms: General American and RP, Standard Hindi, Standard Marathi, Standard German, Metropolitan French, Seoul Korean and Tokyo Japanese. Individual speakers, regions and poetic or sung styles differ. For Devanagari, Hangul and kana the highlighted piece is the written syllable containing the sound (Devanagari and Hangul write a syllable as a unit); romanisation is a transliteration, not IPA. Check anything you will perform with a native speaker or diction coach.


Hindi and Marathi
Both use the Devanagari script. Hindi has the Persian-Arabic sounds [f z x ɣ q] in loanwords, shown with a dot (nuqta) under the letter; many speakers replace them with native sounds. Marathi usually does not write the nuqta; its loan sounds are often assimilated. Marathi च and ज are [t͡s d͡z] before a, ā, u, o, and [t͡ʃ d͡ʒ] before i, e.


Korean
Hangul writes sounds in syllable blocks. The Korean vowel ㅡ is [ɯ], and ㅓ [ʌ]. Final consonants are pronounced differently from initial ones.


Japanese
Written in kana and kanji; the examples give kana. The し and ち sounds are alveolo-palatal ([ɕ], [t͡ɕ]) and ふ is [ɸɯ̟ᵝ].


Symbols without examples
Some symbols (for example ɨ, ʉ, ɘ, ɵ, ɤ, ɞ, ɶ) are on the chart but are not separate sounds in any of the seven languages here. They are shown dashed and have no reference words.

title: Accompaniment Styles
text:
These patterns are built into the accompaniment engine and can be selected on any tune page.
    Each style adapts automatically to the tune's meter and chord chart.
    Styles marked any meter work in 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, and 6/8; fixed-meter styles

            Jazz Charleston

            Cha-cha
            chacha

          Bass on beat 1, chord on 2, then three quick chords on "3–and–4" — the "1·2·cha-cha-chá" count. Evolved from the mambo in 1950s Cuba; named for the shuffling footwork of dancers.

            Cuban

            Calypso / mento
            calypso

          Bass on beats 1 and 3, light chords on every upbeat — the Trinidadian and Jamaican "afterbeat." Mento is the Jamaican root form; calypso developed in Trinidad. Both patterns flowed into ska and reggae.

            Caribbean
            Roots
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Samba
            samba
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Surdo-style kick on beats 2 and 4 (absent on beat 1), snare on beat 3, hi-hat fills every eighth. The rhythmic foundation of Brazilian carnival parade music; transferred to the drum kit from the samba bateria.

            Pop / ballad

            Driving 8ths
            driving8
            any
            ▶

            Country

            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Offbeat chords
            offbeat
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Chord only on the off-beats, silence on the downbeats. The defining rhythmic gesture of ska and reggae; known as the "skank" or "chop." In reggae, the kick lands on beat 3 (the "one-drop").

            Block chords
            block
            any
            ▶

            arpflow

            Arpeggio (root–5th)
            arpcell
            any
            ▶

          Block chordsblockany
          Sustained block voicing on every beat. The starting point for learning chord shapes and for chorale-style writing.

          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Left-hand bass on 1, right-hand chord on 2–3. The standard piano waltz texture from Chopin through the ballroom repertoire.

          Bass on 1 and 3, chords on every beat. Ubiquitous in pop piano; easy to adapt to either hands-together or stride-style playing.

      Guitar & Plucked Strings
      
        
          Folk — alternating bassfolkany
          Thumb alternates root–fifth in the bass; fingers strum the chord on the off-beat. The foundational fingerpicking and flatpicking pattern in folk, bluegrass, and country guitar.
          FolkCountryBluegrass
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving8any
          Steady downstroke eighth notes, no rests. The strum pattern behind countless rock, country, and pop songs.
          RockCountryPop
        
        
          Offbeat chordsoffbeatany
          The ska/reggae "skank": chord only between the beats. In reggae the downstroke is muted, leaving only the upstroke chop.
          SkaReggae
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Tresillo bass with off-beat chords. João Gilberto's original bossa guitar part is the blueprint; the pattern is also widely adapted to keyboard.

          Open-voiced ascending tones per beat. Evokes harp, classical guitar, and lute figuration; widely used in Renaissance and Baroque lute tablature.

          PolkaMarchFolk
        
        
          Tangotango4/4
          Habanera cell in the bass with syncopated upper chords. In Argentine tango this interplay moves between bandoneón and piano; in orchestral tango (Piazzolla) it drives the entire ensemble.

          Bass line (roots)bassrootany

          Backbeatbackbeat4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The universal pop and rock groove; the first drum pattern most students encounter.
          PopRock
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving84/4
          Continuous eighth notes on the hi-hat with backbeat snare. Energetic pop and rock feel; common in anthemic and uptempo styles.
          PopRock
        
        
          Ska / reggae (one-drop)ska4/4
          Kick displaced to beat 3; snare and hi-hat emphasise the off-beats. The rhythmic foundation of ska, rocksteady, and roots reggae.
          ReggaeSka
        
        
          Swing — ride cymbalswing_ride4/4
          Swung ride pattern with kick and snare on beats 2 and 4. The standard jazz ride pattern from Swing through bebop.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Swing — hi-hatswing_hats4/4
          Swung quarter-note hi-hat pulse; lighter texture than ride-cymbal swing. Used in small-group jazz and ballad settings.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Swing — open hi-hatswing_hats_open4/4
          Swung hi-hat opening on beats 2 and 4; airy, washy texture. Common in contemporary jazz and fusion where the drummer wants more cymbal wash than the closed-hat version.
          JazzFusion
        
        
          Swing — brushesswing_brushes4/4
          Wire-brush swirl with soft backbeat. Quiet jazz trio and intimate club setting; the standard brush technique for standards and ballads.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Jazz waltz — ridejazzwaltz_ride3/4

          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Jazz waltz — hi-hatjazzwaltz_hats3/4
          Closed hi-hat pulse in 3 with a light swing feel; more understated than the ride-cymbal version. Used in intimate trio settings where the drummer wants less projection.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Ride cymbal tresillo with side-stick; the drum kit adaptation of Brazilian percussion. Foundational in bossa nova and samba-jazz.
          LatinBossa
        
        
          Tango (habanera)tango4/4
          Habanera kick cell with closed hi-hat. The rhythmic engine of Argentine tango and early-20th-century Latin dance music.
          LatinTango
        
        
          Son montuno (clave)montuno4/4
          Cuban clave rhythm on the kick; snare and hi-hat fill the groove. The drum kit version of the son montuno pattern.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Kick on beat 1, hi-hat on 2 and 3. Straightforward triple-meter groove for waltzes, country, and folksong accompaniment.
          DanceFolk
        
        
          Compound (6/8)compound66/8
          Kick on the two main beats, hi-hat subdivisions filling the compound pulse. Used in jigs, compound-feel pop, and gospel 6/8.
          FolkGospel
        
        
          Half-time feelhalftime4/4
          Snare on beat 3 only; kick and hi-hat fill the rest. Makes the bar feel twice as wide without changing tempo. Widely used in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges.
          PopHip-hopRock
        
        
          Funkfunk4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat on all eighths. The foundational James Brown / Clyde Stubblefield groove.
          FunkR&B
        
        
          New Orleans second linesecondline4/4
          Kick on every beat, snare on the upbeats of 1 and 3. The marching street-parade groove; adopted by the Meters, Dr. John, and rock drummers worldwide.
          FunkNew Orleans
        
        
          Sambasamba4/4
          Surdo kick on beats 2 and 4; snare on beat 3; hi-hat throughout. The drum kit adaptation of the samba bateria; common in Brazilian jazz and fusion.
          LatinBrazilian
        
        
          Mambomambo4/4
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation); snare on beat 3. The driving groove of 1940s Havana; ancestor of modern salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Calypso / mentocalypso4/4
          Floating kick (no downbeat on 1); side-stick on beat 3; hi-hat emphasises the upbeats. The Trinidadian and Jamaican afterbeat; ancestral to ska and reggae.
          CaribbeanReggae
        
      
    

    
      Hand Percussion
      
        
          Bongo — martillobongo_martillo4/4
          Steady eighth-note alternation between hi and lo bongo; the "hammer" pattern. The default timekeeping groove in Cuban son and salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Bongo — quarterbongo_slow4/4
          Quarter-note hi/lo alternation; a relaxed, open texture. Works well as a simplified bongo part for classroom or beginner settings.
          LatinTeaching
        
        
          Conga — tumbaoconga_tumbao4/4
          Open tone on the and-of-4, muted tones elsewhere. The foundational Cuban conga pattern; ubiquitous in salsa and son.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — tumbao (dense)conga_tumbao_dense4/4
          Eight-note tumbao with slap and open tone variations; a fuller, more active feel than the standard four-note version.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — sonconga_son4/4
          Alternating lo-conga open tones across the bar; simpler and more open than the tumbao. Common in son cubano and early salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — waltzconga_waltz3/4
          Conga tones on the three main beats in 3/4; pairs with Latin waltz and compound-feel songs.
          LatinWaltz
        
        
          Conga — 6/8conga_6_86/8
          Open and muted conga tones across the compound-triple pulse. Works with 6/8 Afro-Cuban styles and compound jigs.
          LatinAfro-Cuban

text:
What the entry pages do with the keys you play: which notes are chords and which melody, where each one lands on the bars, how long it is written, how it is spelled. Part 1 runs the engine on a take (a preset, or the log the Chord Entry page keeps) and shows what every rule decided; change a setting and see what it would have written. Part 2 is the rules themselves, with the numbers the engine really uses.

  
    1. Try it
    
      Start from
      Load the last take from Chord Entry
    
    A take log is what the Chord Entry page copies with Copy the take log: every key and pedal event with its time, and the settings. Paste one here and Load it. The settings below then work on the same playing, so you can see what a different rule setting would have written.

    What did I mean?
    
    What was written
    
    
    The take against the bars
    
    a chord's notes as playeda melody note as playedthe melody as writtena chord as placedthe pedal held

    Bars
    Melody notes, one by one
    Chords, one by one
    Pedal
    Copy a report of this run
    The report holds the log, the settings as set here, what was written and every table above. It is everything needed to run the same take again, so it is the thing to send when a take comes out wrong.
  

  
    2. The rules
    In the order the engine applies them. Each rule says what it does, the number it uses (the numbers are read from the engine, not typed here) and where to see it in the tables above. Chords and melody are the same take: the keys you play are sorted into one or the other first (rule 1), and then each follows its own rules.

    Time
    T1The clock: beats from the first downbeat
      Every key and pedal event carries a time in milliseconds from the first downbeat after the count-in (negative in the count-in). A beat is 60 / tempo seconds; in 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 a beat is a dotted quarter, as the band counts it. On a click the page subtracts the sound card's output latency, and the Timing offset or Nudge field moves everything by the milliseconds you give it (a positive number is earlier).
      Seen in: the log's events, and the played column of the note and chord tables.
    T2The bars, and how the pedal changes them
      The take starts with the meter chosen and that many bars. The beat never moves; only where bars begin does. Hold the pedal (MIDI controller ) across two downbeats and the bars from the first of them on are as long as the gap between them, in whole beats. Notes within  beats count as one strike (a chord is one downbeat); only the first and last strike while the pedal is down are used. The gap and the first downbeat are rounded to whole beats.
      A change that falls inside a bar cuts that bar short (a 2/4 bar in a 4/4 tune). A change less than one beat after a bar line moves back to the bar line. In compound meters the new length is counted in dotted quarters, so three beats make 9/8. A second change must come after the first. Over chords already entered the bars are fixed and the pedal is ignored.
      Seen in: the Bars table and the Pedal table (its strikes are the beats it used).
    T3Swing: a swung off-beat is put back on the even grid
      When the playing is read as swung, the second eighth of each beat is taken to sit late: at a fraction s of the beat (0.5 would be straight). s comes from the tempo: 0.68 − 0.08 × clamp((bpm − 100)/120) − 0.05 × clamp((bpm − 220)/80), so it is about 0.68 at a ballad tempo and 0.60 near 220. A time that far into the beat is moved back to the half beat (unswing) before it is rounded to the grid. This is why swung eighths come out as plain eighth notes, and the band swings them again when it plays them. Bars in compound meters are always read straight. Chords are unswung the same way before they snap to the grid.
      Seen in: unswung in the note table (units from the first bar, before rounding) and the Swing setting above.
    T5Pickups: notes before the first bar
      A note (or chord) struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat is taken as on it. Struck earlier than that, in the count-in, it is dropped, unless Notes before bar 1: Write them is on: then the earliest such note sets the length of a short bar in front of bar 1, rounded up to whole beats (never longer than the count-in), and everything is written in it, with no meter mark. The chart then reads it as a pickup (anacrusis). A chart that already has a pickup bar uses its length.
      On the Backing Track page, when the take starts at a later bar (a section, or "Start at bar"), the count-in is the bar before the one recorded from, so notes played in it are written at the end of that bar: a pickup into a verse goes at the end of the interlude before it. Only at the very start of the tune does a pickup get a short bar of its own.
      Seen in: the Bars table (a short first bar), the note table (bar 1 is the pickup) and the roll (the count-in is to the left of the first line).
    T4The grid: rounded to the nearest eighth or sixteenth
      A melody note's start is rounded to the nearest eighth note (or sixteenth, if chosen); the unit is an eighth, so a beat is 2 units in x/4 and 3 in compound meters. A note struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat is moved onto it; one struck earlier than that is dropped. A note that rounds to the same spot as the next one is dropped and the later one stays. A note after the last bar is dropped. Chords snap by the Snap setting instead (a bar, half bar, beat or eighth).
      Seen in: on grid and result in the note table.

    Notes
    N1Which keys are chords and which are melody
      In a chords take every key goes to the chord reader; in a melody take every key goes to the melody line. In a split take the keys below the split key are chords and the split key and those above it are melody. The pedal strikes count notes from either side.
      Seen in: the Entry and Melody-from settings; the roll shows chord notes in orange and melody notes in teal.
    N2Notes struck together
      Melody notes struck within  ms of the first of them are one strike. By default only the highest is written and the others are left out; with Notes struck together are written as a chord all of them are written as an ABC chord, [CEG], with one length. A note struck later than that window is a new note.
      Seen in: left out in the note table, and the notes column (several pitches are one strike).
    N3One note at a time
      The line is one voice: a new note ends the one before it, even if you are still holding it.
    N4How long a note is written
      A note lasts until the next note starts (it is written legato), unless the gap between its release and the next start is  of an eighth or more: then it is written as released (rounded to the grid) and a rest follows. The last note is written to its release. A note is never shorter than one grid step. A note cannot run past the next note or the last bar line.
      So a line played short and detached, as swing is, is written with full note values and no rests unless a gap is clear.
      Where a rest does follow a note longer than an eighth (the end of a phrase), the moment you let go is not much of a guide: with Long notes before a rest: The simplest nearby length (the default) the note ends wherever, near the release, the note and the rest after it are simplest to write. The end may move up to  of the note's length (at least one grid step, at most a beat). The candidates are scored by the written symbols of the note and the rest (a dotted one counts one and a half), an end that is off the beat, and the distance moved; holding the note right on to the next one, losing a rest that was played, costs  more. So a quarter let go a sixteenth early is a quarter, not a dotted eighth and a sixteenth rest, while a dotted quarter and a clear eighth rest stay as played. As released writes the release rounded to the grid.
      Seen in: length in the note table says which case applied and the gap it measured.
    N5Bar lines, chord changes and ties
      A note that runs over a bar line is split and tied. A note that runs over a chord change is split at the change and tied, so each chord symbol sits above the note under it. Only lengths that are written as one note are used:  grid steps (a dotted note is 3 or 6); any other length is split into those and tied.
    N6Spelling: which letter and which accidental
      Notes of the key are spelled as the key spells them. A note outside the key takes whichever of its sharp and flat spellings is nearer the middle of the key on the line of fifths (centre + ); when they are equally near, the flat. So in C: E♭, A♭, B♭, F♯ and D♭; in F: G♭ (not F♯) and A♭.
      An accidental is written only where it differs from the key signature or from what the same letter in the same octave had earlier in that bar. Octaves: middle C is C, the C above it c, then c'; below, C,.

    N7Detached notes: staccato
      By default a short note followed by a rest is written as the note and the rest (an eighth and an eighth rest). With Short detached notes: Staccato note, a note followed by a rest exactly as long as itself, where the two together make a length that can be written, is written as one staccato note of both: eighths with eighth rests become staccato quarters. A staccato note is played by the band at half its length. (Triplet notes are not changed.)
      Seen in: length in the note table ("a note and an equal rest are written as a staccato note of both").
    N8Triplets
      Off by default. When on, each beat of a simple meter whose beat is two units (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, …; not 6/8 and the like, where the beat is already three) is read as three even parts if its notes fit thirds of the beat better than the eighth-note grid by more than  of a beat (summed over the beat's onsets). The check is made on the raw time (a swung off-beat is compared after the swing is taken out, so a swung pair is not mistaken for a triplet; the same pair read as straight is). A beat read as triplets is written under a bracket: three notes (3CDE, or a quarter and an eighth (3:2:2C2D. Only whole beats are triplets (no quarter-note triplets over two beats, no sixteenth sextuplets yet).
      Seen in: triplet in the note table gives the two numbers compared.
    N9Grace notes
      Off by default. When on, a note whose next note starts within the chosen milliseconds (never more than  of a beat, a thirty-second note) is not a note of its own but a slashed grace note of the next one: {/D}E. A run of such notes is all grace notes of the first note after them. This is for the quick note into a blue note; it is why a note that was struck first but let go before the next began is not folded into a chord (rule N2 only joins notes that are still held together). The band does not play grace notes back.
      Seen in: graces in the note table.
    N10Parallel thirds and other double stops
      Above the split key (or in a melody take) two notes struck together are one melody note. With Notes struck together are written as a chord on, both are written in one bracket ([CE], [DF], …) with one length, tied as a pair; with it off only the top one is written. They never reach the chord reader, so they are not named as a chord. Notes of the pair that are struck slightly apart still count as together if they are inside the Together-within window and the first is still held when the second arrives.

    Chords
    C1When a chord is finished
      A chord is closed  ms after its first note. Keys still held from the chord before count as part of the next one, unless three or more new keys arrived. It is timed at its first note.
      Seen in: the Chords table, notes played.
    C2Naming a chord
      Every note played must be accounted for by the chord (the Director page, by contrast, accepts extra notes). Every pitch class played is tried as the root against the table below. A reading in which every note is a chord tone wins; a perfect fifth may be left out of any chord of four or more notes. If two readings fit equally (C6 and Am7), the lowest note played decides; then the reading whose root is nearer the key; then the order in the table. If nothing fits exactly, the closest match is written and the chord is marked as a guess. Two or more different notes are needed. Inversions are written as plain chords unless Slash chords is on (C with E at the bottom is then C/E).
      Seen in: candidates in the Chords table: the five best readings, best first.
      
    C3Where a chord goes
      A chord is timed at its first note. Its position in the bar is unswung (T3), then moved to the nearest point of the Snap setting. A chord struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat goes on it. The chord sits there until the next one.

    Writing it down
    W2Beams
      In ABC a space between notes breaks a beam, so the notation joins eighth notes (and shorter) by writing them without a space: within a beat by default, or within half a bar (four eighths in 4/4; three in 6/8 and the other compound meters are a beat already) with Beams: Within half a bar, or not at all. A rest, a note longer than an eighth, a chord change that starts a new group, or a triplet bracket ends a beam; a triplet is beamed under its own bracket.
    W3Syncopation: ties across the beat
      Jazz writes a quarter note on the “and” of 2 as one quarter. Classical notation writes it as two tied eighths. Syncopation: Tied across the middle of the bar splits a note that starts after the first beat and runs over the middle of the bar (beat 3 in 4/4; a half note on beat 2 too). Tied across every beat also splits a note that starts off the beat and runs over any beat. A note that starts on a beat, or on the bar's first beat, keeps its length. Only the written ABC changes (the band hears the same notes).
    W1The ABC
      Bars of four to a line (the melody bars are written with the beams and ties above); M: is the opening meter and a bar of another meter gets [M:n/d] in front of it. The unit is a quarter note when nothing in an x/4 take sits between the beats, else an eighth, else a sixteenth when sixteenths were used. Chord symbols are quoted above the note or rest at their position. Rests fill what is left.

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
The band’s hammond sound (sounds.js), the organist’s pedal and switch (organist in comp.js), and the panel on the Backing Track page. Written 2026-10-10. Nobody has listened to it. Every level and rule below is either taken from a source (linked) or is a first guess, and the two are kept apart so the guesses are easy to find and change.
What was asked for: all nine tonebars, the upper manual only, the C3 chorus, and a band that works the swell pedal and the Leslie speed by itself. Not built: percussion, the lower manual, bass pedals, the other vibrato settings.


Three kinds, in falling order: technical write-ups read in full (Electric Druid, Scott Healy’s playing tips, Wikipedia); documents quoted in search results but not opened (the Hammond service text, Stefan Vorkoetter); and forum posts quoted in search results, where the link is to the thread the search named and the exact post was not checked (Keyboard Corner, Cantabile, Nord, Fractal). Anything resting only on the third kind is one player’s word.



Nothing is sampled. Each note is three oscillators, a few milliseconds of noise, and then one chain shared by all the notes.



Part
What it does
Where the numbers come from




Tonebars
Nine pitches for a key: 16′, 5⅓′, 8′, 4′, 2⅔′, 2′, 1⅗′, 1⅓′, 1′, at 0.5, 1.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 times the note
Electric Druid


Tonebar steps
0 is silent; each step from 8 down is 3 dB quieter
A clone’s description of the real instrument (Hammy 91); widely repeated, not from a Hammond document


Tempering
The fifths and the third are tempered wheels, not pure harmonics: 1.4988, 2.9976, 5.0409 and 5.9953 times the note. So a note is one oscillator for the octaves, one for the three fifths, one for the third
Electric Druid


Foldback
91 wheels. Key 1 (C2) takes its 8′ from wheel 13. A pitch above wheel 91 is taken an octave lower; the bottom octave’s 16′ an octave higher
Electric Druid (its table did not survive being read by machine; the rule here reproduces its wheel ranges)


Leakage
A closed tonebar still lets a trace through (−48 dB, octaves only)
That it exists: Electric Druid. The amount: a guess


Key click
A key’s nine contacts do not close together. Here: 22 ms of filtered noise as a note starts, with its own slider
The cause: Electric Druid. The sound of it: a guess


Touch
None. A note is the same level however it is played
Scott Healy: “the organ isn’t velocity-sensitive”


C3 chorus
A delay swept up and back 6.87 times a second (412 turns a minute), about 0.9 ms from end to end, mixed half and half with the straight sound
Rate and that the scanner runs up the line and back: Hammond service text. About 50 µs a stage over 18 stages: Stefan Vorkoetter (an M-100, not a B-3). The half-and-half mix: a guess; no source gives the real ratio


Swell pedal
Never silent: 24 dB down at its quietest. Keeps the bass up as it closes. Sits before the tube stage, so opening it also adds growl
That it never closes, lifts bass and treble as it comes down, and drives the amp harder as it opens: Nord forum, quoting a Hammond manual. The 24 dB and the 7 dB of bass: guesses; no source gives figures


Tube drive
The amp-chain drive already in the band, set low
A guess


Rotary speaker
Split at 800 Hz into a horn and a drum. Horn 48 turns a minute slow, 400 fast; drum 85% of that. Two microphones on opposite sides
Crossover and speeds: Wikipedia; 48 / 400 and 40 / 342 measured on a 147: Fractal forum


Speed changes
The horn gets most of the way in about 1.5 s, the drum in about 5 s
“Less than two seconds” and “4 to 10 seconds, depending on belt tension”: one forum post, found by search. No measured figure exists that I could find, so treat it as anecdote



Measured in tests/band/pat/organ.cdp.js: with every tonebar out, all nine pitches of A4 come out within 0.2 dB of each other; the 1⅗′ sits at 2218 Hz, not the pure 2200; C7’s 1′ sounds at 4186 Hz (two octaves folded back); two steps of a tonebar are 6.0 dB; the pedal closed is 24 dB down; the speaker moves the level 0.8 times a second slow and 6.67 fast, and summed to mono the swing all but cancels.



None of these is sourced. The searches named famous registrations (Jimmy Smith, Charles Earland, Groove Holmes, Erroll Garner, “full organ”) but gave no digits, so the menu describes each sound and attributes it to nobody. The default is 88 8000 000.



BandComp.organist decides, bar by bar, where the pedal sits and when the speaker changes speed. It uses no random numbers. Each rule, and what it rests on:
Swell pedal



Rule
Why




It follows how hard the band is playing: about half open when the band plays down, nearly open at full, a little more in a chorus
The organ has no touch, so the pedal is its only dynamics (Healy: “vary the dynamics using the expression pedal”)


The last bar of each four-bar phrase opens through the bar into the next one; more so going into a chorus
“Start with the expression pedal at minimum, then increase the pedal slowly”; a crescendo into the build (Healy)


The first bar of a phrase settles back a little
“Back off the pedal as the speaker slows down” (Healy)


A stop bar is hit and then pulled back sharply
“Pull the expression pedal back suddenly for a sforzando effect” (Healy)


The last chord swells and is let go
A guess



Leslie



Rule
Why




Slow is home
Rock and blues players “lean on that chorale mostly” (a forum post: Keyboard Corner or Cantabile)


Fast through the last bar of a phrase that leads into a chorus or back to the top, or that the band is playing hard; slow again as the next phrase starts
“As your single note starts to build, pop your Leslie or rotary switch to fast, and depress the pedal” (Healy). A forum player describes speeding up at the end of a phrase (Cantabile)


On a chord held two bars or more, a flick to fast for the second half of the phrase’s last bar and straight back
“Flip the Leslie to fast, then immediately flip it back to slow” under pads (Healy)


In swing the speaker stays slow, until the last two bars of the last chorus
Jazz players mostly leave the speaker alone and rely on the chorus (a forum post, Keyboard Corner or Cantabile: they “stop the horn entirely for the vast majority of work”). Slow, not stopped, is my choice


Fast on the final chord
A guess; a common ending



Thresholds that are mine: “playing hard” is an intensity of 0.66 or more; the flick lasts a beat and a half; the pedal’s range is 0.48 to 0.90 of its travel across the band’s intensity.
Nothing was found for gospel. The searches turned up no description of gospel pedal or Leslie habits, so the straight-eighth rules above are rock and blues habits applied to everything that is not swing.



Mixer → Organ: tonebars, swell and Leslie, shown while the organ is the comping instrument or the second one: nine tonebars, a registration menu, Leslie (Automatic / Slow / Fast / Stopped), Swell pedal (Automatic / By hand), key click. The chorus, the pedal’s range, the drive and the speaker’s own numbers are in Mixer → Tone (EQ), in the organ’s amp. Settings are kept in the browser (localStorage.btOrgan, and btAmp for the amp).




Percussion, the lower manual, pedals, V1 to V3 and C1, C2.
Tapering (each wheel’s own level across the keyboard), which a commenter on Electric Druid calls the main reason for the instrument’s scream.
Leakage between neighbouring wheels at other pitches; contact bounce note by note.
The cabinet: no reflections, no horn tone, one tube stage for both rotors.
Tonebar moves, chorus on and off, and registration changes are not played by the band: only the pedal and the speed.
The comping is the piano’s voicings. An organist’s held chords with a moving finger under a held top note (Healy, Ex. 2) are not written.





When do you reach for fast: into every chorus, or only the last one? On held chords? At endings?
In jazz, do you leave the speaker slow, stopped, or off altogether with the chorus doing the work?
Where does your foot sit when comping: about half, or lower? How far do you open into a chorus?
Your comping registration, and whether you change it between verse and chorus.
Chorus C3 always on, or only for some styles?

A guess


Rotary speaker
Split at 800 Hz into a horn and a drum. Horn 48 turns a minute slow, 400 fast; drum 85% of that. Two microphones on opposite sides
Crossover and speeds: Wikipedia; 48 / 400 and 40 / 342 measured on a 147: Fractal forum


Speed changes
The horn gets most of the way in about 1.5 s, the drum in about 5 s
“Less than two seconds” and “4 to 10 seconds, depending on belt tension”: one forum post, found by search. No measured figure exists that I could find, so treat it as anecdote



Measured in tests/band/pat/organ.cdp.js: with every tonebar out, all nine pitches of A4 come out within 0.2 dB of each other; the 1⅗′ sits at 2218 Hz, not the pure 2200; C7’s 1′ sounds at 4186 Hz (two octaves folded back); two steps of a tonebar are 6.0 dB; the pedal closed is 24 dB down; the speaker moves the level 0.8 times a second slow and 6.67 fast, and summed to mono the swing all but cancels.

title: The tonewheel organ
text: None of these is sourced. The searches named famous registrations (Jimmy Smith, Charles Earland, Groove Holmes, Erroll Garner, “full organ”) but gave no digits, so the menu describes each sound and attributes it to nobody. The default is 88 8000 000.

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
BandComp.organist decides, bar by bar, where the pedal sits and when the speaker changes speed. It uses no random numbers. Each rule, and what it rests on:
Swell pedal



Rule
Why




It follows how hard the band is playing: about half open when the band plays down, nearly open at full, a little more in a chorus
The organ has no touch, so the pedal is its only dynamics (Healy: “vary the dynamics using the expression pedal”)


The last bar of each four-bar phrase opens through the bar into the next one; more so going into a chorus
“Start with the expression pedal at minimum, then increase the pedal slowly”; a crescendo into the build (Healy)


The first bar of a phrase settles back a little
“Back off the pedal as the speaker slows down” (Healy)


A stop bar is hit and then pulled back sharply
“Pull the expression pedal back suddenly for a sforzando effect” (Healy)


The last chord swells and is let go
A guess



Leslie



Rule
Why




Slow is home
Rock and blues players “lean on that chorale mostly” (a forum post: Keyboard Corner or Cantabile)


Fast through the last bar of a phrase that leads into a chorus or back to the top, or that the band is playing hard; slow again as the next phrase starts
“As your single note starts to build, pop your Leslie or rotary switch to fast, and depress the pedal” (Healy). A forum player describes speeding up at the end of a phrase (Cantabile)


On a chord held two bars or more, a flick to fast for the second half of the phrase’s last bar and straight back
“Flip the Leslie to fast, then immediately flip it back to slow” under pads (Healy)


In swing the speaker stays slow, until the last two bars of the last chorus
Jazz players mostly leave the speaker alone and rely on the chorus (a forum post, Keyboard Corner or Cantabile: they “stop the horn entirely for the vast majority of work”). Slow, not stopped, is my choice


Fast on the final chord
A guess; a common ending



Thresholds that are mine: “playing hard” is an intensity of 0.66 or more; the flick lasts a beat and a half; the pedal’s range is 0.48 to 0.90 of its travel across the band’s intensity.
Nothing was found for gospel. The searches turned up no description of gospel pedal or Leslie habits, so the straight-eighth rules above are rock and blues habits applied to everything that is not swing.

title: The tonewheel organ
text: Mixer → Organ: tonebars, swell and Leslie, shown while the organ is the comping instrument or the second one: nine tonebars, a registration menu, Leslie (Automatic / Slow / Fast / Stopped), Swell pedal (Automatic / By hand), key click. The chorus, the pedal’s range, the drive and the speaker’s own numbers are in Mixer → Tone (EQ), in the organ’s amp. Settings are kept in the browser (localStorage.btOrgan, and btAmp for the amp).

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
Percussion, the lower manual, pedals, V1 to V3 and C1, C2.
Tapering (each wheel’s own level across the keyboard), which a commenter on Electric Druid calls the main reason for the instrument’s scream.
Leakage between neighbouring wheels at other pitches; contact bounce note by note.
The cabinet: no reflections, no horn tone, one tube stage for both rotors.
Tonebar moves, chorus on and off, and registration changes are not played by the band: only the pedal and the speed.
The comping is the piano’s voicings. An organist’s held chords with a moving finger under a held top note (Healy, Ex. 2) are not written.

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
When do you reach for fast: into every chorus, or only the last one? On held chords? At endings?
In jazz, do you leave the speaker slow, stopped, or off altogether with the chorus doing the work?
Where does your foot sit when comping: about half, or lower? How far do you open into a chorus?
Your comping registration, and whether you change it between verse and chorus.
Chorus C3 always on, or only for some styles?

title: DWIM on the Notation page
text:
“Do what I mean”: select some music, press DWIM, and the page shows the other ways that music could have been written, best first, each with a small score and a Use this button. The Notation page (tools/notation.qmd) offers it; the engine is Chord Entry’s (ChordEntry.alternatives) and the panel is MelodyDwim (apps/shared/melody-dwim.js), shared with the Chord Entry page.
This file is the plan and the record: what works now, how it stays working long after a take, and what is still to build. Keep it up to date when DWIM changes.











Kind
Needs
Examples
Status




Re-reading a take
the take’s log (every key down/up with its time, and the settings)
staccato vs note + rest, triplets or not, swing or straight, eighth vs sixteenth grid, plainest vs as-released note ends, grace notes, pickup
built


Re-writing what is written
only the notes on the page
enharmonic spelling (F♯ / G♭), a chord’s other names (C6 / Am7), tie vs dotted note, octave of a passage, meter (6/8 vs 3/4), key
planned, below



Re-reading is the stronger kind: it goes back to how the music was played and reads it again, so it can recover things the first reading threw away (a note too short to keep, a triplet read as eighths). It can only work where the page still has the playing.



On the Chord Entry page a take’s log lives only until the next take. Here it is kept with the chunk:
chunk.takes = [{ voice, log, from, bars, sig: [per-bar signature] }]

log is ChordEntry.take(...).log(): { v, cfg, events }. It is small (a few kilobytes for a page of music) and is saved with the piece (localStorage), so DWIM works after a reload, tomorrow, next month.
voice is the voice the take was written into (a take for voice 2 does not answer for voice 1).
from is the chunk bar where the take’s first bar sits (0 when it was recorded into the chunk; it moves when a split or merge moves the take), and bars is how many bars the take wrote.
sig[b] is a signature of what the take wrote in bar b (its rhythm and pitches, NotationDoc.barSig).

When it still applies. DWIM compares each selected bar’s signature now with the one recorded. A bar that is unchanged is fully “the take’s”. A bar that was edited (a note moved, a rhythm pattern added) is reported: “Bar 3 was changed after the take: using a reading replaces your changes in that bar.” Using a reading is still allowed: it is your call. Bars outside the take (added later) cannot be re-read.
What survives what.







Operation
What happens to the take




editing notes elsewhere in the chunk
nothing; only the edited bars report a change


splitting the chunk on a bar line
each half keeps the take, with its bars counted from where the half starts (from)


splitting inside a bar
the take is kept by the first half only for its whole bars; the bar that was cut is reported as changed


merging two chunks
both takes are kept, the second one’s bars shifted by the first chunk’s length


duplicating a chunk or a section
the copy keeps the take: DWIM works on the copy too


a new take into the same bars and voice
replaces the old one there


reading ABC or ChordPro in
takes are not in ABC: they are dropped (the page says so)



Using a reading replaces only the selected bars of that voice (NotationDoc.replaceBars) and puts the new signatures in the take, so those bars count as “the take’s” again. The take’s own settings are not changed: the next DWIM still lists every reading, and its “As first written” card is the take’s original reading, not the one you chose.




Select on the staff: click a note (that bar), or shift-click a second note (all the bars between).
DWIM is enabled when the selection lies in one chunk and that chunk has a take for that voice.
The DWIM panel opens with those bars; its own From / To boxes can widen or narrow the range.
Each card: what the reading changes, why someone would mean it, its cost (lower is plainer; notes left out cost most), and Use this.

Takes come from Play it in time. Chords from a take have their own DWIM (below) and are not touched by melody readings.



These work on any music on the page, typed, pasted or played. Each is a list of candidates with a cost, in the same panel, so the user sees one DWIM, not several tools.

Chords. Every chord played in (one a bar, or in a take) keeps the notes that were played (chord.midis). ChordEntry.analyse(midis, { all: true }) already returns every reading that fits (C6 / Am7, slash or not); DWIM on a chord lists them. Typed chords have no notes; for those, offer enharmonic names only (C♯m / D♭m).
Spelling. A selected note or span: the other spelling of each note out of the key (F♯ / G♭), using ChordEntry.spellNotes with the chord of the bar, which is what Chord Entry does for takes. Needs a spelling override on the note (pitches hold MIDI numbers; add spell: { k: "Gb" } beside them).
Rhythm, plainer. Without the playing, the written durations can still be re-read: a note and rest pair as one staccato note, a dotted note vs a tie, sixteenth pairs as eighths when the meter allows.
Meter. A chunk’s rhythm read in another meter with the same length of bar (6/8 vs 3/4, 2/2 vs 4/4), scored by how many notes cross beats; useful after a take recorded in the wrong meter.
Octave. A passage that sits far from the voice’s clef: one octave up or down.
Key. The key guess (NotationDoc.guessKey) with its runners-up and their scores, so a doubtful key can be compared and chosen; still confirmed by the user.

Order of work: 1 (data is already there), 2, then 3–6 as they are wanted.

node tests/abc/notation.cdp.js: a take recorded (synthetic events), saved, the page reloaded, DWIM run on a bar, a reading used.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text: Open the Emo / pop-punk style in the Backing Track

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
What it is
Guitar-band rock at punk tempos with melodic, often confessional singing: a distorted guitar chugging palm-muted power chords in the verse, ringing open in the chorus, over root eighths and a rock beat, with half-time choruses and breakdowns.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
A little history
Emo (“emotional hardcore”) began in Washington, D.C., in 1985 with Rites of Spring and Embrace, who took hardcore punk’s speed into more personal songs. The 1990s brought a quieter, intricate “Midwest emo” (Cap’n Jazz, American Football). Pop-punk runs from the Buzzcocks and the Ramones to Green Day’s Dookie (1994), which sold millions, then Blink-182. Around 2000-2007 the two merged into a mainstream sound: Jimmy Eat World, My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy, Paramore. It came back in the 2020s, from Olivia Rodrigo to a revival of the bands themselves.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root eighths. Comping: palm-muted chugging in verses, open strumming in Chorus bars.
Drums: rock backbeat; mark bars Half-time for a half-time chorus or breakdown.

title: Boogaloo
text: Open the Boogaloo style in the Backing Track

title: Boogaloo
text:
What it is
A jazz band playing straight (not swung) eighth notes over a repeated bass figure, with piano or organ chords locked to the riff and a backbeat on the drums. It sits between hard bop, R&B and Latin music.

title: Boogaloo
text:
A little history
The word covers two related things from the mid-1960s. Latin boogaloo was a New York dance music that mixed Cuban son and mambo with R&B; Joe Cuba’s Bang! Bang! (1966) and Pete Rodríguez’s I Like It Like That (1967) were hits. In jazz, soul jazz players on labels like Blue Note took up the same straight eighths. Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man (1962) and Lee Morgan’s The Sidewinder (recorded 1963) came first, and Lou Donaldson’s Alligator Bogaloo (1967) put the name on the jazz version. Drummers such as Idris Muhammad and Bernard Purdie played a backbeat with busy sixteenth-note hi-hats; the tunes were often blues forms over one riff. Mongo Santamaría’s cover of Watermelon Man (1963) carried the Latin side, with congas, back into the charts, which is why the band adds a conga tumbao.

title: Boogaloo
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogaloo riff: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, fifth and flat seventh on 4.
Comping: stabs on the same rhythm as the riff.
Drums: straight-eighth backbeat. Congas: a tumbao.
Voicings: rootless jazz voicings.

title: Swing
text: Open the Swing style in the Backing Track

title: Swing
text:
What it is
The rhythm section of small-group jazz from the late 1930s onward: a bass that plays a note on every beat, a drummer whose main voice is the ride cymbal (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a) with the hi-hat closing on 2 and 4, and a piano or guitar that “comps” (accompanies, complements): short chords placed off the beat, answering the soloist instead of marking time.

title: Swing
text:
A little history
In the 1920s the bass part of a jazz band was usually a tuba or a slapped string bass playing on beats 1 and 3 (the two-beat feel; see Jazz ballad). In the Count Basie band of the mid-1930s, bassist Walter Page walked four even beats a bar, guitarist Freddie Green strummed a quiet chord on every beat, and drummer Jo Jones moved the time-keeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. Basie himself played sparse fills instead of a full stride left hand. That “All-American Rhythm Section” is where the modern swing feel comes from.
In the 1940s bebop drummers (Kenny Clarke, then Max Roach) moved the pulse to the ride cymbal and used the snare and bass drum for accents (“dropping bombs”). Pianists such as Bud Powell stopped playing on every beat and comped in short syncopated stabs. By the late 1950s, rootless left-hand voicings (Bill Evans, Wynton Kelly, Red Garland) became the standard piano sound: the bassist has the root, so the pianist plays the 3rd, 7th and colour tones. That is the sound the band’s piano uses here.

title: Swing
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Walking: root on beat 1, chord tones and scale steps, an approach note on beat 4.
Comping: syncopated rhythms chosen from a set of figures (the Charleston, anticipations, and so on).
Drums: ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, light comping on the snare.
Voicings: rootless piano voicings, shell voicings on guitar. Players add unmarked 9ths and 13ths.

Real walking lines move far more freely than any rule set; the band’s bassist is a beginner’s model.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text: Open the Hymn (four parts) style in the Backing Track

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
What it is
Congregational hymn accompaniment: soprano, alto, tenor and bass moving together, one chord per melody note or two, each held until the next, no drums. The organ is the obvious instrument.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
A little history
Martin Luther’s chorales (from the 1520s) gave Protestant congregations hymns to sing; J. S. Bach’s four-part harmonisations of them in his cantatas and passions (1720s-40s) became the model of how to write harmony, and still are in theory classes. In England, Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley in the 1700s wrote the texts; the collection Hymns Ancient and Modern (1861) and The English Hymnal (1906, music edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams) set the four-part style of the Anglican hymnal. American hymnals, gospel song and shape-note singing grew from the same roots.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Held roots. Comping: hymn: three voices over the root. Drums: none.
Choose Church organ as the instrument for the other obvious sound.

title: Dance pop
text: Open the Dance pop style in the Backing Track

title: Dance pop
text:
What it is
The disco beat and its descendants: a kick drum on every beat (four on the floor), the open hi-hat on every off-beat, a bass jumping between the root and its octave, and chords on a 3+3+2.

title: Dance pop
text:
A little history
Disco grew out of New York and Philadelphia clubs in the early 1970s. Earl Young, the drummer of Philadelphia International’s house band MFSB, is often credited with the steady kick and open hi-hat (The Love I Lost, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, 1973). The octave bass became disco’s other mark (Chic’s Bernard Edwards). Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer’s I Feel Love (1977) put the beat on synthesizers and pointed toward house and techno (Chicago and Detroit, mid-1980s). Since then the four-on-the-floor beat has stayed at the centre of dance pop: Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Daft Punk, Dua Lipa.

title: Dance pop
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Octaves. Comping: a 3+3+2, on the electric piano. Drums: four on the floor.

What it is

title: Folk carol

A little history
Many English carols are older than the hymns sung beside them: dance songs and wassails collected by Cecil Sharp and Ralph Vaughan Williams in the early 1900s and published in The Oxford Book of Carols (1928). The British folk revival of the 1960s and the folk-rock bands that followed (Steeleye Span, Fairport Convention) played them with guitars, fiddles and drums, and many carol albums since have done the same.

title: Calypso

title: Calypso
text:
What it is
The topical song of Trinidad: a singer (the calypsonian) with a witty, often political lyric over a bouncing 2/4, with a strummed guitar or cuatro, a bass on root and fifth, and chords on the off-beats.

title: Calypso
text:
A little history
Calypso (earlier kaiso) grew out of the songs of Trinidad’s Carnival in the 1800s: the chantwell leading call-and-response songs in French Creole, stick-fighting songs, and the music of the Spanish Venezuelan string bands. By the 1910s-20s it was sung in English and recorded in New York. Calypso tents competed each Carnival season, and singers took grand names: Atilla the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader, Lord Kitchener, the Mighty Sparrow. Lord Invader’s Rum and Coca-Cola (sung at the 1943 Carnival) became an American hit for the Andrews Sisters in 1945, and Invader later won a lawsuit over its royalties; and Harry Belafonte’s album Calypso (1956) was the first LP to sell a million copies. Jamaica’s mento is a cousin, and in the 1970s Lord Shorty mixed calypso with Indian rhythms into soca, now Carnival’s main music.

text:

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: chords on every off-beat. Drums: a calypso beat.

title: Jazz ballad
text: Open the Jazz ballad style in the Backing Track

title: Jazz ballad
text:
What it is
A slow standard played by a jazz rhythm section: the bass on beats 1 and 3 (a two-feel), held chords on the piano, and brushes stirring the snare or a soft ride. The band leaves room for the melody.

title: Jazz ballad
text:
A little history
The two-feel is older than walking bass. New Orleans and 1920s dance bands put the tuba or string bass on 1 and 3, and when the bass began walking in the 1930s (see Swing), the two-feel stayed on as the lighter gear: bands play the head of a tune in two and start walking for the solos. On ballads it never has to leave. Brushes, used on drums since the 1920s, became the ballad sound through drummers such as Jo Jones and later Philly Joe Jones and Ed Thigpen. Pianists filled the long chords with the rich voicings that came from Ellington, Billy Strayhorn and later Bill Evans.

title: Waltz (in one)
text: Open the Waltz (in one) style in the Backing Track

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
What it is
A fast 3/4 in which the listener feels one beat a bar, not three: the bass on 1, light chords on 2 and 3, brushes, bars grouped in fours.

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
A little history
The waltz rose from Austrian and South German country dances in the late 1700s and took over the ballrooms of Vienna in the early 1800s with Joseph Lanner and the Strauss family (Johann Strauss II’s The Blue Danube, 1867). Played fast, the pulse is one per bar, and phrases come in fours and eights. The waltz then spread everywhere: music-hall and parlour songs, country waltzes (Tennessee Waltz), jazz waltzes, and many carols and folk songs that are sung in a quick 3/4.

title: Tango
text: Open the Tango style in the Backing Track

title: Tango
text:
What it is
The dance music of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in 2/4 or 4/4, played here on its oldest rhythm: the habanera (dotted eighth, sixteenth, two eighths), which also underlies the 3+3+2 of a lot of later pop.

title: Tango
text:
A little history
The habanera was a Cuban song and dance of the mid-1800s that spread through Spain, Mexico and the Río de la Plata ports (Bizet borrowed one for Carmen, 1875). In the poor neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires in the 1880s and ’90s it mixed with the milonga, Spanish and Italian song, and African Argentine candombe into the tango. Early groups were flute, violin and guitar; the bandoneón (a German button accordion) arrived around 1900 and became the tango’s voice. Carlos Gardel’s Mi noche triste (1917) began the sung tango. The 1940s orquestas típicas (Juan D’Arienzo, Aníbal Troilo, Osvaldo Pugliese) moved to a driving marcato in four; from the 1950s Astor Piazzolla’s nuevo tango added jazz and classical counterpoint.
The band plays the habanera rhythm, the older and more widely useful of tango’s rhythms; the four-beat marcato of the dance orchestras is not modelled.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text: Open the John Prine Fingerpicking style in the Backing Track

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:
What it is
A steel-string guitar played with the thumb and fingers at once: the thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat while the fingers pluck the chord on the off-beats or pinch with the thumb. No drums, an upright bass doubling the thumb.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:
A little history
Alternating-thumb picking runs back to Black guitarists in the South of the 1920s: Mississippi John Hurt recorded for OKeh in 1928, and Elizabeth Cotten played Freight Train left-handed. In Kentucky, Arnold Shultz, Ike Everly and Mose Rager handed it to Merle Travis, after whom “Travis picking” is named, and Chet Atkins spread it through country guitar. The 1960s folk revival brought it to singer-songwriters. John Prine (1946-2020), the Chicago postman whose first album (John Prine, 1971) contains Paradise, Hello in There and Angel from Montgomery, played a plain thumb-and-fingers style under plain-spoken songs.

text:

title: Reggaeton
text: Open the Reggaeton style in the Backing Track

title: Reggaeton
text:
What it is
Spanish-language dance music from Puerto Rico and Panama, built on the dembow: the kick on every beat, and the snare on the last sixteenth of beat 1 and the and of 2 (and again in beats 3 and 4), a 3+3+2 in sixteenths over each half bar, under long synth chords and a rapped or sung vocal.

title: Reggaeton
text:
A little history
The rhythm is named after Shabba Ranks’ Jamaican dancehall record Dem Bow (1990), whose riddim (the backing track, by Steely & Clevie, built on their Poco Man Jam) was copied everywhere. In Panama, artists such as El General sang Spanish lyrics over dancehall riddims (reggae en español). In Puerto Rico in the 1990s DJ Playero and others made underground mixtapes on the same beats; the name reggaeton took hold around the turn of the century. Daddy Yankee’s Gasolina (2004) was the international breakthrough, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s Despacito (2017) one of the most-streamed songs ever, and Bad Bunny the genre’s biggest star of the 2020s.
