title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text: Tonal patterns are short groups of pitches we learn by ear first, with solfège, before we ever name a key signature. The foundation is the major tonic and dominant.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Stepwise motion
The most basic tonal pattern is stepwise: Do – Re – Mi – Fa – Sol and back down. Sing it on a neutral syllable first, then with solfège, then connect it to what you see on the staff.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Tonic and dominant

Tonic (Do – Mi – Sol): the “home” chord, restful.
Dominant (Sol – Ti – Re): the “tension” chord that wants to resolve home.

Hearing the difference between these two is the single most important tonal skill in beginning band.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Practice steps

Sing Do, then find Sol.
Sing the tonic arpeggio, then the dominant.
Go to Practice → Tonal Patterns and play major stepwise patterns, singing along with solfège.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Pop singing sounds like talking on pitch. The words come first, the tone stays close to your speaking voice, and the style lives in small things: how a note starts, a little cry or breath, a run at the end of a line. This lesson builds those things one at a time, from breathing to riffs and harmony.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. The exercises are written for a middle voice. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower, as usual. Exercises marked Step up climb a half step each time you press it, the way a warm-up works through the range. Click a heading to fold a section away.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Breath and posture
Stand as if you were about to talk to a friend across the room: feet under the hips, knees soft, head level, shoulders loose. Breathe in low and quietly, so the belly and lower ribs widen and the shoulders don’t rise. Then let the air out slowly and steadily, without squeezing.
Exercise: hiss out on “sss” for a count of 8, then 12, then 16, keeping the sound even. Then do the same on a hum.
The aim isn’t a huge breath. It’s a steady one you don’t have to fight.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Starting the note: the onset
A note can start three ways:

Breathy: air first, then sound, as in a sigh, “hhhey”.
Hard: a little click of the vocal folds first, as in “uh-oh!”.
Balanced: air and sound together.

Pop uses all three for effect, but a balanced onset is home base. Sing the five notes below on “mum”, starting each note gently with the M.



Now sing the first note three times, once with each onset: “hhhum”, “’um” and “um”. Hear the difference, then go back to the balanced one.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Speech level and the mix
Your speaking voice and your high, light voice (head voice) join somewhere around the middle of your range. Pop singers keep the sound speech-like through that join. That blend is the mix. The safest way to find it is with exercises that keep the throat easy: lip trills (a horse’s “brrr”) and a bratty “nay”.
Sing this on a lip trill first, then on “nay” (bright and a bit nasal, like a teasing kid). Let the sound stay small at the top. Don’t shout up there.



As you step up, the top note will want to “flip” into a lighter sound. Let it flip at first. Over weeks, the “nay” helps the flip smooth out into a mix.

If your jaw juts or your neck tightens at the top, go back down two steps and make the sound smaller. Pop high notes come from a lighter, more speech-like voice, not from more push.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Vowels and words
Sing the words the way you’d say them: “love” is “luv”, not an operatic “lahv”. Two habits help.

Sing on the vowel and get to the consonant late. In “night”, hold “ah” and save the “-eet” ending for the very end of the note.
Narrow the vowel a little on high notes. “Ah” leans toward “uh”, and “ee” toward “ih”. The word still reads, and the throat stays easier.

Sing this line on “I can’t stop thinking ’bout you”, holding the vowels and putting the consonants late.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Belt, carefully
Belting is the strong, speech-like sound of pop and musical theatre on high notes, like a call across a playground: “Hey!”. Done well it is bright and forward, not shouted. Keep it short at first, and keep it well inside your comfort zone.




Belt for a few minutes at a time, not a whole session. If you feel any squeeze in your throat, go back to “nay” (the previous section). A teacher in person is the best guide for belting.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Riffs and runs
A run is a quick string of notes on one syllable, usually at the end of a phrase. Most pop runs come from the pentatonic scale. Learn each run slowly, on “ah”, until every note is clean. Then speed it up.
This run starts on A minor pentatonic: A, C, D, E, G.



And a common descending one from C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A.



Practice: sing each run at half speed with a metronome, then at full speed. A clean slow run is worth more than a fast blur.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Style: cry, breath and flips
These colours are what make a singer sound like pop:

Cry: a slight whimper or sob in the tone, like the edge of tears. It lightens the sound and helps it climb.
Breathy tone: let a little air into the start of a quiet phrase for intimacy. Don’t use it all the time, or the voice tires.
Flip (a yodel break): let the voice jump into a lighter sound for a moment on the way up, as in many folk and R&B lines.
Fry: the creaky sound at the bottom of the voice, used to start a phrase. Keep it light and brief.

Sing the line below twice: plainly, then adding a flip on the high note and a little breath at the start.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Phrasing and the mic

Sit a little behind the beat. Pop singers often land a word just after the beat, like a relaxed conversation. Try a line both ways with the Backing Track playing.
Shape each phrase. Most lines rise toward an important word and fall away after it.
Use the mic. Sing close (a finger or two away) for quiet, intimate lines. Pull back a few inches for loud notes, so they don’t blast. Point the mic at your mouth, not your chin.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Harmony: singing a third above
Backing vocals often sing a third above the melody: two scale steps higher, moving in parallel with it. Sing the melody below, then sing the harmony line written above it.



Practice: play it and sing the melody (the lower line), then the harmony. Then sing the harmony while the recording plays the melody.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Where to go next

Jazz singing: swing, scat and singing the changes.
Classical singing: breath, pure vowels and legato.
Four-chord loops: sing melodies and harmonies over the loops of most pop songs.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
This lesson is for a drummer who can already play a basic beat: the bass drum on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4, and something steady on top. It is about the “something on top”, and about everything the hi-hat can do besides keeping time. You need a hi-hat with a pedal, a snare and a bass drum. Each step is a little harder than the one before; stay on a step until you can play it through the whole chorus without watching your hands.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the groove written large and the whole chorus on a drum staff. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the note that is sounding lights up in the notation. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. The straight steps are played over four bars of F7 by the Straight-eighth rock or Acoustic strum band, and the swing steps over the 12-bar blues by the Swing band. Each step starts at its own tempo; the strip at the bottom changes the tempo, and the Feel menu changes the band. If you cannot yet play a step at its tempo, slow it down until you can.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 0. The three sounds of the hi-hat
text:
0. The three sounds of the hi-hat
The hi-hat is two cymbals on a stand, one above the other, with a pedal that opens and closes them. That gives it three sounds you will use all through this lesson.

Closed, with the stick. The pedal is down, the cymbals are together, and you hit the top one. A short, tight “tick”. This is the hi-hat sound you hear in most rock.
Open, with the stick. You let the pedal up a little, so the cymbals are apart, and hit. The sound rings and hisses until something stops it.
Closed, with the foot. You press the pedal and the cymbals come together on their own, with no stick. A soft “chick”.

Click a button to hear each one, and the last button to hear an open note being closed.


Closed, stick


Open, stick


Closed, foot


Open, then the foot


Here is how each is written. All three are an ✕, because they are cymbals. A closed note sits above the staff. An open note is the same ✕ with a small circle over it. A note played with the foot is an ✕ below the staff, and its stem points down like the bass drum’s. Click a head to hear it.



The foot closes the cymbals, and that stops an open note. When the cymbals come together, whatever was ringing ends. So an open hi-hat rings until the next closed note or the next foot note cuts it off, whichever comes first. On this page the band’s drummer does the same: press “Open, then the foot” and listen to the open note stop dead. Hearing where an open note ends is as important as hearing where it starts.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat
text:
1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat
The plainest rock beat. The closed hi-hat plays all four beats, the bass drum plays on 1 and 3, and the snare plays on 2 and 4. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud and make the hi-hat as even as the clock.



Two things at once, then three. Start with the hi-hat and the snare alone; add the bass drum when the hands are steady. The hi-hat does not slow down when the snare lands.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat
text:
2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat
Now the hi-hat plays twice as often, eight notes to the bar. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. The notes on the numbers fall with the bass drum and the snare; the notes on the “ands” fall in between. The bass drum is still on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4.



Keep the right hand moving in one smooth, even stroke, down on the beat and down on the “and”, and let the snare and the bass drum fit themselves around it.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
3. Accents
The same eighth notes, but now they are not all the same. Lean on the notes that fall on the beats and play the “ands” lightly. The usual way to get this is to hit the beats with the shoulder of the stick, on the edge of the hi-hat, and the “ands” with the tip, on top of it; the beats come out louder and brighter, the “ands” softer. The groove starts to breathe.
In the notation, an accent mark (>) is written over each note that is meant to be louder than its neighbours. Look for the mark over the beats in the staff below; the “ands” have none.



Listen with Drums alone. Then play it on a practice pad and try making the difference between the two kinds of note smaller and larger.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
4. The off-beats alone
Take the hi-hat off the beats and play it only on the “ands”: and of 1, and of 2, and of 3, and of 4. The bass drum plays on every beat, and the snare is still on 2 and 4. The beats are now played by the feet and the left hand, and the right hand plays in the gaps.



Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud, and tap your foot on the numbers. The hi-hat sits on the words you say between the taps.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
5. Opening the hi-hat
Go back to the eighth notes of step 2, and open the hi-hat once: on the and of 4, the last note of the bar. Open it as you hit, let it ring through the end of the bar, and close it on the 1 of the next bar, with the stick and the foot together. Because the cymbals come together, the open note stops right where beat 1 starts.



The open note is written with the small circle. The foot note under the staff, on beat 1 of each bar, is the pedal closing the cymbals. Play it once with the stick alone and once with the foot as well, and listen for the difference.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor
text:
6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor
The groove of a dance floor. The bass drum plays on every beat, the snare on 2 and 4, and the hi-hat plays closed on the beats and open on every “and”. Each closed note on the next beat shuts the open one before it, so you hear a “tss-tick, tss-tick” pattern. Your foot has to lift the pedal for each “and” and press it down again for each beat.



This is the same groove as “Four on the floor” in the Drums menu of the Backing Track, with the clap taken off so that you can hear the hi-hat by itself.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
7. Sixteenth notes with one hand
At a slow tempo the hi-hat can play four notes to every beat: sixteenths. Count “1 e and a 2 e and a 3 e and a 4 e and a”. One hand plays them all, sixteen to the bar. Play the beats a little stronger than the rest. The bass drum is on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4.



Start very slowly. A slow tempo is the whole point of this step: you are learning to keep sixteen even notes going while the other hand and both feet do something else. Speed up by a few beats a minute at a time.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
8. Sixteenth notes with two hands
Now use both hands on the hi-hat, right, left, right, left on the four notes of a beat. Both hands play on the hi-hat. On beats 2 and 4 the right hand has a different job: it comes off the hi-hat to play the snare. So the hi-hat is silent on those two notes, and you play fourteen hi-hat notes to the bar instead of sixteen.



The gap in the hi-hat on 2 and 4 is where the snare sits. Listen for it: the left hand keeps the sixteenths going without a break, and the snare lands in the space the right hand leaves.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
9. The foot alone
Now the hi-hat’s foot, which keeps time in a different way. First the jazz setting: time is played on the ride cymbal, and the hi-hat foot closes the cymbals on 2 and 4. The foot is the “chick” that goes with the ride pattern.



Next, a rock beat played on the ride cymbal, with eighth notes on the ride, the bass drum on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4, and the foot closing the hi-hat on all four beats. The right hand is on the ride cymbal, so the hi-hat is played by the foot alone. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” with your foot first, then add the rest.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
10. The swing hi-hat
The ride pattern of swing time, played on the hi-hat itself. The pattern is the same as on the ride: a note on each beat, with a skip note after beats 2 and 4. The cymbals are open on 1 and 3, so they ring, and closed on 2 and 4, where the foot closes them with the stick. The skip notes after 2 and 4 are closed. The eighths are swung: the first is long and the second short.



The foot notes on 2 and 4 under the staff are what stop the open notes, and so make the “tss-chick” of swing time. Listen with Drums alone, and notice where the open notes end.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
Where to go next

Play step 2 or 3 with the drums left out and keep the form of the vamp for ten choruses.
For the beat that goes with the 12-bar blues, the ride pattern and the shuffle, go to Blues for Drums.
Tools → Backing Track has every groove on this page in its Drums menu, under the names that start “Hi-hat”. The Cymbal menu has “Closed hi-hat”, which puts the hi-hat in place of the ride in the other grooves.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
A hammer-on and a pull-off make a second note without a second pick stroke. The fretting hand does the work. This lesson builds both from one finger on one string up to licks, scale runs and chord embellishments. Each step says what makes it easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong, then gives something to practice. The same technique is the left-hand half of Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs.
How to read the examples. Each exercise is written on a staff and in tablature. Tablature has one line a string, the high E on top, and a number for the fret. A slur between two notes is a hammer-on (the second note is higher, marked H) or a pull-off (the second note is lower, marked P), and both notes lie on one string. The staff is written an octave above where a guitar sounds, as guitarists read it. Press ▶ to hear it. The player picks every note, so on the recording the hammer-ons and pull-offs are separate soft attacks. Listen for the pitches and the rhythm and make the legato yourself. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger).

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
1. One finger on one string
Pick the open G string once. Then bring finger 2 down on the 2nd fret from above, quickly, with the tip, just behind the fret wire. The string rings the higher note with no pick. That is a hammer-on.




Easy because: one finger, one string and one pick stroke.
Hard because: the finger has to land hard enough to sound a note with nothing but its own speed. A soft landing gives a faint or no note.
What goes wrong:

The finger lands flat or too far back from the fret, and the note is dull or buzzes.
The hand lifts the finger a long way before it falls. A short, quick drop is enough, and it keeps the hand relaxed.
The other fingers fly up in sympathy. Let them hang near the strings.


Practice: ten hammer-ons in a row, each one picked once, with a rest between. Listen for the hammered note being as loud as the picked one. That takes some weeks to get.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
section: 2. From an open string: each finger
text:
2. From an open string: each finger
An open string is the easiest start, because no finger is holding the lower note. On the high E string, hammer each finger in turn: finger 1 at fret 1, finger 2 at fret 2, finger 3 at fret 3, finger 4 at fret 4.




Easy because: the open string is a fixed, ringing starting point.
Hard because: fingers 3 and 4 are weaker than 1 and 2, and they land softly at first.
What goes wrong: the weak fingers give the faintest notes. A finger landing next to the fret rather than behind it, a thumb riding over the neck, and the wrist drooping all make it worse.

Practice: the same drill on every string. Spend most of the time on fingers 3 and 4.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
3. Fretted to fretted
Now the lower note is fretted too. Press finger 1 down on the 2nd fret of the A string and pick. Finger 1 stays down while finger 2 hammers onto fret 3. When the higher finger lands it shortens the string, and the higher note sounds. Then try fret 4 with finger 3, then move up one fret and do it again.




Easy because: you already know both halves. The picked note is a plain fretted note, and the hammer is the move from section 2.
Hard because: two fingers have to be placed at once, one to keep the lower note ringing and one to hammer.
What goes wrong: the lower finger relaxes when the upper one lands and the first note dies. The hammer lands on a different string from the one picked. The hammered note is quieter than the picked one.

Practice: hold finger 1 down and hammer with finger 2, then 3, then 4, up and down the neck on one string.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
4. Pull-offs
A pull-off is the mirror image. Put two fingers down on the same string, the upper one at the higher fret and the lower one at the lower fret. Pick, then pull the upper finger off, and as it leaves, pull it a little sideways, toward the floor, so that it plucks the string. The lower finger or the open string rings.



Then with the lower note fretted:




Easy because: a pull-off is a hammer-on backwards. Section 3’s two-finger shape is the same.
Hard because: the lower finger must already be in place before the pull. A pull-off that only lifts the finger sounds weak. It has to flick.
What goes wrong:

The upper finger lifts straight up and the lower note is barely heard.
The finger drags across the next string and mutes it or sounds it.
The lower finger is not down yet when the upper one leaves.


Practice: put both fingers down, pick, and pull off. Play the picked note and the pulled note at an even loudness. Do the open-string version on every string, then the fretted one.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
5. Trills and hammer-pull loops
Put the two together. Pick once, hammer on, pull off, hammer on, and keep going, and the picked note turns into a trill. This is how guitarists get a long, fluttering note out of one pick stroke, and it is a fine test of both techniques at once.



Make it faster by halving the note values. Then end with a picked note, so the trill has a landing.




Easy because: nothing new: a hammer-on, a pull-off and a repeat.
Hard because: the notes have to stay even and loud while the hand tires.
What goes wrong: the notes fade away as the hand tires. The rhythm rushes. The lower finger gets pushed off when the upper finger hammers.

Practice: one measure at a slow tempo, with a metronome, and then speed up 4 beats a minute at a time. Stop when the notes begin to fade. Try it with fingers 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 and 3-4.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
6. In licks and scale runs
A lick is a short phrase. Written below are three, all in the key of A minor, in the first of the pentatonic positions, with the index finger on the 5th fret. Each slur is on one string. The first goes up with hammer-ons and the second comes down with pull-offs:



The third is in the open position and mixes both. The hammer-on from the open D string, and the pull-off back to the open G string, are the sound of a lot of blues and country playing:




Easy because: a pentatonic run is only two notes a string, and each pair is a hammer-on or a pull-off you know.
Hard because: the picks and the slurs alternate, and the hand has to change strings after each pair.
What goes wrong: the picked note at the start of each pair is rushed, and then the slurred notes sound like they are in a hurry. Playing it fast without the pick on the first note of each pair is the quickest way to lose the beat.

Practice: play the first two bars with a metronome at 70, and say the rhythm out loud, “one-and two-and”. When the slurred notes are as loud as the picked ones, speed up.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
section: 7. Inside chord shapes: the Sus embellishment
text:
7. Inside chord shapes: the Sus embellishment
Hammer-ons and pull-offs also decorate a chord. The best known is the Sus embellishment: strum an open chord, then hammer one finger onto a note next to a chord tone, so that the chord briefly becomes a sus chord, and pull it off to come home again. Jimi Hendrix used the idea all through Little Wing and Castles Made of Sand, and rock, folk and country guitarists use it all the time. On D, A and C the moving finger is the little finger or the ring finger on the top strings, and the rest of the chord stays put.
D. Strum D. The finger on the high E string (fret 2) stays down. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of the same string: the 3rd of the chord (F♯) becomes the 4th (G), and D becomes Dsus4. Pull off to come back.






A. Strum A. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of the B string, over the finger that holds fret 2: A becomes Asus4.






C. Strum C. The high E string is open. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of that string, then pull off. The top note moves from E to G and back.







Easy because: the chord is already under your hand. Only one finger moves, and only one fret.
Hard because: the hammering finger is the little finger, and it has to land without touching the next string or lifting a finger that is holding the chord.
What goes wrong:

The chord gets thinner because a finger of the shape lifted when the pinky came down.
The pinky lands on the pad instead of the tip, and mutes the string next to it.
It is played so fast and so loud that it stops sounding like a chord with a flourish.


Practice: strum the chord once, then hammer and pull off with a steady pulse, one decoration to a chord. Play along with the band: the chart is D, A, C, D, one bar each. Do the embellishment on each chord in time.



Unlocks: Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs; the open-chord decorations of pop changes for guitar; guitar chord shapes by hand.

title: Drum groove: Light time
text:
The pattern
Very quiet eighths on the hi-hat, a soft kick on 1 and 3 and a light cross-stick on 2 and 4. No fills. A stand-in for brushes.
It belongs in Folk carol, Acoustic strum, Boom-chick and Piano ballad. Here it is in the folk carol style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Light time
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

The pattern
Two bars of sixteenth notes: eight groups of three, then four groups of two to square it up. Ghostbusters, Raise Your Glass. For slow and medium tempos.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth on every beat
text:
The pattern
Root, fifth, root, fifth: a note on every beat, short. Now and then, mostly at the end of a four-bar phrase, the last three eighth notes of the bar run up the scale (5-6-7) into the next bar’s root. In 3/4 it is root, fifth, fifth.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth on every beat
text:

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth on every beat

title: Comping rhythm: Driving eighths
text:
The pattern
The chord on every eighth note, the beats a little louder than the off-beats.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Driving eighths
text:
Step 1: Quarter-note chords
Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Driving eighths
text:
Step 2: Driving eighths, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The chord on every eighth note, beats a little louder. On piano, the right hand bounces from the wrist; on guitar, all downstrokes. Keep it tight with the hi-hat.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: Driving eighths
section: Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band
text:
Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

title: Comping rhythm: Driving eighths
text:
Step 4: On the guitar
The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

title: Comping rhythm: Driving eighths
section: Step 5: Two chords in a bar

title: Bass line: Killer Joe: two-bar vamp
text:
The pattern
A two-bar figure for two chords a whole step apart: the root held for two beats, then two quarter notes that climb into the next root from below (C, G, A into B flat; B flat, G, B into C).
It belongs in Swing and Boogaloo. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Killer Joe: two-bar vamp
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Killer Joe: two-bar vamp
text:
Step 2: Two-feel
Half notes on beats 1 and 3, root then fifth, with an occasional pickup into the next bar. The lighter feel a band often plays on the head before the bass starts to walk.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Two chords a whole step apart, two bars each. Hold the root for two beats, then two quarter notes climbing into the next root from below. The same shape takes you down from C7 to B♭7 and back up.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
The pattern
One note on every beat (four quarter notes in 4/4, three in 3/4, dotted quarters in 12/8): the root on beat 1 when the chord changes, chord tones and scale steps in between, and an approach note on beat 4 that leads into the next bar.
It belongs in Swing and Jazz ballad. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
Step 2: Two-feel
Half notes on beats 1 and 3, root then fifth, with an occasional pickup into the next bar. The lighter feel a band often plays on the head before the bass starts to walk.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
Step 3: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
Step 4: Walking, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Beat 1: the root. Beats 2 and 3: any two other chord tones or scale steps. Beat 4: a note one fret above or below the next bar’s root. Start from the chord tones of the step before and change only beat 4, then free up beats 2 and 3.

The whole band, at 120 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s bass off and take the part yourself.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: swing time
text:
The pattern
The ride pattern played on the hi-hat itself: open on 1 and 3, closed on 2 and 4 with the skip note after them, the foot closing the cymbals on 2 and 4. Swung. Nothing else.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: swing time
text:
Step 1: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: swing time
text:
Step 2: Ride pattern (learning swing, 2)
The swing ride pattern and nothing else: the cymbal on every beat with a skip note before 3 and before 1 (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a), and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The ride pattern played on the hi-hat: open on 1 and 3, closed on 2 and 4 with the skip note. The foot closes the cymbals on 2 and 4.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: syncopated
text:
Step 2: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
Three held chords in a bar of eight eighth notes, grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Clocks, Shape of You, Eye of the Tiger.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

text:
The pattern
The root on every beat and the root an octave up on every off-beat.
It belongs in Dance pop. Here it is in the dance pop style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Octaves (disco)
text:
Step 1: Roots on every beat
Start with something simpler. The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Octaves (disco)
text:
Step 2: Root eighths
The root on every eighth note, the beats a little louder: the rock bass line under With or Without You and a thousand others.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Octaves (disco)
text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Root on the beat, the same note an octave higher on the off-beat. The octave is two strings up and two frets up: the hand stays in one place and the plucking hand jumps strings. Keep both notes short and the off-beats as loud as the beats.

text:

text:
Step 2: Root and fifth
The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

The pattern
The strum most songbooks start with: down on 1, down-up on 2, then up, down-up through 3 and 4 (the hand misses the strings on beat 3).

title: Drum groove: 12/8
text:

Three eighths to every beat on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, backbeat on 2 and 4. In 4/4 the eighths are triplets.
It belongs in 12/8 doo-wop. Here it is in the 12/8 doo-wop style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: 12/8
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: quarter notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The first rock beat. In 3/4: hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: 12/8
text:
Step 2: Blues shuffle
Swung eighths all the way through on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. The Chicago blues beat.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: rocking
text:
The pattern
Quarter notes: the chord on 1, the thumb on 2, the top two notes on 3, the thumb on 4, over held left-hand octaves on the root. On the piano with the Standard voicing the chord is a triad in first inversion.
It belongs in Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Folk carol, Hymn (four parts) and 12/8 doo-wop. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: rocking
text:

Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: rocking
text:
Step 2: Hymn: four parts
Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart’s chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

How to play it. Left hand: an octave on the root, held. Right hand in quarter notes: the whole chord on 1, the thumb on 2, the top two notes on 3, the thumb on 4. The right hand rocks between the thumb and the top.

Snare on 2 and 4 with a syncopated kick: beat 1, the and of 2 and the and of 3. Eighths on the cymbal.

text:

Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.

title: Drum groove: Funk
text:

Eighths on the cymbal and a full snare on 2 and 4. The kick changes over four bars: 1, 3 and the and of 3; then 1, the and of 2 and 3; the last bar adds a pickup on the and of 4. Sixteenth-note fills.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:
The pattern
A repeated straight-eighths figure: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, then a fifth and flat seventh on beat 4 leading back to the root. The kind of line under Watermelon Man. In 6/8 and 12/8 it becomes a shuffle: each beat played long-short, climbing root, 3rd, 5th, 6th.
It belongs in Boogaloo. Here it is in the boogaloo style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:

The root on beat 1, again on the and of 2 and on beat 3, the same rhythm as the kick drum. Every second bar ends with an eighth note that leads into the next chord.

title: Comping rhythm: Strum: 3-3-2 accents
text:

The D, D-U, U-D-U strum with the weight moved to beat 1, the and of 2 and beat 4, the 3+3+2 grouping under a great many pop songs.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Strum: 3-3-2 accents
text:
Step 2: Strum: D, D-U, U-D-U
The strum most songbooks start with: down on 1, down-up on 2, then up, down-up through 3 and 4 (the hand misses the strings on beat 3).
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

The basic conga part, on one drum with the hands alternating: left-hand heel on 1, left-hand toe on the and of 1, a right-hand slap on 2, left toe on the and of 2, left heel on 3, left toe on the and of 3, then two right-hand open tones on 4 and the and of 4. Heel and toe are quiet; slap and open tones carry.
It belongs in Son montuno, Cha-cha and Boogaloo. Here it is in the cha-cha style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
section: Step 1: Open tones only (learning the tumbao, 1)
text:
Step 1: Open tones only (learning the tumbao, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the two right-hand open tones of the tumbao, on 4 and the and of 4. The first thing to play.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Conga part: Tumbao

Step 2: Right hand alone (learning the tumbao, 2)
The right hand of the tumbao by itself: a slap on 2, then open tones on 4 and the and of 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Conga part: Tumbao

text:
Step 3: Left hand alone (learning the tumbao, 3)
The left hand of the tumbao by itself: heel on 1, toe on the and of 1, toe on the and of 2, heel on 3, toe on the and of 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Conga part: Tumbao

Step 4: Tumbao, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Both hands: heel, toe, slap, toe, heel, toe, open, open. Heel and toe quiet; slap and open tones carry.

Step 5: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s congas off and take the part yourself.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text: The chord instruments fill the middle of the band. They play the notes the bass leaves out, in a rhythm that fits between the drums’ hits. This is called comping (short for accompanying). How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
1. The rhythm is the part
A guitar part is mostly a rhythm. The chords here never change, only the strumming pattern. Each one gives the same song a different energy.



Under a singer, long chords and fingerpicking leave the most room. Down-up eighths fill everything and suit a loud chorus. Many arrangements go from sparse in the verse to full in the chorus with the same chords.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
2. Voicing: which notes, how high
The same chord can be played with all six strings ringing (an open chord) or as three notes higher up the neck (a triad). Open chords fill the whole range from low to high. A small triad stays out of the bass’s way and out of the singer’s.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
3. Off the beat: the chop
In reggae and ska the guitar plays only on the off-beats: short and choked. Motown guitarists did something similar on 2 and 4, doubling the snare. A chord instrument that plays very little can still be the part everyone remembers.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
4. Jazz comping: piano and guitar
In jazz, the piano doesn’t play a pattern. It plays short chords, mostly off the beat, and answers the soloist. It also leaves out the root (the bass has it) and plays rootless voicings: the 3rd, 7th and colour notes.



A swing-era guitarist (Freddie Green in the Count Basie band) did the opposite: a short three-note chord on every beat, felt more than heard. Here are the two together. That’s what the next section is about.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
5. Two chord players at once
Two chord instruments that both play busy patterns in the same register fight. The fix is to give them different jobs: one plays the rhythm, the other holds long chords, or one plays low and the other high. The band does this by itself when a second chord player is added: switch each one off in turn.
Swing: piano comps, the guitar plays four to the bar.



Rock: the guitar strums, an organ holds long chords behind it. This is the classic “pad” organ of 60s and 70s rock and soul.



The organ is its own world. The next lesson takes it apart.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
6. Try it

In section 2, pick Open chords and turn the bass off. Then pick Triads. Which one needs the bass more?
In section 5, switch off the drums and bass and listen to only the two chord players. Can you hear which one keeps the rhythm and which one holds the harmony?

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
This is how a guitarist plays chords in a band on a 12-bar blues without a single barre chord: two or three well-chosen notes, moved by a fret at a time. You need to know how to fret a note and how the strings are numbered (6 is the low E, 1 is the high E). For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear it. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its guitarist plays exactly the notes in the diagrams, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the guitar to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. Find the key note on string 6. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on string 5. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on string 5. Three chords, three notes, and the hand stays where it is.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.



Play one long note per bar with the band and count the form: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Knowing where the roots are is what lets you find every chord shape that follows.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Play only those two notes and a listener still hears the chord, especially with a bass player underneath. The diagrams show all four notes of each chord, with the guide tones filled in. Click a chord name to hear the four notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



From the root: the 3rd is one string up and one fret back, the 5th is one string up and two frets on, and the ♭7th is two strings up at the same fret as the root.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
3. Guide tones on strings 5 and 4
Now play just the 3rd and 7th, as a two-note chord on strings 5 and 4. Look at the Superimposed view to see what makes this worth learning: the three chords are the same two-finger shape, one fret apart. From the I chord, move both fingers down one fret for IV and up one fret for V.
That works because the 3rd of one chord is a half step from the 7th of the next. Going from I7 to IV7, the 3rd drops a fret and becomes the ♭7th, and the ♭7th drops a fret and becomes the 3rd. Switch the labels to chord tones and watch the two notes swap names.
Up a tritone. The 3rd and ♭7th of a dominant chord are six frets’ worth of pitch apart, an interval called a tritone, and a tritone turned upside down is still a tritone. So the same two-finger shape six frets higher gives the same two notes of the same chord, with the 3rd and ♭7th changing places. Press Up a tritone to move all three chords there. That gives every chord two homes on each pair of strings. In keys where the lower home would run off the end of the neck (F and G♭ here), the diagrams start in the upper one, so the three shapes always stay one fret apart.



The hollow dot is the root. Where one is shown it is in reach on string 6 and you can add it; where none is shown, leave it to the bass player.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
text:
4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
The same pairs one string set higher sit under roots on both low strings, so every chord can have its root added. These three-note chords are shell voicings: root, 3rd and 7th with the 5th left out. A chord with its root on string 6 has the 7th on string 4 and the 3rd on string 3. A chord with its root on string 5 has the 3rd on string 4 and the 7th on string 3. Mute string 5 with the side of your finger when the root is on string 6.
First the two notes alone:



Then with the root. This is the rhythm guitar sound of the swing era. Up a tritone here moves each chord to its other shell: the root changes string and the 3rd and 7th change places above it.



The band’s guitarist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm, then try four even strokes to the bar (set the feel and tempo to taste).

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is one fret lower than a dominant chord’s. In a shell with the root on string 6, that puts the 7th and the minor 3rd at the same fret, under one finger.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Press Superimposed to see how little the hand moves through ii7, V7 and I7.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is with the shells from step 4 underneath.



Comp under the tune with a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3, and leave the riff room. Then look at the guide tones alone. The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a fret to become the ♭7th of IV, which is exactly what your guide-tone shape does at the same moment.

text:

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
The first lesson on this page’s loops stayed in major. Minor is different in one important way: the scale you play on is not the scale the chords come from. Natural minor has no leading tone, so the V chord is changed to get one. This lesson writes everything in A minor.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
1. The basic minor changes
Am, Dm, Em, Am: i, iv, v, i, all from the natural minor scale. The v chord, Em, is minor. It is pleasant and it is also weak: it has G, not G♯, so there is no leading tone to pull to A.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
2. The harmonic-minor V7
Am, Dm, E7, Am. One note changes, G to G♯, and the chord becomes the dominant. The G♯ is the leading tone and it rises to A. This is the chord that makes minor feel like a key and not a mode.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
3. The Picardy third
Am, Dm, E7, A. Finish on a major chord. The C of the A minor chord is raised to C♯. It is an old trick, for a hymn or a baroque piece: the music goes dark and the last chord turns the lights on.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
4. A walking bass
Am Am/G | Dm/F Dm | E7 | Am. The bass steps down A, G, F, then falls a third to D, and E7 and Am follow. The slash chord Am/G is an A minor chord over a G in the bass.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
5. ii° to V to i
Am, Dm, Bm7♭5 E7, Am. Put the half-diminished ii chord in front of the dominant. It is the minor version of the two-five: B, D, F, A, then E7. The bass falls a fifth from B to E, and again from E to A, the same circle-of-fifths motion as in the major two-five-one.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
Build your own
Choose each chord. The shaded bars differ from the basic minor changes.

title: Sound 14: The Vocoder
text:
A vocoder makes an instrument talk. It takes two sounds: a modulator (usually a voice) and a carrier (usually a synth playing chords). It measures how loud each band of frequencies is in the voice, moment by moment, and sets the loudness of the same bands in the synth to match. The synth keeps its pitch and chords; the voice supplies the words. It’s the robot voice of Kraftwerk, Herbie Hancock, Daft Punk and Laurie Anderson. It was invented at Bell Labs in the 1930s to squeeze speech down telephone lines.
How to use the page. Put on headphones: the microphone hears the speakers otherwise. Choose Microphone as the modulator (or the built-in Robot voice if there’s no mic), press ▶, then talk or sing while you play chords on the computer keys, the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Until you play, a chord is held for you.

title: Sound 14: The Vocoder
text: The vocoder

title: Sound 14: The Vocoder
text:
How it works
The vocoder is built from parts you have already met:

Split the voice into bands. A row of band-pass filters, each a different frequency from low to high, splits the voice into 16 or so bands.
Measure each band. An envelope follower on each band turns the wobbling band into a smooth level: how loud that band is right now. The bars under the controls show those levels.
Split the synth the same way. A second row of band-pass filters, at the same frequencies, splits the carrier.
Let the voice turn the synth up and down. Each band of the synth is turned up and down by the level of the matching band of the voice, and the bands are added back together.

A vowel is a pattern of loud bands (the formants, from the filter lesson), so the synth takes on the vowel. The pitch comes from the synth, which is why you can speak in a monotone and have it sing in chords.

title: Sound 14: The Vocoder
text:
Things to try

Bands. With 4 bands the words are barely understandable; with 16 they’re clear; with 32 it sounds almost like a voice through a synth-shaped filter. Old hardware vocoders had 8 to 20.
Band sharpness. Higher Q makes each band narrower: more ringing and more “robot”.
Envelope speed. Slow (5 Hz) blurs the words into a smooth pad; fast (60 Hz) keeps every consonant but gets gritty.
Let “s” sounds through. A synth has little energy in the very top, so “s”, “t” and “f” disappear. Real vocoders pass the voice’s top end straight through to keep the words clear.
Carrier. A sawtooth is best, because it has energy in every band for the voice to shape. A square works less well (it is missing every other harmonic). Noise as the carrier gives a whisper with no pitch at all.
Listen to the modulator or the carrier alone to hear what goes in.
Drum loop as the modulator makes the chord pulse in the rhythm of the drums, a trick used in dance music.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
This lesson is about making up your own melody over a twelve-bar blues, using Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet as the model. It is for any instrument. You should already be able to play the tune (it is taught in Blues for Violin and Saxophone, section 7) and know what the chords are (Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues).
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom sets up the page for you.
Where this page says “concert”, it means the note as the piano hears it.
How to use the page. Every line of notation has a ▶ Play button, and the note that is sounding lights up. The chord charts have ▶ Play with the band; the piano plays the written line unless you tick Leave out the melody. Under each note is its place in the chord (R = root) or its number in the scale.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
1. Start from the melody
The best first solo on any tune is the tune. It already fits the chords, it already has a rhythm, and the listener already knows it.



Three things about this melody are worth stealing.

It is a riff. One two-bar idea, played three times. A solo built from one idea that is repeated and changed a little sounds like it means something. A solo of new ideas in every bar does not.
It uses four notes: the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. You do not need many.
It leaves space. Each line ends on a long note. Half of each phrase is silence or holding.

Exercise. Play the tune. Then play it again and change one thing: leave a note out, repeat a note, or play the rhythm of the riff on a single pitch. Keep the long notes where they are. Do that for several choruses before you go on.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
2. Hitting the change
The most important moment in a blues is bar 5, where the home chord gives way to IV. In this tune the melody marks it with one note. In bars 1 to 4 the riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord (concert A when the tune is in F). In bars 5 and 6 that note drops a half step (concert A♭), and it is now the ♭7th of the IV chord. In bar 7 it goes back up.
A soloist who plays the higher note in bar 5 sounds lost: it is a half step away from a note the chord needs. A soloist who plays the lower one sounds like they know the tune. That is what players mean by hitting the change (or making the change).
Here is that move alone: one note per bar, the 3rd or 7th of each chord, taking the nearest one at every change.



Exercise. With Leave out the melody ticked, improvise using only the rhythm of the riff and the notes of this line: the upper note in bars 1 to 4, the lower one in bars 5 and 6, the upper again in bar 7. It is very little to play with. Hit the change every time, exactly on bar 5, before you add anything else.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
3. The minor blues scale
Six notes, and it can be played over the whole twelve bars without changing anything. That is why it is the first scale most improvisers learn.



Counted from the key note it is R, ♭3, 4, ♯4, 5, ♭7. Two of those are blue notes:

The ♭3 is the same pitch as the note that hit the change in section 2 (concert A♭ in F). Over the IV chord it is a chord tone. Over the home chord it rubs against the chord’s major 3rd, and that rub is the sound of the blues.
The ♯4 is a passing note between 4 and 5. Slide through it; do not sit on it.

What this scale does not have is the major 3rd of the home chord. Played for a whole chorus it sounds dark and tough, and it never quite says which chord you are on.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
4. The major blues scale
The brighter one. Counted from the key note: R, 2, ♭3, 3, 5, 6.



It has both thirds: the ♭3 and the major 3rd, side by side. That is the same pair of notes the melody uses to hit the change. Sliding from the ♭3 up to the 3 is one of the most recognisable sounds in the music. This scale fits the home chord perfectly, because its 3, 5 and 6 belong to it.
It fits the IV chord less well. Its major 3rd is the note that section 2 told you to leave in bar 5.
Putting the two together. Use each scale where it is strongest:








Bars
Chord
Scale to favour




1 to 4
I7
major blues: lean on the 3


5 and 6
IV7
minor blues: lean on the ♭3


7 and 8
I7
major blues again


9 to 12
ii7, V7, I7, V7
either; the minor blues scale covers all four



That table is the melody’s own plan. Blues in the Closet uses the major 3rd on the home chord and the lowered one on IV.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
5. The pentatonic scales
Take the ♯4 out of the minor blues scale and five notes are left: the minor pentatonic.



Take the ♭3 out of the major blues scale and you have the major pentatonic.



Why bother with scales that have fewer notes?

Nothing in them clashes. Neither scale has a half step in it, so no two of its notes rub against each other, and any of them can be held. They are the safest notes there are.
They fall under the hand. On guitar and bass the minor pentatonic is the first position most players learn, two notes on every string. On a wind or string instrument it is five notes with no awkward corners.
The minor pentatonic covers the whole chorus, exactly as the minor blues scale does. Use it when you want to think about rhythm and phrasing and not about notes.
A major pentatonic built on a chord’s own root always fits that chord. It is the chord’s root, 3rd and 5th plus its 2nd and 6th: no 4th and no 7th, the two notes that cause trouble. So one more way through the form is three pentatonics: the home chord’s in bars 1 to 4, the IV chord’s in bars 5 and 6, and so on.
Two for the price of one. The major pentatonic of the key has the same five notes as the minor pentatonic that starts a minor 3rd below it. Compare the scale below with the major pentatonic above. If you know one shape, you know the other.




The blues scales are these two pentatonics with one extra note each: the ♯4 added to the minor, the ♭3 added to the major. Those added notes are the blue notes.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
section: 6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
text:
6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
The blues scales treat the whole chorus as one sound. The other way to improvise is to give each chord its own scale. A dominant seventh chord takes the Mixolydian scale: a major scale with the 7th lowered. Its 1, 3, 5 and ♭7 are the chord, and the notes between join them up. (Where that lowered 7th comes from is explained in the “flat 7” panel of the instrument lessons.)
For the home chord:



For the IV chord:



Compare them note by note. They share every pitch but one. The home chord’s scale has its major 3rd; the IV chord’s scale has that note a half step lower, as its ♭7. It is the same half step as in section 2, the one the melody plays. Hitting the change and changing scale are the same act.
For the V chord:

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The two-five: Dorian
Bars 9 and 10 are ii7 then V7. A minor seventh chord takes the Dorian scale: a major scale with the 3rd and the 7th lowered.



Now look back at the V chord’s Mixolydian scale above. It is the same seven notes, started from a different place. The ii chord and the V chord of a two-five share one scale, so bars 9 and 10 need only one set of notes, and the melody shows it: the riff passes over both chords unchanged.
That scale is also the plain major scale of the key. So the whole chorus comes down to three sets of notes, each one note different from the last:

Bars 9, 10 and 12 (ii7 and V7): the major scale of the key.
Bars 1 to 4, 7, 8 and 11 (I7): lower its 7th. That is the home chord’s Mixolydian.
Bars 5 and 6 (IV7): lower the 3rd as well. That is the IV chord’s Mixolydian.

To hear the notes that tell these scales apart, this line plays the ♭7, 6, 5 and 3 of every chord, one bar each:

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. Your chorus
Nothing is written here. The band plays the changes and the chorus is yours. Tick Loop in the strip at the bottom to keep it going.



A plan for practice, one item per session:

The melody, varied a little more each chorus (section 1).
Only the two notes of the change, in the riff’s rhythm (section 2).
Only the minor blues scale, in two-bar phrases with two bars of rest after each.
Major blues scale on the home chord, minor blues on IV, following the table.
Three major pentatonics: the root’s own, for whichever chord is sounding.
Chord scales: one chorus where every phrase ends on the 3rd or ♭7 of the chord of the moment.
Trade fours with the band: you play four bars, rest four, play four.

In every one of them, hit the change in bar 5.
To hear what the chords are doing under your solo, see guide tones and the changes lesson.

title: Sound 11: Reverb
text:
Clap in a cathedral and the sound goes on for seconds after your hands stop. It bounces off the walls, the floor and the ceiling, thousands of times, each echo a little quieter and a little duller, until they blur into a smooth wash. That wash is reverberation, and every room has its own. A reverb effect puts a dry recording into a room that isn’t there.
How to use the page. The source starts as single hits, so you can hear each hit’s tail die away. The strip under the controls is the room’s impulse response: what one instant click would sound like in this room.

title: Sound 11: Reverb
text:
The room




Decay time (RT60): how long the tail takes to fall by 60 dB, which is about until you can’t hear it. A living room is about 0.5 s, a concert hall about 2 s, a cathedral 5 s or more.
Pre-delay: the gap before the reverb starts. In a big room the first reflection takes a while to come back. A little pre-delay keeps a voice clear in front of its reverb.
Damping: in real rooms the high frequencies die first, absorbed by air, carpet and people. Lower damping makes a darker, warmer tail.
Early reflections: the first few distinct echoes from the nearest walls. They tell your ear how big the room is before the tail arrives.
Mix: how far away the sound seems. More wet signal pushes it to the back of the room.

Try the presets: a small room, a hall, a cathedral, a plate (a big steel sheet with a pickup, used in studios since the 1950s: bright and dense, no early reflections) and reverse, the impulse response played backwards so each sound swells into itself.

title: Sound 11: Reverb
text:
How it is made: convolution
This reverb is a convolution reverb. It needs one thing: the impulse response of the room. To capture a real room, engineers play a click (or a sweep) in it and record what comes back. The computer then replays that recording once for every sample of the input, scaled by that sample’s level, and adds them all up. That’s a lot of arithmetic, which the browser does for us.
The impulse responses here aren’t recordings. They are made from decaying noise that gets duller as it fades, plus a few early reflections. That’s close to what a real room does, and it means every control can change the room instantly.

title: Sound 11: Reverb
text:
On music
Switch the source to the chords, the drum loop or your microphone (headphones on). Long reverb makes chords smooth and huge but turns drums to mush; fast music wants short reverb or a lot of pre-delay. Singing into the cathedral preset and listening to your own voice come back is the best way to learn what reverb does.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Watermelon Man is a 16-bar blues that a conga player can learn in an afternoon, once the tumbao is under the hands. If you have not played the tumbao yet, start with How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao. This page assumes the heel, toe, slap and open tones, and the part Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to take over. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both. The sounds are General MIDI stand-ins, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones are approximations: listen to a real player for the sound.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
The tune and its history
Herbie Hancock wrote Watermelon Man for his first album, Takin’ Off (Blue Note, 1962), with Freddie Hubbard, Dexter Gordon, Butch Warren and Billy Higgins on drums. No conga player is listed on that record. It is in F, in even eighths: Hancock said Higgins played “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. It goes at roughly 120 to 130 beats a minute.
Late in 1962 Hancock filled in on piano in the band of the conga player Mongo Santamaría for a weekend at a club in the Bronx, and Donald Byrd urged him to play the tune for Mongo. Mongo’s band recorded it on 17 December 1962 “in a cha-cha beat”, with Kako Baster on timbales, Victor Venegas on bass and Ray Lucas adding a backbeat on drums. The single came out on Battle in 1963 and reached the top ten or eleven of the Billboard Hot 100 (sources differ). It is slower than Hancock’s, and is often named as a starting point of boogaloo and Latin soul. A much later remake, on Head Hunters in 1973, has Bill Summers blowing into beer bottles after the Central African hindewhu.
What this lesson teaches, and what it does not. No published transcription of the conga part on Mongo’s record was found. What you learn here is the standard tumbao, the part a conga player plays in a cha-cha beat. Listen to the record and copy what you hear.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Reading the part
Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space; a low drum, when there is one, sits on a lower space. A plain head is the open tone (or the bass tone), an ✕ is the slap, a triangle is heel or toe, and a diamond is the muted tone. Two lines of words sit under the notes: the stroke (H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass) and the hand (L or R).

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
The form
It is a 16-bar blues: a 12-bar blues whose bars 9 and 10 (C7 and B♭7) are played three times. In F, with one chord to a bar:

Bars 1 to 4: F7, F7, F7, F7
Bars 5 to 8: B♭7, B♭7, F7, F7
Bars 9 to 12: C7, B♭7, C7, B♭7
Bars 13 to 16: C7, B♭7, F7, F7

The Backing Track has the same form as its “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset, with the band stopping on bar 14 (the break). The steps below use it.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
section: 1. The form, with the open tones only
text:
1. The form, with the open tones only
Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4, and nothing else. Count the sixteen bars out loud. Listen for the three C7 to B♭7 pairs in bars 9 to 14: that is the part of the form a 12-bar blues does not have.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
2. The right hand
Add the slap on 2. The right hand plays the slap, then the two open tones. The slap on 2 lands with the backbeat.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
3. The tumbao, slowly
Now the whole part: Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, hands L L R L L L R R, one bar at a time, in a cha-cha beat at about 100 beats a minute. Do not speed up to catch the band; keep the left hand quiet and the slap and open tones clear.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
4. The break
On bar 14 the band stops. The congas play one open tone on beat 1 with the band, then nothing, and come back in on bar 15 with the band. Count the silent beats. The two bars shown large are bars 13 and 14.



The bar after the stop is the hard part: nothing in the band tells you the time but your own counting. Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud through bar 14.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
5. With the melody
The tune, written in F, above the chart. The band plays it on the piano with the congas. Tick Leave out the tune to hear the congas and the band alone. In this step the band plays straight through the break, so the melody is not cut off.



Read the melody as you play. The riff in bars 1 and 2 is the line everyone knows.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
6. Mongo’s way and Herbie’s way
The same part in two styles. The first plays the congas in the Cha-cha at a moderate tempo, as Mongo’s band recorded it, with the break on bar 14. The second is the Boogaloo at about 126, with straight eighths and the break, nearer Hancock’s own tempo. Change between them with the Feel menu at the bottom. The part is the same tumbao in both.
Mongo’s way: Cha-cha, a moderate tempo.



Herbie’s way: Boogaloo, about 126.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
7. Two drums
As an extension, the same form with two drums in the Son montuno: every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. Which bar of the pair takes the low drum depends on the clave, and this lesson does not say which way the clave runs on the record. A one-bar tumbao avoids the question: stay with step 6 until you can play it through without thinking.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Where to go next

Play step 6 with the congas left out and the tumbao in your hands for ten choruses.
Learn the five strokes properly in How to Play Congas.
Blues for Drums has the same kind of steps for a drum kit.
Tools → Backing Track has the “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset and a Congas menu that works in any style.
Listen to Mongo Santamaría’s record and copy what you hear.
