title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
This lesson is for a guitarist who knows open chords and strumming but hasn’t played jazz. Its thirteen steps go in order of how simple the voicing is. First come more chord types in familiar shapes, then fewer strings, then fewer chord tones, then more colour. Guitar chord shapes by hand has the same chords in the order the hand finds them easy.
How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left and the nut at the top. Each dot shows its chord tone: R is the root, and 3, 5, ♭7, 9 and so on are counted up from it. The fret numbers under each diagram run from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Press ▶ to hear a shape. The staff writes the chords an octave above where they sound, which is how guitar music is written.
Each step has an ID, such as G-A3, that other lessons use to point back here.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A1 Open triads
A triad is root, 3rd and 5th. A guitar has six strings, so some of those three tones are doubled: C x32010 is C–E–G–C–E, with the 3rd on two strings. The doubled tones and ringing open strings give the bright sound of folk and pop. The 3rd decides major or minor, and it is the only difference between E and Em.



Practice: loop C, Am, F, G (four-chord loops, loop 1) until the changes land in time with no gap. Play F as the small shape xx3211 until you reach the barre (G-A3).
Unlocks: the strummed styles of the Backing Track: Acoustic strum, Straight-eighth rock, Boom-chick.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A2 Fifths (power chords)
Root and 5th, sometimes with the octave on top. There is no 3rd, so the chord is neither major nor minor. Fifths stay clear under distortion, where the 3rds of two chords would clash, and they fit whatever 3rd the bass or the singer supplies. This is also the first time a chord leaves a tone out, which every later step does too. The shape is the same with the root on string 6 or on string 5, so one fingering moves anywhere.



Practice: play a 12-bar blues in fifths. Then rock between the 5th and the 6th on the middle string (E5 to E6 to E5), the classic rock-and-roll rhythm figure.
Unlocks: palm-muted eighth notes in rock and pop-punk.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
section: G-A3 Barre chords: the E and A shapes
text:
G-A3 Barre chords: the E and A shapes
Any open shape can move up the neck if your index finger replaces the nut. The root is under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape and on string 5 for the A shape. Those two shapes give all twelve major and minor chords, and this is the point where the neck becomes a map rather than a list of chords. The physical side is in G-B8 and G-B9.



Practice: play one four-chord loop in three keys, naming each root as you land on it.
Unlocks: the same strums in every key; Motown / soul.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A4 Sus and add9
A sus chord replaces the 3rd with the 2nd (sus2) or the 4th (sus4). With no 3rd it is neither major nor minor, and it leans toward resolving: Dsus4 falls to D as G moves down to F♯. Add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 9th, the 2nd an octave up. It is sweet rather than tense. These are the colours of pop and 80s rock guitar, and the first chords in this sequence that go beyond a triad.



Practice: D, Dsus4, D, Dsus2, one bar each. Then alternate C and Cadd9.
Unlocks: sixteenth-note strums with hammer-ons, and fingerpicking (Travis pattern).

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A5 Dominant 7th
A dominant 7th is root, major 3rd, 5th and flat 7th. The 3rd and the ♭7 are a tritone apart, and a tritone wants to resolve. Going from G7 to C, the 3rd (B) rises a half step to C and the ♭7 (F) falls a half step to E. That pull is what makes a chord dominant, and it drives the blues and every jazz tune.



Practice: play G7 to C slowly and find the two notes that move by one fret. Then see blues for guitar.
Unlocks: Blues shuffle, and a 12-bar blues on I7, IV7 and V7.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A6 Minor 7th and major 7th
A minor 7th is a minor triad plus a ♭7. It sounds soft and open rather than dark. A major 7th is a major triad plus the 7th one fret below the root, and it sounds dreamy. Pop already uses both: Am7 and Cmaj7 turn up all over pop changes for guitar. In jazz these two types, together with the dominant 7th, make up most of the harmony.



Practice: Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7 (I–vi–ii–V) in open shapes. Then play it in F with barre shapes.
Unlocks: Bossa nova, and slow Charleston comping.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A7 Half-diminished and diminished 7th
Half-diminished (m7♭5) is a minor 7th with a flat 5th. It is chord vii in a major key (Bm7♭5 in C) and the ii chord in a minor key (see minor changes). A diminished 7th is a stack of minor 3rds, so the shape repeats every three frets with the same four notes. The F♯dim passing chord in pop changes is this chord.



Practice: slide a dim7 shape up three frets at a time. You’ll hear the same chord four times, with four different names.
Unlocks: the passing chords in turnarounds, and the minor-key ii–V–i.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A8 Shell voicings (root, 3rd, 7th)
The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones: they say what kind of chord it is. The 5th adds the least, because the bass and the key already imply it, so a shell leaves it out. Root, 3rd and 7th make a chord thin enough to sit under a singer or a solo, which is how a rhythm guitarist plays in a jazz band. Shells come with the root on string 6 (strings 6, 4 and 3) or on string 5 (strings 5, 4 and 2). The Chord Library calls these Shell (R-3-7).



Practice: play C7, F7 and G7 as shells and watch the 3rd and the 7th: each moves a fret or two when the chord changes.
Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, Reverse Charleston, and the Shell voicing in the Backing Track’s guitar menu.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
section: G-A9 Triads on the top strings
text:
G-A9 Triads on the top strings
Three strings and three notes, with nothing doubled. This is the cleanest chord on the guitar, and it sounds best in a band with a keyboard or a second guitar because it takes only a thin slice of the range. A triad has three positions, and each one moves the lowest note to the top. The shapes are small, so you can chain them with almost no movement. The Backing Track calls this Voice-led triads.



Practice: play C, F and G, choosing each time the shape nearest to the last.
Unlocks: funk sixteenths and reggae or ska off-beats on the top three strings.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A10 Drop 2 voicings
Start with a seventh chord in close position, its four tones packed inside an octave. Take the second note from the top and drop it an octave. The chord opens up enough to fit the fingers, and it still has all four tones. On strings 4, 3, 2 and 1, a ii–V–I in C moves every voice by a fret or two. That smooth movement between chords, the voice leading, is what jazz chord shapes are for.



Practice: play that ii–V–I, then move the same three shapes up five frets to F.
Unlocks: the Drop 2 guitar voicing in the Backing Track, with Bossa nova and Charleston comping.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A11 Drop 3 voicings
Drop the third voice from the top instead of the second, and the bass note moves down a string, leaving a string skipped in the middle. From the bottom up the tones are root, 7th, 3rd, 5th. Drop 3 sounds bigger than a shell and still has four notes. Guitarists use drop 3 when the chord needs a low root and weight, and drop 2 when it should sit higher and lighter.



Practice: play the ii–V–I in drop 3 (Dm7 x5x565, G7 3x343x, Cmaj7 x3x453), then in drop 2, and listen to how close the voice leading is.
Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing in the Backing Track, and slow ballad comping.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A12 Extensions: 9th and 13th
The 9th is the 2nd an octave up, the 11th is the 4th and the 13th is the 6th. An extension adds colour without changing what the chord does. C9 still pulls to F, only richer, and C13 is the dominant chord of a blues band’s horn section. Here’s a shortcut: an Em7 shape over a C bass note is Cmaj9, because E–G–B–D are the 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th of C.



Practice: swap each dominant 7th of a 12-bar blues for a 9th or a 13th.
Unlocks: funk, Boogaloo stabs, and the jazz blues.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A13 Altered dominants
An altered dominant raises or lowers the 5th or the 9th to add tension just before the chord resolves. The ♭9 and ♯9 pull down toward the chord that follows, and the ♯5 pulls up toward its 3rd. Altered chords are short and high-energy, and they usually come at the end of a phrase. The 7♭9 shape, without its root, is a diminished 7th, which is why a dim7 shape can stand in for a 7♭9.



Practice: in a ii–V–I in C, play G7♯9 instead of G7 and listen to the tension release into Cmaj7.
Unlocks: endings, turnarounds and the last bar of a chorus in jazz comping.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
Where to go next

Guitar chord shapes by hand has the same chords in physical order, with what makes each one hard.
Piano chord voicings has the same ideas on the keyboard.
The Chord Library has every voicing of every chord: search drop2, shell, caged:E and so on.

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Subtractive synthesis starts with a wave full of harmonics and takes some away with a filter. It was the design of the Moog, the ARP, the Prophet-5 and the Minimoog that defined synth bass and synth lead, and most software synths still start from it. It is three parts in a row, each with a helper:
Oscillators (the raw tone) → filter (the brightness) → amplifier (the loudness). Envelopes shape the filter and the amplifier over the length of each note, and an LFO adds movement.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo to hear the synth play, or play it from the computer keys (a w s e d…), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. It plays chords. Start with the presets, then change one control at a time.

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text: The synth

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
1. Oscillators
Two oscillators, each with a shape from Sound 2. A sawtooth is the usual starting point because it has every harmonic for the filter to work on. A square or narrow pulse is hollower. Osc 2 detune sets the second oscillator a few cents off the first: the two drift in and out of phase and the sound becomes thick and moving. 5 to 15 cents is the classic “fat” sound; 0 is thin and still. Set Osc 2 octave to −1 for weight under a bass, or +1 for brightness. Noise adds breath, from Sound 3.

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
2. Filter
The low-pass filter is where the character comes from. Cutoff sets how bright the note is, resonance adds the peak at the cutoff. The filter here is the steep 24 dB-per-octave kind.

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
3. Envelopes: ADSR
An envelope is a shape that runs once each time you play a note. It has four stages:

Attack: how long it takes to rise from nothing to full when the key goes down.
Decay: how long it takes to fall from full to the sustain level.
Sustain: the level it holds while the key stays down (a level, not a time).
Release: how long it takes to fade to nothing after the key comes up.

The amp envelope shapes the loudness: a piano has fast attack, long decay, no sustain; an organ has instant attack, full sustain, instant release; a string pad has slow attack and slow release.
The filter envelope moves the cutoff, by up to Envelope amount octaves. This is the secret of most good synth sounds: real instruments are brightest at the start of a note. A fast filter attack and short decay give the “pew” of a synth bass; a slow attack gives a brass “swell”. The drawing under the controls shows both envelopes.

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
4. LFO
The LFO (Sound 5) adds vibrato (→ Pitch) or a slow filter sweep (→ Cutoff).

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Recipes to try

Bass. Press Bass. Turn Envelope amount to 0: the note goes dull and loses its “pluck”. Put it back and change Decay in the filter envelope: short is a click, long is a wow.
From brass to strings. Press Brass, then raise the amp Attack to 0.3 s and set the filter Envelope amount to 0. The swell becomes a bowed string pad.
Pluck. Press Pluck and play fast. Everything happens in the filter envelope: sustain at 0, so every note closes down by itself.
No oscillator at all. Press Wind (noise): noise through a resonant band-pass, with the LFO moving the band. Play different keys: nothing changes, because noise has no pitch.

title: Sound 6: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Next

Sound 7: FM synthesis, a completely different way to make harmonics.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
The twelve-bar blues is three four-bar phrases on three chords. Almost everything players have done to it since is one of a small number of moves: go to a chord sooner, approach a chord with its own dominant, split a dominant into a two-five, or replace a dominant with the one a tritone away. This lesson adds those moves one at a time. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays two choruses after a one-bar count-in. Section 8 has a tune written in notation, where the note that is sounding lights up. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
1. The three-chord blues
Four bars of I, two of IV and two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Every chord is a dominant seventh, including the home chord. That is the sound of the blues: a tonic that carries a flat seventh and does not need to resolve.



Listen for the two places the form turns. Bar 5 is the first move away from home. Bar 9 is the highest point of tension, and the last four bars walk it back down.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 2. The quick change and the turnaround
text:
2. The quick change and the turnaround
Two small changes, both very common. In bar 2 the band goes to IV for one bar and comes straight back (the quick change), which breaks up four bars of the same chord. In bar 12 the band plays V instead of resting on I, so the end of the chorus pulls into the top of the next one (a turnaround).



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
text:
3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
Swing and bebop players turned the last line round. Instead of V then IV, they play ii7 then V7: the bass now moves by fifths (G, C, F in the key of F) all the way home. To set up the ii chord, bar 8 becomes VI7, the dominant of ii. The turnaround in bars 11 and 12 is the same idea at twice the speed: I, VI7, ii7, V7, two beats each.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 4. Getting to IV, and getting back
text:
4. Getting to IV, and getting back
Three more moves, each of them a way to make an arrival stronger.

Bar 4: a two-five into IV. The I7 chord in bar 4 is already the dominant of IV, so put its ii chord in front of it (v7 I7, two beats each).
Bar 6: the bass climbs a half step from IV to ♯iv°7, and that chord pulls back to I in bar 7. This one is as old as the blues on the piano.
Bar 8: split VI7 into its own two-five, iii7 VI7.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
5. Tritone substitution
A dominant seventh chord and the dominant seventh a tritone away share the same third and seventh (swapped). So either can stand in for the other, and the substitute’s root arrives by a half step from above instead of by a fifth. Here it is in four places: the end of bar 4 (♯IV7 falling to IV), the end of bar 8 (♭III7 falling to ii), bar 10 (♭II7 falling to I), and a turnaround built entirely of substitutes: I, ♭III7, ♭VI7, ♭II7.



Listen to the bass. Wherever a substitute is used, the line slides down by half step.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
6. The Bird blues
Charlie Parker’s “Blues for Alice” keeps only three landmarks of the form: I in bar 1, IV in bar 5 and the two-five in bars 9 and 10. Everything between is a chain of two-fives. Bars 2 to 4 descend by step to reach IV. Bars 6 to 9 descend by half step to reach ii. The home chord is a major seventh, not a dominant.



Compare it with the jazz blues of section 3. The shaded bars show how little is left.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
7. The minor blues
The same twelve bars with minor i and iv chords. The last line is usually ♭VI7 to V7: a dominant a half step above the dominant (the tritone substitute of V’s own dominant). The turnaround uses a half-diminished ii chord. “Mr. P.C.” and “Equinox” are both built this way.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet is a good first tune because its changes are the three-chord blues with just two of the moves above.

Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five, ii7 then V7, as in the jazz blues of section 3.
Bar 12 is V7, the turnaround of section 2.

Everything else is plain. There is no quick change in bar 2 (four full bars of I), bars 5 and 6 are IV, bars 7 and 8 stay on I with no VI7, and bar 11 is one bar of I. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the three-chord blues of section 1.



The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and the note that is sounding lights up as it plays. Listen to bars 5 and 6: one note of the riff is a half step lower there than in bars 1 and 2, because the 3rd of the I chord has become the ♭7th of the IV chord. The changes are in the melody. In bars 9 and 10 the riff does not change at all, even though the chords under it are new: every note of it belongs to both the ii chord and the V chord.
To build this chorus yourself in the next section, choose Stay on I, Stay on I, Stay on IV, Stay on I, Two-five and V in the last bar. Open in the Backing Track puts the tune on that page in a new tab, where the bass line, comping and drums can each be chosen. The instrument lessons each end with this tune, and the improvising lesson is built on it.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
Build your own chorus
Choose one option for each pair of bars and the chart rewrites itself. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. All of the options fit together, so there is no wrong combination: try the plainest first line with the busiest turnaround, or the reverse.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
Test your ear
The band plays a plain blues with one pair of bars changed. The question tells you which bars to listen to; the counter shows where the band is. Pick what you heard.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
Where to go next

Play along. Set the strip at the bottom to Loop, pick a key and improvise over each version in turn. Bars 4, 8 and 12 are where the new chords ask for new notes.
Take a chorus you built to Tools → Backing Track (use Copy as ABC above and paste it into Edit the changes (ABC) there) to choose the bass line, comping rhythm and drum groove part by part.
Learn each version in the keys you play most: F and B♭ for horns, E, A and G for guitar.
Chord changes beyond the blues: cadences, turnarounds and rhythm changes, guide tones and borrowed chords.

title: Sound 8: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
A wavetable is a list of different single-cycle wave shapes, one after another. The oscillator plays one shape, and a position control chooses which. Move the position while a note is playing and the sound morphs smoothly from one shape to the next. Wolfgang Palm’s PPG Wave (1981) made the idea famous; today it’s the heart of software synths like Serum and Vital.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo or play the keys or MIDI. Drag Position in the table while a note plays. The drawing shows every shape in the table, front to back, with the current one in red.

title: Sound 8: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
The synth



This table has eight shapes: sine, triangle, sawtooth, square, a narrow pulse, a vowel (“ah”), a hollow wave and a sparse glassy one. Between two shapes the oscillator mixes them: halfway between sawtooth and square is half of each. Look at the spectrum as you drag: each shape is a different recipe of harmonics (see Sound 1), and the morph moves smoothly from one recipe to the next.

title: Sound 8: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
Scanning the table
A wavetable is most interesting when the position moves by itself. Raise Scan LFO depth and the LFO sweeps the position back and forth through the table. A slow scan (0.1 Hz) gives a pad that slowly changes colour. A fast scan (4 Hz or more) gives a talking, rhythmic wobble.
In a full wavetable synth an envelope can also move the position, so that every note starts on one shape and ends on another. That’s the same idea as the filter envelope in subtractive synthesis, but the movement can be through any timbres at all, not just from bright to dark.

title: Sound 8: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
How it is built here
A full wavetable synth stores each shape as hundreds or thousands of samples and plays them back very fast. For a lesson that is more than we need. The browser can build an oscillator from a list of harmonic strengths (as in the additive widget in Sound 1), so each shape in this table is stored as 48 harmonic strengths, and the position mixes neighbouring lists about thirty times a second. Mixing harmonic recipes and mixing wave shapes give exactly the same result, so it sounds and looks the same as the real thing, just with a smaller table.

title: Sound 8: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
Next

Sound 9: Distortion, the first of the effects.

title: Sound 7: FM Synthesis
text:
FM (frequency modulation) synthesis makes harmonics by a different route from subtractive synthesis. Instead of starting rich and filtering, it starts with two plain sine waves and uses one to wobble the pitch of the other so fast that the wobble becomes new frequencies. John Chowning found this at Stanford in 1967; Yamaha built it into the DX7 in 1983, and its electric piano, bells and slap bass are all over the music of the 1980s.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo or play the keys or MIDI. Choose a preset, then change one control at a time. The dashed lines on the spectrum mark where FM puts its new frequencies.

title: Sound 7: FM Synthesis
text:
Carrier and modulator




The carrier is the sine wave you hear. Its frequency is the note you play.
The modulator is a second sine wave that you don’t hear directly. It moves the carrier’s pitch up and down.
The ratio is the modulator’s frequency divided by the carrier’s.
The index is how far the modulator pushes the pitch. At 0 there’s no modulation: a plain sine.

This is the vibrato from the LFO lesson, sped up into the audio range. Below about 20 Hz you hear a wobble; above it you hear a new timbre.

title: Sound 7: FM Synthesis
text:
Sidebands
With the preset Steady (to study) loaded, hold a note and slowly raise the index from 0. New spikes appear on the spectrum on both sides of the carrier, spaced by the modulator’s frequency: carrier ± 1 × modulator, ± 2 ×, ± 3 × and so on. These are sidebands. The higher the index, the more sidebands, and the brighter the sound.
Now change the ratio:

Whole-number ratios (1, 2, 3…) put every sideband on a harmonic of the note. The sound is pitched and “musical”. Ratio 1 gives every harmonic, like a sawtooth; ratio 2 gives only odd harmonics, like a square or a clarinet.
Other ratios (1.41, 3.5…) put the sidebands between harmonics. The sound is inharmonic: metallic, bell-like, clangorous. That’s how FM makes bells and gongs so easily, which subtractive synths find hard.
Modulator fine tune detunes the modulator a few cents: the sidebands beat against each other and the sound shimmers.

title: Sound 7: FM Synthesis
text:
Envelopes make FM come alive
In FM the index does the job of the filter in a subtractive synth: it sets the brightness. Give the index its own envelope and the brightness changes during each note, the way real instruments do.

Bell: index starts high and dies away, the volume dies away more slowly. The clang at the start fades into a pure hum.
Electric piano: ratio 1, a quick index decay: a bright “tine” attack and a mellow body.
Brass: the index rises with the attack, so the note gets brighter as it swells.
Bass: a short burst of index gives the slap at the start of each note.

Try the Bell preset and change only the ratio: 3.5, 1.4, 2.76, 5.19. Each is a different metal.

title: Sound 7: FM Synthesis
section: FM and the spectrum, in one sentence
text:
FM and the spectrum, in one sentence
Subtractive starts with all the harmonics and removes some; additive (Sound 1) sets each harmonic by hand; FM makes a whole family of frequencies from two sine waves, controlled by just two numbers: the ratio decides where they go and the index decides how many.

title: Sound 7: FM Synthesis
text:

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
A cadence is how a phrase ends. Every ending has a different feel, and the feel comes from the two chords that make it. This lesson plays the five you will meet most, each as a four-bar phrase, and then asks a harder question about one of them: is it a cadence at all?
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I
text:
1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I
C, F, G7, C. The strongest ending there is. G7 contains the leading tone B and the note F, which are a tritone apart. Both are unstable: B wants to rise a half step to C and F wants to fall a half step to E. The tonic chord that follows is where they land. The bass falls a fifth, and everything leans the same way.



Learn this one first. Every other ending on the page is compared with it.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 2. The half cadence: ending on V
text:
2. The half cadence: ending on V
C, F, C, G. The phrase stops on the dominant, with the tension still in the air. It is a comma, not a full stop: the ear expects an answer, and the next phrase usually supplies it.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi
text:
3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi
C, F, G7, Am. Everything points at C, and then the last chord is Am, which shares two notes with C (C and E). The leading tone still rises to C, but the chord on top of it is Am. The listener expects a full stop and gets a surprise.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one
text:
4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one
C, Am, F, C. IV to I, the “Amen”. Most books call this a cadence. This lesson does not, and here is the argument.

A cadence is made by the dominant. What ends a phrase in tonal music is the leading tone rising to the tonic and the tritone of V7 resolving inward. IV to I has neither. No note in F is pulled toward C, so nothing is resolved.
IV is a neighbour of I. I, IV, I leaves home and comes back, exactly as I, vi, I does. That is a prolongation of the tonic chord, not an arrival.
It comes after the real cadence. The “Amen” at the end of a hymn follows a V to I that has already closed the phrase. The plagal is tacked on afterwards, so it cannot be what made the ending.
Some theorists agree. William Caplin’s Classical Form counts only authentic and half cadences, and does not count IV to I as a cadence.




Here is the “Amen” in its usual place: an authentic cadence first, then the plagal after it. Listen to bars 1 and 2, which end the phrase, and then to bars 3 and 4, which only soften it.



There is a fair reply. In the blues, in gospel and in much rock, IV to I really is how a tune ends, because those styles never relied on a leading tone. So whether “fake” means “not a cadence” or “a different kind of ending” depends on the style. In the classical tradition the first reading is the one with the support.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
5. The backdoor: ♭VII to I
C, F, B♭, C. The chord on the flat seventh is B♭, and it falls a whole step to C. There is no leading tone here either. The ending sounds relaxed, a door left open instead of shut. Compare it with the plagal ending: both arrive without a dominant.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
Build your own
Choose how the phrase opens and how it ends, and the chart and the staff rewrite themselves. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the plain authentic ending.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
Test your ear
Two questions. The first asks which ending the band played. The second plays one of three endings and asks how the last chord feels, so you can decide for yourself whether the plagal is a cadence.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
Where to go next

Play the five endings in a row at the same tempo and note which ones you could end a song on.
Take any of the phrases to Tools → Backing Track (Copy as ABC, then paste into Edit the changes (ABC)) to choose the bass line and drums.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the drum chair, starting with nothing but the beat. You need to be able to hit the ride cymbal (or hi-hat), the snare and the bass drum, and to work the hi-hat pedal. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the beat written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a drum staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. Each step starts in its own feel and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Reading a drum part
Each line or space of the staff is one part of the kit. Cymbals and anything struck on the rim are written with an ✕. What the hands play has stems up; what the feet play has stems down. Click a piece to hear it: the picture shows where each one is written, and the line under it has the same notes in the same places, so you can click those too. Hover over any drum note on this page and it tells you which piece it is.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
1. The beat and the form
A drummer has two jobs on a blues: keep the time, and know where in the twelve bars the band is. Start with the plainest time there is. The ride cymbal (or the closed hi-hat) plays all four beats. The left foot closes the hi-hat on 2 and 4. Nothing else.



Count the bars out loud while you play: four bars, then four more, then the last four. The chords change at bar 5, bar 7 and bar 9. Listen for the bass moving and learn to hear those moments coming.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
2. The ride pattern
Swing time on the ride cymbal is the four beats plus a skip note just before beats 3 and 1: ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a. It is written as two eighth notes, but the first is long and the second short, as if the beat were divided in three and you played the first and last parts. Keep the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.



Listen with Drums alone to hear how late the skip note sits. Slow the tempo down and it gets later still.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
3. Swing time
Now the other two limbs. In swing the bass drum is played very quietly on all four beats, felt more than heard (feathering), and it is not written. The snare does not keep time: it answers the band with a note here and there, often on the last part of a beat. The band’s drummer improvises this, so the notation changes every chorus.



Start with the ride pattern and the hi-hat foot. Add one snare note per bar, on the “a” of beat 4, and leave it at that until it is comfortable.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
4. Showing the form
A fill tells the band where it is. On a blues the places to mark are the ends of the three four-bar phrases: bar 4, which leads to the IV chord; bar 8, which leads to the last line; and bar 12, which leads back to the top. The small ones need only a beat or two. The one in bar 12 can be bigger, and the crash on beat 1 of the next chorus is its landing.



Keep the time going right up to the fill and come out of it on beat 1. A fill that loses the beat is worse than no fill.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
5. The shuffle
The beat of Chicago blues. The cymbal plays the swung eighths all the way through, long, short, long, short, with the bass drum on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. This is the first beat on this page with a backbeat.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
6. The slow blues in 12/8
At a slow tempo every beat divides in three, and the cymbal plays all three parts. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. It is written here in 4/4 with triplets; the same beat is often written in 12/8.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
7. Straight eighths
Not every blues swings. In a boogaloo or a rock blues the eighth notes are even. The cymbal plays eight to the bar, the bass drum is on 1 and 3, and the left hand plays a cross-stick on 2 and 4.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
8. Grabbing the crash
A crash cymbal rings for a long time. Sometimes you want the accent without the ring: hit the crash, then catch its edge with the other hand straight away, so that it stops. Drummers call this a choke. It is written as a short crash with choke over it.
Here the band plays the straight-eighths beat from step 7 with a small fill at the end of bars 4 and 8, and the crash is grabbed on beat 1 of bar 5 and bar 9, the first bar of the second and third lines. Hit the crash together with the bass drum, and have the hand on the cymbal before beat 2. Then go straight back to the time. When the band stops at the end, the last crash is grabbed too.



Try it with the loop on and listen to the gap the choke leaves. A grabbed crash says “here” louder than a ringing one, because of the silence after it.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
section: 9. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
9. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues, at a medium swing. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and each time it ends on a long note, in bars 4, 8 and 12. Those are the same three places step 4 marked with fills. The tune leaves the space; the drummer fills it and sets up the next phrase.



Play time through the riff and stay out of its way: no snare on top of the melody’s accents. Read the melody while you play. A drummer who knows the tune plays the form without counting.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Where to go next

Loop each step with the drums left out and play it for ten choruses without losing the form.
Play the fills step with your own fills in bars 4, 8 and 12.
Take a chorus from the changes lesson: the busier the chords, the more the band needs the form marked clearly.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
A filter turns some frequencies down and lets others through. It is the most-used control on a synthesizer and on a mixing desk: the treble and bass knobs on a stereo, the “wah” in a wah-wah pedal and the “wow” in a synth bass are all filters.
How to use the page. Press ▶. The Source menu picks what goes into the filter: noise shows the filter’s shape most clearly; the riff and chords show what it does to music; Your keyboard plays the keys or MIDI; Microphone filters your own voice (wear headphones). The red line on the spectrum is the filter’s response: above the middle line it boosts, below it cuts. Bypass switches the filter out so you can compare.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Low-pass and high-pass



A low-pass filter lets the lows through and cuts the highs. The frequency where it starts cutting is the cutoff. Drag Cutoff down slowly with noise playing: the hiss becomes a rush and then a rumble. Switch the source to the synth riff and do the same: the sound goes from bright to muffled, as if behind a wall.
A high-pass does the opposite: it removes the lows. That’s how a sound is made thin, like a telephone or a small radio, and how mixing engineers clear rumble out of everything except the bass and kick drum.
The slope is how fast the filter cuts beyond the cutoff: 12 dB per octave is gentle, 24 dB per octave is the steep, classic “Moog” low-pass.

Why low-pass sounds “darker”. From the harmonic series lesson: brightness is the strength of the high harmonics. A low-pass removes those harmonics, starting from the top. On a sawtooth (all harmonics) you can hear them go one by one as the cutoff passes them.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Resonance
Resonance (or Q) boosts a narrow band right at the cutoff. With the riff playing and the cutoff around 800 Hz, turn Resonance up to 10 or more. A whistling peak appears on the red line and you can hear it ring. Now press Sweep: the cutoff moves up and down by itself, and the resonant peak sweeps through the harmonics. That’s the classic synth “wow”, and with a guitar it’s a wah pedal.
At very high resonance the filter rings at the cutoff frequency on its own, almost like a sine wave. Some synths let the filter self-oscillate and play it as an extra oscillator.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Band-pass, notch and EQ




Band-pass keeps a band around the cutoff and cuts both sides. Higher Q, narrower band. It’s the sound of a telephone or a megaphone, and it’s how a vocoder splits a voice into bands (Sound 14).
Notch is the opposite: it removes a narrow band and leaves everything else. Engineers use it to remove a hum. A phaser is several moving notches.
Peak (bell), low shelf and high shelf are the filters of an equaliser (EQ). They boost or cut (the Boost/cut slider) instead of removing. A shelf lifts or lowers everything above or below the cutoff, like the treble and bass knobs. A bell lifts or lowers a band in the middle.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Filters on your voice
Choose Microphone as the source (with headphones on), choose Band-pass and sweep the cutoff while you talk. The vowels in speech are themselves made by filters: your mouth and throat are resonant tubes, and moving your tongue and lips moves their resonances (the formants). Say “ee-ah-oo” slowly and watch the bumps in the spectrum move.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Next

Sound 5: LFOs
Sound 6: Subtractive synthesis: oscillator, filter, envelope.

title: Sound 5: LFOs
text:
An LFO, or low-frequency oscillator, is an oscillator too slow to hear as a pitch, typically between a tenth of a beat and twenty times a second. Instead of being listened to, it moves a control: the pitch, the volume, a filter, the stereo position. Almost every effect that “moves” (vibrato, tremolo, wah, chorus, phaser, PWM) is an LFO turning a knob for you.
How to use the page. Press ▶ or play the keys. The strip above the scope draws the LFO itself over the last two seconds; the red dot is where it is now.

title: Sound 5: LFOs
text:
What an LFO can move



Leave the shape on Sine and try each target with Rate about 5 Hz:

Pitch gives vibrato: the note bends slightly sharp and flat. Singers and string players use 5 to 7 cycles a second. Too deep and it sounds seasick; too fast and it sounds nervous.
Volume gives tremolo: the note gets louder and softer. The “tremolo” on a guitar amp is this, and so is a vibraphone with its motor on.
Filter cutoff gives an automatic wah. Slow it right down (0.2 Hz) for a slowly opening and closing sound; speed it up for a “wobble” bass.
Pan moves the sound between your left and right ear (auto-pan). Use headphones.

Depth is how far the LFO moves the control, and Rate is how fast. Those two plus the shape are all an LFO has.

title: Sound 5: LFOs
text:
Shapes

Sine and triangle: smooth back-and-forth.
Square: jumps between two values. On pitch it’s a trill; on volume, a chopped “gate”.
Sawtooth (ramp): rises slowly, then drops. On pitch it sounds like a siren.
Random (sample & hold): jumps to a new random value every cycle. On the filter it’s the bubbling “computer” sound of 1970s science fiction.

title: Sound 5: LFOs
section: When an LFO gets fast enough to hear
text:
When an LFO gets fast enough to hear
Set the target to Volume, the shape to Sine and slowly push the rate past 20 Hz. The tremolo stops sounding like a pulse and becomes a rough, buzzy tone, and new pitches appear on the spectrum on both sides of the note. That is amplitude modulation. Do the same with Pitch and past about 30 Hz the vibrato becomes a metallic, bell-like timbre: that is frequency modulation, the subject of Sound 7. An LFO and an audible oscillator are the same thing at different speeds.

title: Sound 5: LFOs
text:
LFOs elsewhere on these pages

The PWM in Sound 2 is an LFO on the pulse width.
Chorus (Sound 12) is an LFO on a very short delay.
A phaser (Sound 13) is an LFO sweeping a chain of filters.
The Leslie speaker in the organ lesson is a mechanical LFO: a spinning horn moves pitch, volume and direction all at once.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
A great many songs are one loop of four chords, played round and round while the melody, the words and the arrangement change on top. The loops are not very different from each other: they are the same handful of chords (I, ii, IV, V, vi, and a few borrowed from the minor) in a different order, or with one of them swapped. This lesson goes through the loops one at a time. Each has the chords, the same four bars on a grand staff (block chords in the treble, the bass note below) and the site’s backing band, which plays it round and round so that you hear it as a loop.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four times round after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key: C G Am F in the key of C is the same loop as D A Bm G in the key of D. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the first loop.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 1. The axis loop: I V vi IV
text:
1. The axis loop: I V vi IV
C, G, Am, F. The loop that is under Let It Be, No Woman, No Cry and the verse of Don’t Stop Believin’, among a great many others. The bass drops from C to G, rises a step to A and falls a third to F. Three major chords and one minor: the minor chord keeps it from sounding simply happy.



Play it until you can hum the bass note of each bar. Every other loop is compared with this one.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V
text:
2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V
Am, F, C, G. The four chords are the same; the loop starts on the minor chord, so that it sounds like a minor song, and the major chord C arrives in the middle. Zombie by the Cranberries is this loop (in E minor), and so is the chorus of Despacito.



Compare the two charts: there is no new chord. Where a loop starts is what the ear takes for home. The other two starting points are IV I V vi (F, C, G, Am) and V vi IV I (G, Am, F, C).

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V
text:
3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V
C, Am, F, G. The doo-wop loop. It has the chords of the axis loop, but with the minor chord second, so the bass steps down by thirds: C, A, F, and then the G climbs to C again. Stand by Me is built on it. Listen to bar 4: the V chord is the last bar and it leads straight back to C.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 4. The turnaround: I vi ii V
text:
4. The turnaround: I vi ii V
C, Am, Dm, G. Replace the IV with its relative minor, ii. The bass now moves round the circle of fifths: C, A, D, G, and back to C. This is the turnaround of jazz, and the A section of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (the “rhythm changes”) begins this way. Put a seventh on each chord and it is the sound of a standard.



Bar 3 is the only difference from the fifties loop. The ii chord and the IV chord share two of their three notes (F and A), so one can stand in for the other.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 5. Out and back: I IV V IV
text:
5. Out and back: I IV V IV
C, F, G, F. The loop of Louie Louie and Wild Thing. There is no minor chord and no change of direction; the loop goes up to the dominant and back down by the same step. Because the bar-4 chord is IV, not I, it does not feel finished, and the loop goes round again and again.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I
text:
6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I
C, B♭, F, C. B♭ is not in the key of C. It is the chord on the flat seventh, borrowed from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat seventh) and the note that the blues calls the flat seven. Sweet Home Alabama goes I, ♭VII, IV this way. In C the bass goes down a step, then down a fourth, then down a fourth again.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
7. The minor loops
Two loops in the minor, written here in C minor (three flats in the signature).

i ♭VII ♭VI V: Cm, B♭, A♭, G. The Andalusian loop. The bass falls by step, C, B♭, A♭, G, and the last chord is a major V, with the leading tone B, so that it pulls hard back to Cm. Hit the Road Jack is this loop.
i ♭VI ♭III ♭VII: Cm, A♭, E♭, B♭. The four chords of the axis loop in E♭ major, started on the vi chord: loop 2 in its minor key. It is the sound of much current pop.







Play the two minor loops and then loop 2. The notes are different, but the shape, down by steps then up by a third, is the same.

Choose a chord for each bar, or start from one of the loops above, and the chart and the staff rewrite themselves. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. The numeral next to each chord is its place in the key of C.

title: Sound 9: Distortion
text:
Distortion changes the shape of a wave by squashing its loudest parts. A changed shape means a changed recipe of harmonics (Sound 1), so distortion adds harmonics that weren’t there. A little gives warmth; a lot gives the roar of a rock guitar.
How to use the page. Every effect on these pages has a Source menu (what goes in), a Mix (how much of the effect you hear), and Bypass to switch it out and back in. The square graph is the distortion curve: the input level runs across, the output level up. The dashed diagonal is “no change”.

title: Sound 9: Distortion
section: A sine wave in, harmonics out
text:
A sine wave in, harmonics out



The source starts as a pure sine tone: one spike on the spectrum. Raise Drive slowly.

The curve bends over at the ends: loud parts of the wave can’t get any louder.
The scope shows the sine’s peaks being flattened toward a square.
New spikes appear on the spectrum at 3, 5, 7… times the frequency: odd harmonics, because the top and bottom of the wave are squashed the same way. That’s the square-wave recipe.

Now try the other curves:








Curve
What it does
Sound




Soft clip
bends over gradually
overdrive: a warm, singing tone, like a valve amp turned up


Hard clip
flat-tops the wave at a fixed level
fuzz: buzzy and aggressive


Uneven (tube-like)
squashes the top and bottom differently
adds even harmonics (2, 4, 6) too, which sound sweeter and fuller


Wavefolder
folds the peaks back down instead of flattening them
the West-coast synth sound: glassy, metallic, changes wildly with drive


Bit crusher
rounds the wave to a few steps
the gritty sound of old computers and samplers



Tone is a low-pass after the distortion: almost every guitar amp has one, to tame the fizz that heavy distortion adds at the top.

title: Sound 9: Distortion
text:
On music
Switch the Source to Chords or the Synth riff. Distorting a chord sounds much messier than distorting one note: every note’s harmonics clash with the others’, and the curve also creates new frequencies at the differences between the notes (intermodulation). That’s why heavy rock guitar plays power chords (root and fifth only). The difference frequencies of a fifth are another octave of the root, so it stays clean.
Try your own voice or instrument through it with Microphone (and headphones).

title: Sound 9: Distortion

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
A note played on a real instrument is never one frequency. It is a stack of frequencies, all at whole-number multiples of the lowest one. That stack is the harmonic series, and it explains why a violin and a flute playing the same A sound different, why the octave and the fifth sound “pure”, and how every synthesizer on the following pages works.
How to use the page. Every widget has a ▶ button, a picture of the wave’s shape (an oscilloscope) and a picture of its spectrum (how loud each frequency is, low on the left, high on the right). The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume. You can play the widgets from the computer keyboard (a w s e d f t g y h u j k is one octave, z and x move it), from the on-screen keyboard, or from a MIDI keyboard. Notes go to the widget you clicked last. Click a heading to fold a section away. Start with the volume low.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
A string vibrates in pieces
Pluck a string and it swings as a whole, but it also swings in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, all at once. Half the length vibrates twice as fast, a third of it three times as fast. If the whole string gives 100 Hz, the halves give 200 Hz, the thirds 300 Hz, and so on. The same happens in the air column of a trumpet or a clarinet, and in your voice.
Each of those frequencies is a harmonic. The first harmonic, the whole string, is the fundamental, and it’s the pitch you name. The others are overtones. You don’t hear them as separate notes. You hear them as the colour (the timbre) of the one note.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
The series, written out
Here are the first sixteen harmonics written as notes. The number under each note is the harmonic’s number: harmonic n vibrates n times as fast as the fundamental. The number above is how far the real harmonic is from the piano’s version of that note, in cents (100 cents = one half step). Choose a different fundamental and the whole series is transposed. The pattern of steps never changes.



Things to notice:

The octaves are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Doubling the frequency always gives an octave.
The gaps shrink as you go up. Octave, then a fifth (2 to 3), a fourth (3 to 4), a major third (4 to 5), a minor third (5 to 6), and then steps smaller than a minor third. The higher harmonics are close enough to make scales.
Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 are a major triad (C, E, G over a C fundamental). The major chord is built into every pitched sound.
Harmonic 7 is about a third of a half step flat of the piano’s B♭, harmonic 11 sits almost exactly between F and F♯, and harmonic 13 is well sharp of A♭. Press Harmonic, then tempered and listen at those three. Piano tuning (equal temperament) moves every note slightly so that all keys work. The pure intervals are the harmonics.
The 5th harmonic is 14 cents flat of the piano’s major third. Barbershop singers and string quartets lean their major thirds that way, toward the harmonic.

Press Build the tone to hear the harmonics enter one at a time, each a little quieter than the one before (harmonic n at strength 1/n). With all sixteen it no longer sounds like a chord. It sounds like one buzzy note: a sawtooth wave.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
section: Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves
text:
Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves
The sine wave is the simplest sound there is: one frequency and nothing else. It sounds pure and a little dull, like a tuning fork or a whistle.
In 1807 Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating wave, whatever its shape, can be built by adding sine waves at whole-number multiples of its frequency. Each sine wave has its own strength (and it can be upside down). The recipe of strengths is the wave’s spectrum. Going from a wave to its recipe is the Fourier transform; going from the recipe back to the wave is Fourier synthesis.
You don’t need the maths to use the idea:

The shape of a wave (the oscilloscope) and its recipe (the spectrum) are two views of the same sound. Change one and the other changes.
Sharp corners and sudden jumps need lots of high harmonics. Smooth, rounded shapes need few. Bright sounds have strong high harmonics; dark, mellow sounds don’t.
The ear mostly hears the recipe, not the shape. Flip a harmonic upside down and the shape changes a lot while the sound hardly changes.

The spectrum display under every widget on these pages is a Fourier transform done about sixty times a second, by the browser.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
Build waves from harmonics
Each slider is one harmonic. Up is louder; below the middle line it is upside down. The numbers under the sliders play that harmonic alone. The drawing shows the harmonics faintly and their sum in bold. Press ▶ and move the sliders while it plays.



Try this:

Press Sine. One harmonic, one frequency. The spectrum shows a single spike.
Press Sawtooth: every harmonic, harmonic n at strength 1/n. Now turn Harmonics used down to 1 and slowly back up. Each added harmonic sharpens the ramp. With few harmonics the edge wobbles; the wobble (the Gibbs effect) gets narrower but never quite goes away.
Drag the slider for harmonic 2 to zero. The note now sounds hollow, a little like a clarinet.
Press Organ. Organ stops add harmonics 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and so on (see the organ lesson): the tonebars are an additive synthesizer.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
Square, triangle, sawtooth, pulse
These four shapes are the raw material of almost every synthesizer, because each has a simple, recognisable recipe.









Wave
Harmonics
Strength of harmonic n
Sound




Sine
1 only
—
Pure, flute-like, no edge


Sawtooth
all
1/n
Bright, buzzy, brassy and string-like


Square
odd only (1, 3, 5…)
1/n
Hollow, woody, clarinet-like


Triangle
odd only
1/n², alternating up and down
Soft, between sine and square


Pulse
depends on width
a pulse 1/k wide has no harmonics at multiples of k
Thin and nasal as it narrows



Press each preset above and compare the spectrum. A square is a pulse exactly half a cycle wide, so it’s missing every 2nd harmonic. Press Pulse 1/3 and harmonics 3, 6, 9 and 12 drop out. Pulse 25% loses 4, 8, 12 and 16. The next lesson makes the pulse width move, which is PWM.
The triangle’s harmonics fall away as 1/n², much faster than the square’s 1/n, which is why it sounds so much softer even though both have only odd harmonics.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
In a seventh chord the 3rd and the 7th say what the chord is. A line made of those notes, one for each chord, is called a guide-tone line, and it moves by step or by nothing at all. This lesson writes that line over four-chord loops, on a staff, so that you can hear what the chords are doing inside.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart. Under each chart is a one-voice staff with the line, and the band’s piano plays the line over the chords.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
1. Just the 3rds
C, G, Am, F as plain triads, with the 3rd of each chord on the staff. The 3rd is the note that makes a chord major or minor. Listen to the line E, B, C, A: it is the loop with the chords taken away.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
2. Sevenths, and the 3rds again
Cmaj7, G7, Am7, Fmaj7. The same loop with a 7th on every chord. The 3rds are the same notes. The 7ths are new, and they are what the next step uses.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
3. Just the 7ths
The 7ths of those chords: B, F, G and E. The 7th of one chord is often the 3rd of the next, or a step from it: the B of Cmaj7 is the 3rd of G7, and the G of Am7 rises a step to the A that is the 3rd of Fmaj7.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
4. The guide-tone line
For each chord, take whichever of its 3rd and 7th is nearer the last note you played. The line now moves by a step or a skip, and it holds a note where it can.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
5. Over a two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. The most important use of the line. The F is the 3rd of Dm7 and the 7th of G7: it does not move at all. It then falls a half step to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7, which is the note that tells you the chord has changed to major.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
6. Over the turnaround
Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Four chords, and the line moves by half steps and whole steps through all of them. A bass player and a pianist who both play the guide tones will be in tune with each other without having said a word.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
Build your own
Choose a progression and what the staff shows: the chords, the 3rds, the 7ths or the guide-tone line. The band plays the line when the staff shows one.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones

Where to go next

Play each line on your instrument over the band, then try singing it.
The guitar and piano lessons on the blues use the same 3rd and 7th as their shell chords.
In turnarounds the line is the same, with a tritone substitution in the V.

title: Sound 13: Phaser
text:
A phaser sweeps a few notches up and down the spectrum, and the result is a soft, swirling “whoosh”. It’s the sound of the electric piano in a thousand 1970s records, and Eddie Van Halen’s guitar on the first Van Halen album.
How to use the page. The source starts as chords. The red line on the spectrum shows the notches moving. Turn Mix to 100% and the effect disappears (to the ear), which says something about how it works.

title: Sound 13: Phaser
text: The effect

title: Sound 13: Phaser
text:
How it works
A phaser passes the sound through a chain of all-pass filters. An all-pass filter is a strange kind of filter: it doesn’t change how loud any frequency is. It only delays some frequencies more than others, so it shifts their phase. On its own you can’t hear it.
But mix that phase-shifted copy back with the original, and wherever the copy has been shifted exactly half a cycle the two cancel. Those cancellations are the notches. The stages here are the browser’s all-pass filters, each of which makes one notch, so Stages = 4 gives four notches. (A guitar pedal uses simpler stages, and needs two of them per notch.) An LFO sweeps the all-pass filters up and down, and the notches sweep with them.
That’s why the wet sound alone (Mix at 100%) sounds plain. The notches only exist when the shifted copy meets the original. 50% gives the deepest notches.

title: Sound 13: Phaser
text:
The controls

Stages: more stages, more notches, a stronger effect. The MXR Phase 90 has two notches; 12 here is very dramatic.
Centre and Sweep: where the notches sit and how far up and down they move.
Rate: slow for a swirl, fast for a warble.
Width (Q): how sharp the phase change in each stage is, and so how narrow the notches are.
Feedback: feeds the output back to the input; the areas between the notches turn into resonant peaks and the effect becomes more vocal and whistling. (The red line doesn’t show the feedback.)

title: Sound 13: Phaser
text:
Phaser or flanger?
Both sweep notches. A flanger uses a short delay, which makes many evenly spaced notches, like the teeth of a comb, so it sounds metallic and jet-like. A phaser uses all-pass filters, which make a few notches that aren’t evenly spaced, so it sounds softer and more liquid. Switch the source to noise on both pages and compare the spectrum.

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
The band’s hammond sound (sounds.js), the organist’s pedal and switch (organist in comp.js), and the panel on the Backing Track page. Written 2026-10-10. Nobody has listened to it. Every level and rule below is either taken from a source (linked) or is a first guess, and the two are kept apart so the guesses are easy to find and change.
What was asked for: all nine tonebars, the upper manual only, the C3 chorus, and a band that works the swell pedal and the Leslie speed by itself. Not built: percussion, the lower manual, bass pedals, the other vibrato settings.


Three kinds, in falling order: technical write-ups read in full (Electric Druid, Scott Healy’s playing tips, Wikipedia); documents quoted in search results but not opened (the Hammond service text, Stefan Vorkoetter); and forum posts quoted in search results, where the link is to the thread the search named and the exact post was not checked (Keyboard Corner, Cantabile, Nord, Fractal). Anything resting only on the third kind is one player’s word.



Nothing is sampled. Each note is three oscillators, a few milliseconds of noise, and then one chain shared by all the notes.



Part
What it does
Where the numbers come from




Tonebars
Nine pitches for a key: 16′, 5⅓′, 8′, 4′, 2⅔′, 2′, 1⅗′, 1⅓′, 1′, at 0.5, 1.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 times the note
Electric Druid


Tonebar steps
0 is silent; each step from 8 down is 3 dB quieter
A clone’s description of the real instrument (Hammy 91); widely repeated, not from a Hammond document


Tempering
The fifths and the third are tempered wheels, not pure harmonics: 1.4988, 2.9976, 5.0409 and 5.9953 times the note. So a note is one oscillator for the octaves, one for the three fifths, one for the third
Electric Druid


Foldback
91 wheels. Key 1 (C2) takes its 8′ from wheel 13. A pitch above wheel 91 is taken an octave lower; the bottom octave’s 16′ an octave higher
Electric Druid (its table did not survive being read by machine; the rule here reproduces its wheel ranges)


Leakage
A closed tonebar still lets a trace through (−48 dB, octaves only)
That it exists: Electric Druid. The amount: a guess


Key click
A key’s nine contacts do not close together. Here: 22 ms of filtered noise as a note starts, with its own slider
The cause: Electric Druid. The sound of it: a guess


Touch
None. A note is the same level however it is played
Scott Healy: “the organ isn’t velocity-sensitive”


C3 chorus
A delay swept up and back 6.87 times a second (412 turns a minute), about 0.9 ms from end to end, mixed half and half with the straight sound
Rate and that the scanner runs up the line and back: Hammond service text. About 50 µs a stage over 18 stages: Stefan Vorkoetter (an M-100, not a B-3). The half-and-half mix: a guess; no source gives the real ratio


Swell pedal
Never silent: 24 dB down at its quietest. Keeps the bass up as it closes. Sits before the tube stage, so opening it also adds growl
That it never closes, lifts bass and treble as it comes down, and drives the amp harder as it opens: Nord forum, quoting a Hammond manual. The 24 dB and the 7 dB of bass: guesses; no source gives figures


Tube drive
The amp-chain drive already in the band, set low
A guess


Rotary speaker
Split at 800 Hz into a horn and a drum. Horn 48 turns a minute slow, 400 fast; drum 85% of that. Two microphones on opposite sides
Crossover and speeds: Wikipedia; 48 / 400 and 40 / 342 measured on a 147: Fractal forum


Speed changes
The horn gets most of the way in about 1.5 s, the drum in about 5 s
“Less than two seconds” and “4 to 10 seconds, depending on belt tension”: one forum post, found by search. No measured figure exists that I could find, so treat it as anecdote



Measured in tests/band/pat/organ.cdp.js: with every tonebar out, all nine pitches of A4 come out within 0.2 dB of each other; the 1⅗′ sits at 2218 Hz, not the pure 2200; C7’s 1′ sounds at 4186 Hz (two octaves folded back); two steps of a tonebar are 6.0 dB; the pedal closed is 24 dB down; the speaker moves the level 0.8 times a second slow and 6.67 fast, and summed to mono the swing all but cancels.



None of these is sourced. The searches named famous registrations (Jimmy Smith, Charles Earland, Groove Holmes, Erroll Garner, “full organ”) but gave no digits, so the menu describes each sound and attributes it to nobody. The default is 88 8000 000.



BandComp.organist decides, bar by bar, where the pedal sits and when the speaker changes speed. It uses no random numbers. Each rule, and what it rests on:
Swell pedal



Rule
Why




It follows how hard the band is playing: about half open when the band plays down, nearly open at full, a little more in a chorus
The organ has no touch, so the pedal is its only dynamics (Healy: “vary the dynamics using the expression pedal”)


The last bar of each four-bar phrase opens through the bar into the next one; more so going into a chorus
“Start with the expression pedal at minimum, then increase the pedal slowly”; a crescendo into the build (Healy)


The first bar of a phrase settles back a little
“Back off the pedal as the speaker slows down” (Healy)


A stop bar is hit and then pulled back sharply
“Pull the expression pedal back suddenly for a sforzando effect” (Healy)


The last chord swells and is let go
A guess



Leslie



Rule
Why




Slow is home
Rock and blues players “lean on that chorale mostly” (a forum post: Keyboard Corner or Cantabile)


Fast through the last bar of a phrase that leads into a chorus or back to the top, or that the band is playing hard; slow again as the next phrase starts
“As your single note starts to build, pop your Leslie or rotary switch to fast, and depress the pedal” (Healy). A forum player describes speeding up at the end of a phrase (Cantabile)


On a chord held two bars or more, a flick to fast for the second half of the phrase’s last bar and straight back
“Flip the Leslie to fast, then immediately flip it back to slow” under pads (Healy)


In swing the speaker stays slow, until the last two bars of the last chorus
Jazz players mostly leave the speaker alone and rely on the chorus (a forum post, Keyboard Corner or Cantabile: they “stop the horn entirely for the vast majority of work”). Slow, not stopped, is my choice


Fast on the final chord
A guess; a common ending



Thresholds that are mine: “playing hard” is an intensity of 0.66 or more; the flick lasts a beat and a half; the pedal’s range is 0.48 to 0.90 of its travel across the band’s intensity.
Nothing was found for gospel. The searches turned up no description of gospel pedal or Leslie habits, so the straight-eighth rules above are rock and blues habits applied to everything that is not swing.



Mixer → Organ: tonebars, swell and Leslie, shown while the organ is the comping instrument or the second one: nine tonebars, a registration menu, Leslie (Automatic / Slow / Fast / Stopped), Swell pedal (Automatic / By hand), key click. The chorus, the pedal’s range, the drive and the speaker’s own numbers are in Mixer → Tone (EQ), in the organ’s amp. Settings are kept in the browser (localStorage.btOrgan, and btAmp for the amp).




Percussion, the lower manual, pedals, V1 to V3 and C1, C2.
Tapering (each wheel’s own level across the keyboard), which a commenter on Electric Druid calls the main reason for the instrument’s scream.
Leakage between neighbouring wheels at other pitches; contact bounce note by note.
The cabinet: no reflections, no horn tone, one tube stage for both rotors.
Tonebar moves, chorus on and off, and registration changes are not played by the band: only the pedal and the speed.
The comping is the piano’s voicings. An organist’s held chords with a moving finger under a held top note (Healy, Ex. 2) are not written.





When do you reach for fast: into every chorus, or only the last one? On held chords? At endings?
In jazz, do you leave the speaker slow, stopped, or off altogether with the chorus doing the work?
Where does your foot sit when comping: about half, or lower? How far do you open into a chorus?
Your comping registration, and whether you change it between verse and chorus.
Chorus C3 always on, or only for some styles?

title: DWIM on the Notation page
text:
“Do what I mean”: select some music, press DWIM, and the page shows the other ways that music could have been written, best first, each with a small score and a Use this button. The Notation page (tools/notation.qmd) offers it; the engine is Chord Entry’s (ChordEntry.alternatives) and the panel is MelodyDwim (apps/shared/melody-dwim.js), shared with the Chord Entry page.
This file is the plan and the record: what works now, how it stays working long after a take, and what is still to build. Keep it up to date when DWIM changes.











Kind
Needs
Examples
Status




Re-reading a take
the take’s log (every key down/up with its time, and the settings)
staccato vs note + rest, triplets or not, swing or straight, eighth vs sixteenth grid, plainest vs as-released note ends, grace notes, pickup
built


Re-writing what is written
only the notes on the page
enharmonic spelling (F♯ / G♭), a chord’s other names (C6 / Am7), tie vs dotted note, octave of a passage, meter (6/8 vs 3/4), key
planned, below



Re-reading is the stronger kind: it goes back to how the music was played and reads it again, so it can recover things the first reading threw away (a note too short to keep, a triplet read as eighths). It can only work where the page still has the playing.



On the Chord Entry page a take’s log lives only until the next take. Here it is kept with the chunk:
chunk.takes = [{ voice, log, from, bars, sig: [per-bar signature] }]

log is ChordEntry.take(...).log(): { v, cfg, events }. It is small (a few kilobytes for a page of music) and is saved with the piece (localStorage), so DWIM works after a reload, tomorrow, next month.
voice is the voice the take was written into (a take for voice 2 does not answer for voice 1).
from is the chunk bar where the take’s first bar sits (0 when it was recorded into the chunk; it moves when a split or merge moves the take), and bars is how many bars the take wrote.
sig[b] is a signature of what the take wrote in bar b (its rhythm and pitches, NotationDoc.barSig).

When it still applies. DWIM compares each selected bar’s signature now with the one recorded. A bar that is unchanged is fully “the take’s”. A bar that was edited (a note moved, a rhythm pattern added) is reported: “Bar 3 was changed after the take: using a reading replaces your changes in that bar.” Using a reading is still allowed: it is your call. Bars outside the take (added later) cannot be re-read.
What survives what.







Operation
What happens to the take




editing notes elsewhere in the chunk
nothing; only the edited bars report a change


splitting the chunk on a bar line
each half keeps the take, with its bars counted from where the half starts (from)


splitting inside a bar
the take is kept by the first half only for its whole bars; the bar that was cut is reported as changed


merging two chunks
both takes are kept, the second one’s bars shifted by the first chunk’s length


duplicating a chunk or a section
the copy keeps the take: DWIM works on the copy too


a new take into the same bars and voice
replaces the old one there


reading ABC or ChordPro in
takes are not in ABC: they are dropped (the page says so)



Using a reading replaces only the selected bars of that voice (NotationDoc.replaceBars) and puts the new signatures in the take, so those bars count as “the take’s” again. The take’s own settings are not changed: the next DWIM still lists every reading, and its “As first written” card is the take’s original reading, not the one you chose.




Select on the staff: click a note (that bar), or shift-click a second note (all the bars between).
DWIM is enabled when the selection lies in one chunk and that chunk has a take for that voice.
The DWIM panel opens with those bars; its own From / To boxes can widen or narrow the range.
Each card: what the reading changes, why someone would mean it, its cost (lower is plainer; notes left out cost most), and Use this.

Takes come from Play it in time. Chords from a take have their own DWIM (below) and are not touched by melody readings.



These work on any music on the page, typed, pasted or played. Each is a list of candidates with a cost, in the same panel, so the user sees one DWIM, not several tools.

Chords. Every chord played in (one a bar, or in a take) keeps the notes that were played (chord.midis). ChordEntry.analyse(midis, { all: true }) already returns every reading that fits (C6 / Am7, slash or not); DWIM on a chord lists them. Typed chords have no notes; for those, offer enharmonic names only (C♯m / D♭m).
Spelling. A selected note or span: the other spelling of each note out of the key (F♯ / G♭), using ChordEntry.spellNotes with the chord of the bar, which is what Chord Entry does for takes. Needs a spelling override on the note (pitches hold MIDI numbers; add spell: { k: "Gb" } beside them).
Rhythm, plainer. Without the playing, the written durations can still be re-read: a note and rest pair as one staccato note, a dotted note vs a tie, sixteenth pairs as eighths when the meter allows.
Meter. A chunk’s rhythm read in another meter with the same length of bar (6/8 vs 3/4, 2/2 vs 4/4), scored by how many notes cross beats; useful after a take recorded in the wrong meter.
Octave. A passage that sits far from the voice’s clef: one octave up or down.
Key. The key guess (NotationDoc.guessKey) with its runners-up and their scores, so a doubtful key can be compared and chosen; still confirmed by the user.

Order of work: 1 (data is already there), 2, then 3–6 as they are wanted.

node tests/abc/notation.cdp.js: a take recorded (synthetic events), saved, the page reloaded, DWIM run on a bar, a reading used.
